109887.q: What does the state of a substance depend on?
a: On the shape of the container
109887.e: Whether a substance is solid, liquid or gas is mainly decided by temperature and pressure.
109887.m: Temperature and pressure decide the state of matter.

109888.q: Which of these substances is a gas at room temperature?
109888.e: Oxygen only becomes liquid at around -183 °C. So at room temperature it is a gas.
109888.m: Oxygen is a gas at room temperature.

109889.q: What does not change when a substance changes state?
109889.e: Ice, water and water vapour are all made of water molecules. Only the way the particles are arranged and move changes.
109889.m: When the state changes, the substance stays the same.

109890.q: How are the particles arranged in a solid?
a: Close and regular, vibrating in place
Far apart and free to move
109890.e: In solids, strong forces hold the particles in fixed places. They can only vibrate back and forth.
109890.m: In solids, particles vibrate in fixed places.

109891.q: How do the particles in a liquid move?
a: They fly far away from each other
109891.e: In liquids the particles are close together but can move around. That is why a liquid can flow.
109891.m: In liquids, particles slide past each other.

109892.q: How is a substance imagined in the particle model?
a: As tiny particles that are always moving
As a solid mass without particles
As large balls that always stand still
As particles you can see with the naked eye
109892.e: All substances are made of very small particles. They are far too small to see and are constantly moving.
109892.m: In the particle model, every substance is made of tiny moving particles.

109893.q: Why can a gas easily be compressed?
a: There is a lot of empty space between the particles
109893.e: In gases the distances between the particles are very large. When you press, they simply move closer together, like in a bicycle pump.
109893.m: Gases can be compressed because there is lots of space between the particles.

109894.q: What do you see under a microscope when tiny grains float in water?
a: They keep jiggling back and forth
109894.e: The invisible water particles keep bumping into the grains. So they jiggle randomly back and forth; this is called Brownian motion.
109894.m: Brownian motion shows that particles are always moving.

109895.q: What is it called when a drop of ink spreads through water by itself?
109895.e: In diffusion, substances mix through the constant movement of their particles, without any stirring.
109895.m: Through diffusion, substances mix by themselves.

109896.q: At what temperature would particles have the least possible movement?
109896.e: Absolute zero is 0 kelvin, which is -273.15 °C. It can't get colder.
109896.m: At absolute zero, particle movement is smallest.

109897.q: Why do most substances expand when heated?
a: The particles move more and need more space
109897.e: The particles themselves stay the same size. Because they vibrate more strongly, the distances between them grow.
109897.m: Heated substances expand because the gaps between particles grow.

109898.q: In which state of matter are the forces of attraction between particles smallest?
109898.e: Gas particles are far apart and hardly attract each other. That is why they spread out freely.
109898.m: In gases the particles hardly attract each other.

109899.q: At what temperature does ice melt at normal air pressure?
109899.e: The melting point of ice is 0 °C. Anders Celsius used it as one of the fixed points of his temperature scale.

109900.q: Which metal melts even in a warm hand?
109900.e: Gallium has a melting point of about 30 °C. Body heat is enough to make it liquid.

109901.q: Which metal has the highest melting point?
109901.e: Tungsten only melts at around 3400 °C. That is why it used to be used for the filaments in light bulbs.
109901.m: Tungsten has the highest melting point of all metals.

109902.q: Roughly at what temperature does iron melt?
109902.e: Pure iron melts at about 1538 °C. That is why blast furnaces are extremely hot.

109903.q: Why is salt spread on roads in winter?
a: It lowers the freezing point of water
109903.e: Salt water only freezes below 0 °C. So water on the road stays liquid even in light frost.
109903.m: Salt lowers the freezing point of water.

109904.q: For a pure substance, how does the freezing point compare with the melting point?
109904.e: Melting and freezing happen at the same temperature. For water both are at 0 °C.
109904.m: Melting point and freezing point are the same.

109905.q: What does it show if a substance melts at a lower temperature than expected?
109905.e: Impurities lower the melting point. That is why laboratories use the melting point to test how pure a substance is.

109906.q: Roughly at what temperature does gold melt?
109906.e: Gold melts at about 1064 °C. That is why goldsmiths need very hot flames or furnaces.

109907.q: Which is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature?
109907.e: Mercury melts at around -39 °C. It used to be used in clinical thermometers.
109907.m: Mercury is liquid at room temperature.

109908.q: How does the boiling point of water change when you dissolve a lot of salt in it?
109908.e: Dissolved substances make evaporation harder. So salt water boils slightly above 100 °C, but when cooking pasta the effect is very small.
109908.m: Salt water boils slightly higher than pure water.

109909.q: Roughly at what temperature does water boil on the summit of Mount Everest?
109909.e: At around 8800 metres the air pressure is only about a third of that at sea level. Water boils there at about 70 °C.
109909.m: On Mount Everest water boils at about 70 °C.

109910.q: Why are thermometers with mercury hardly used any more?
109910.e: Mercury evaporates a little even at room temperature, and its vapour is poisonous. If a thermometer breaks, that is dangerous.

109911.q: Roughly at what temperature does ethanol (alcohol) boil?
109911.e: Ethanol boils at about 78 °C, lower than water. This is used when distilling spirits.
109911.m: Alcohol boils at a lower temperature than water.

109912.q: Roughly at what temperature does liquid nitrogen boil?
109912.e: Nitrogen is a gas at room temperature. At normal air pressure it is only liquid below about -196 °C.

109913.q: How can you tell that water in a pan is boiling?
a: Large steam bubbles form inside it
109913.e: When boiling, water also turns to steam inside the liquid. The steam bubbles rise and make the water bubble.
109913.m: Boiling water bubbles because of steam bubbles.

109914.q: What happens to the temperature of boiling water when you turn the hob up?
109914.e: The extra energy only makes more water evaporate. In an open pan the temperature stays at the boiling point.
109914.m: Boiling water doesn't get hotter if you heat it more.

109915.q: Which element has the lowest boiling point?
109915.e: Helium only boils at around -269 °C, just a few degrees above absolute zero.
109915.m: Helium has the lowest boiling point of all substances.

109916.q: What is the change from liquid to gas called?
109916.e: During evaporation, particles break away from the liquid and become gas.
109916.m: When it evaporates, a liquid becomes a gas.

109917.q: What is the difference between evaporating and boiling?
a: Evaporation happens below the boiling point at the surface
Evaporation only happens with salt water
109917.e: During evaporation, single fast particles leave the surface, even at low temperatures. When boiling, steam forms throughout the liquid.
109917.m: Evaporation happens even below the boiling point.

109918.q: Why does a cloth spread out dry faster than a crumpled one?
a: The surface for evaporation is bigger
It is attracted by the sun
109918.e: Water only evaporates at the surface. The bigger the surface, the more particles can escape at the same time.
109918.m: A large surface speeds up evaporation.

109919.q: What happens to the temperature of boiling water while it evaporates in an open pan?
a: It keeps jumping up and down
109919.e: The energy supplied is used for evaporating, not for further heating. That is why boiling water stays at about 100 °C.

109920.q: Why does hot steam scald the skin worse than water at the same temperature?
a: It releases a lot of extra heat when it condenses
It is always much hotter than 100 °C
109920.e: When steam turns back into water on the skin, it releases the energy it took in while evaporating. This gives the skin a great deal of heat.
109920.m: Hot steam is especially dangerous for the skin.

109921.q: How does the volume change when water at 100 °C turns into steam?
109921.e: At normal pressure, one litre of water makes about 1700 litres of steam. This expansion used to drive steam engines.
109921.m: Steam needs much more space than water.

109922.q: Why does a puddle evaporate faster on a hot day?
a: More particles have enough energy to escape
The sun sucks up the water
109922.e: At higher temperatures, more water particles move fast enough to leave the surface.
109922.m: The warmer it is, the faster water evaporates.

109923.q: How do the Swiss salt works get table salt from brine?
a: They dry it in the wind
109923.e: Brine is salty water from underground. In large plants the water is evaporated and the salt is left behind.
109923.m: Salt is left behind when salt water evaporates.

109924.q: What is the change from gas to liquid called?
109924.e: During condensation a gas cools down and its particles gather together into a liquid.
109924.m: During condensation a gas becomes liquid.

109925.q: Where does the water dripping from the hose of an air conditioner come from?
a: From humidity condensing on the cold cooling part
From the rain on the roof
109925.e: The air conditioner cools the room air on cold fins. Water vapour condenses there and is drained away as condensate.
109925.m: Air conditioners remove water from the air by condensation.

109926.q: How does dew form in the morning?
a: Water vapour in the air condenses on cool surfaces
109926.e: On clear nights, grass and leaves cool down a lot. The air next to them cools too, and the water vapour turns into dew drops.
109926.m: Dew forms when water vapour condenses on cool surfaces.

109927.q: What often forms in autumn when damp air over the Swiss Plateau cools a lot?
109927.e: When the air near the ground cools below the dew point, the water vapour condenses into tiny droplets that float in the air.
109927.m: Fog is a cloud lying on the ground.

a: Damp air rises, cools and water vapour condenses
Water evaporates directly in the sky
The wind squeezes water out of the sea
109928.e: As air rises it cools. The water vapour condenses on tiny dust and salt particles into droplets.
109928.m: Clouds form through condensation high up.

109929.q: What is the temperature called at which water vapour starts to condense in cooling air?
109929.e: At the dew point the air is saturated with water vapour. If it cools further, water droplets form.
109929.m: At the dew point water vapour starts to condense.

109930.q: What is the part in fridges and power stations called where steam is turned back into liquid?
109930.e: In the condenser the vapour gives off heat and becomes liquid again. On a fridge, it is the warm grille at the back.
109930.m: In the condenser vapour turns back into liquid.

109931.q: What is the separation method called in which a liquid is evaporated and the vapour condensed again?
109931.e: Distillation separates substances with different boiling points. It is used, for example, to get pure water or essential oils.
109931.m: In distillation, liquid is evaporated and condensed again.

109932.q: What is the change from liquid to solid called?
109932.e: During solidification the particles arrange themselves into a solid structure. For water this is called freezing.
109932.m: When it solidifies, a liquid becomes solid.

109933.q: What happens to the volume of water when it freezes?
a: It increases by about 9 per cent
109933.e: In ice, water molecules form a loose lattice with gaps. That is why ice needs about 9 per cent more space.

109934.q: What is the process called in which liquid metal is poured into a mould and solidifies there?
109934.e: In casting, the metal takes on the shape of the mould as it solidifies. Church bells, for example, are made this way.
109934.m: In casting, liquid metal solidifies in a mould.

109935.q: What happens to rock when water in its cracks freezes again and again?
a: It becomes as soft as clay
109935.e: Freezing water presses hard against the sides of the cracks. This frost shattering makes stones break off in the Alps and creates scree slopes.
109935.m: Frost shattering breaks up rock in the mountains.

109936.q: What forms when liquid lava solidifies?
109936.e: Lava cools in the air and becomes solid. This creates rocks such as basalt or pumice.

109937.q: Why do fruit growers spray their blossoms with water when there is frost?
a: The freezing water gives off heat
109937.e: When water freezes, it gives off heat. As long as water keeps freezing, the blossom under the ice stays at about 0 °C and does not freeze to death. This is done in Valais, for example.
109937.m: Freezing water can protect blossoms from frost.

109938.q: What is it called when water is cooled below 0 °C without freezing?
109938.e: Very pure, still water can stay liquid below 0 °C. With a jolt or a touch it freezes suddenly; this is how freezing rain makes black ice.

109939.q: How does the volume of most substances change when they solidify?
109939.e: In most substances the particles move closer together when they solidify. That is why leftover candle wax often gets a dip in the middle.
109939.m: Most substances contract when they solidify.

109940.q: What does a solid need in order to sublimate?
a: Energy in the form of heat
109940.e: The particles have to break completely out of the solid structure. To do this they take in heat from their surroundings.

109941.q: What can happen to snow in very dry, cold air and sunshine, even below 0 °C?
a: It turns directly into water vapour
109941.e: A layer of snow can lose mass this way without melting. This is especially easy to see in dry mountain air.
109941.m: Snow can disappear even without melting.

109942.q: In which process is ice removed from frozen food at very low pressure?
109942.e: In freeze-drying, the ice turns directly into vapour in a vacuum. This is how instant coffee or astronaut food is made, for example.
109942.m: In freeze-drying, the ice disappears without melting.

109943.q: Which substance slowly turns into violet vapour even at room temperature?
109943.e: Iodine forms dark crystals. In a closed jar you soon see violet vapour above them.
109943.m: Iodine forms violet vapour even at room temperature.

109944.q: Which state of matter does a substance skip during sublimation?
109944.e: The substance goes straight from solid to gas. It does not pass through the liquid state.
109944.m: In sublimation the liquid state is missing.

109945.q: What is the damage called on badly wrapped food in the freezer, where ice sublimates?
109945.e: The ice in the surface of the food turns into vapour. Dry, grey patches are left behind.
109945.m: Good wrapping protects against freezer burn.

109946.q: What happens when a comet comes close to the sun?
a: Frozen substances turn into gas and form a tail
109946.e: Comets are made of ice and dust. Near the sun the ices turn directly into gas; this forms the coma and the tail.
109946.m: A comet's tail forms through sublimation.

109947.q: Why do naphthalene mothballs get smaller over time?
109947.e: Naphthalene is solid but constantly gives off vapour. The smell is meant to keep moths away.

109948.q: What is the direct change from gas to solid called?
109948.e: In deposition, a gas becomes a solid directly without becoming liquid.
109948.m: In deposition, a gas becomes solid directly.

109949.q: How does hoar frost form on branches and grass?
a: Water vapour turns directly into ice
109949.e: On cold, clear nights, water vapour settles on cold surfaces as fine ice crystals.
109949.m: Hoar frost forms directly from water vapour.

109950.q: Which patterns form on cold window panes in winter through deposition?
109950.e: Damp room air meets ice-cold glass. There the water vapour grows directly into branching ice crystals.
109950.m: Frost flowers grow from water vapour on a cold window.

109951.q: How do snow crystals mainly form in clouds?
a: Water vapour settles directly as ice on tiny particles
Rain only freezes on the ground
109951.e: In cold clouds, ice crystals grow as water vapour settles directly on them. This creates the delicate shapes of snowflakes.
109951.m: Snow crystals grow directly from water vapour.

109952.q: Why do snow crystals usually have a six-sided shape?
a: Because of how water molecules are arranged in ice
Because the wind grinds them that way
Because they break as they fall
109952.e: In ice, water molecules form a hexagonal lattice. This order shows in the shape of snow crystals.
109952.m: Snow crystals are six-sided because of the ice lattice.

a: A gas becomes solid directly, without becoming liquid
A solid becomes a gas directly
109953.e: In deposition, water vapour, for example, turns directly into ice. This is how hoar frost and frost flowers form. The opposite process is called sublimation.
109953.m: In deposition, a gas becomes solid directly.

109954.q: What does a gas give off to its surroundings during deposition?
109954.e: When changing into a more ordered state, energy is released. It is given off to the surroundings as heat.

109955.q: Why does a layer of ice form on the walls of a freezer that is opened often?
a: Moisture from the room air turns directly into ice there
109955.e: Each time it is opened, damp air flows in. On the very cold walls the water vapour settles as frost, which is why freezers have to be defrosted.
109955.m: Damp air freezes onto the walls of the freezer.

109956.q: What happens to the temperature of an ice and water mixture while the ice is melting?
109956.e: All the heat supplied is used for melting. Only when all the ice has melted does the temperature rise.

109957.q: What is the heat supplied during melting used for?
a: To break the bonds between the particles
109957.e: In a solid the particles are held firmly in place. The heat of fusion provides the energy to break up this structure.
109957.m: The heat of fusion breaks up the solid order of the particles.

109958.q: Why does an ice cube cool a drink so well?
a: It takes in a lot of heat as it melts
It gives off cold to the drink
109958.e: To melt, the ice cube takes in a lot of heat from the drink. This makes the drink colder.
109958.m: Melting ice takes heat from its surroundings.

109959.q: How much energy do you need to melt 3 kg of ice at 0 °C if 1 kg needs 334 kJ?
109959.e: You multiply the mass by the heat of fusion: 3 times 334 kJ makes 1002 kJ.
109959.m: The melting energy grows with the mass of the ice.

109960.q: Why is the heat of fusion also called “hidden” heat?
a: It is taken in without the ice getting warmer
It can only be measured in the dark
It is only found inside the Earth
109960.e: While ice melts, it takes in heat, but the thermometer stays at 0 °C. The heat seems to disappear, so it is called hidden or latent heat.
109960.m: The heat of fusion is hidden heat: it does not change the temperature.

109961.q: Why do snowfields in the Alps last a long time in spring, even though the air is above 0 °C?
a: Melting ice takes a great deal of energy
New snow is delivered at night
109961.e: Before snow melts, a lot of energy must be supplied to it. That is why it takes weeks for thick snow cover to disappear.
109961.m: Snow melts slowly because melting needs a lot of energy.

109962.q: Which needs more energy: melting 1 kg of ice at 0 °C or heating 1 kg of water from 0 °C to 80 °C?
a: Melting needs no energy at all
109962.e: Melting needs about 334 kJ. Heating needs 4.19 kJ times 80, so around 335 kJ.
109962.m: Melting ice needs as much energy as heating water by 80 degrees.

109963.q: What is the heat called that is released during solidification and is the same as the heat of fusion?
109963.e: The energy a substance takes in when melting is given off again when it solidifies.
109963.m: The heat of solidification is the same as the heat of fusion.

a: The evaporating water cools the skin
109964.e: Sweat evaporates on the skin. For this it needs heat, which it takes from the body.

109965.q: Why does alcohol hand sanitiser feel cold on your skin?
a: The alcohol evaporates quickly and takes away heat
It is kept in the fridge
109965.e: Alcohol evaporates very easily. It takes the energy it needs from the skin, which therefore feels cool.
109965.m: Quickly evaporating liquids cool the skin.

109966.q: Why does water stay cool in an unglazed clay jug?
a: Water seeps through and evaporates outside
109966.e: Water gets through the pores to the outside and evaporates there. This takes heat from the jug and its contents.
109966.m: A clay jug cools through evaporation.

109967.q: Why does sweating cool you poorly in humid, muggy air?
a: You don't sweat at all then
109967.e: If the air is already almost saturated with water vapour, only a little sweat can evaporate. It drips off without cooling.
109967.m: In muggy air sweat hardly cools you.

109968.q: Where does an evaporating liquid get the energy it needs?
109968.e: The fastest particles escape and take energy with them. The remaining liquid and its surroundings cool down as a result.
109968.m: Evaporation takes heat from the surroundings.

109969.q: Which principle does a fridge use inside?
a: A refrigerant evaporates and takes away heat
109969.e: Inside, the refrigerant evaporates and takes in heat. Outside it is turned back into liquid and gives off the heat.
109969.m: In a fridge an evaporating refrigerant does the cooling.

109970.q: You wrap a wet cloth around a thermometer. Why does it show less than a dry thermometer next to it?
a: The water evaporates and takes away heat
109970.e: Water evaporates from the wet cloth and takes heat from the thermometer. The drier the air, the bigger the difference.
109970.m: Evaporating water cools a thermometer too.

109971.q: What is dry ice made of?
109971.e: Dry ice is carbon dioxide (CO₂) in solid form. It looks like white ice.
109971.m: Dry ice is solid carbon dioxide.

109972.q: At what temperature does dry ice sublimate at normal air pressure?
109972.e: Dry ice turns directly into gas at about -78.5 °C. So it is much colder than a freezer compartment.

a: It does not become liquid when it warms up
109973.e: At normal air pressure there is no liquid carbon dioxide. So dry ice leaves no puddle.

109974.q: Where does the mist from dry ice collect, because carbon dioxide is heavier than air?
109974.e: The cold gas and the mist sink downwards. That is why stage fog creeps across the floor.
109974.m: Dry ice mist creeps along the floor.

109975.q: Why must you never touch dry ice with bare hands?
109975.e: Because of the very low temperature, the skin can freeze. That is why you use thick gloves or tongs.
109975.m: Only touch dry ice with gloves.

109976.q: Why must you never put dry ice in a tightly closed bottle?
a: The gas produced can make it burst
109976.e: A little dry ice makes a lot of gas. The pressure in the bottle rises sharply until it can explode.
109976.m: Dry ice never goes in a tightly sealed container.

109977.q: What danger is there when a lot of dry ice sublimates in a small, closed room?
109977.e: The carbon dioxide pushes the oxygen out of the air. That is why rooms with dry ice must be well ventilated.

109978.q: What is dry ice often used for?
109978.e: Dry ice is used, for example, to keep food, medicines and lab samples cold when they are sent.
109978.m: Dry ice keeps goods cold during transport.

109979.q: What do the arrows in a drawn food chain show?
a: The direction in which food is passed on
The direction in which the animals migrate
109979.e: The arrow points from the living thing that is eaten to the one that eats it. This shows where food and energy flow.
109979.m: The arrow always points from what is eaten to the eater.

109980.q: What is a food chain called that begins with dead material such as leaves or droppings?
109980.e: A decomposer chain, also called a detrital food chain, begins with dead plant parts or animal remains. Soil animals feed on them and are eaten in turn.
109980.m: Not every food chain begins with a living plant.

109981.q: Why do food chains usually have only four or five links?
a: Because a lot of energy is lost at every level
Because animals eat four species at most
Because plants have too little water
109981.e: Only a small part of the energy is passed on from one level to the next. There is usually not enough energy left for a sixth or seventh link.
109981.m: Long food chains are rare because energy is lost along the way.

109982.q: What happens if the plants at the start of a food chain disappear?
a: All the following links lack food
Only the last link is affected
The animals make their own food
109982.e: All the animals in the chain depend directly or indirectly on the plants. If the plants are missing, all the other links have no food.
109982.m: Without plants at the start, the whole food chain collapses.

109983.q: What does the blue whale mainly eat?
109983.e: The blue whale filters huge amounts of small crustaceans, called krill, out of the water. The krill in turn eat tiny algae.
109983.m: The largest animal on Earth eats tiny crustaceans.

109984.q: Why did the insecticide DDT build up especially in birds of prey?
a: Because it accumulates along the food chain
Because birds of prey drink the poison directly
Because birds of prey nest in fields
Because the poison only attacks birds
109984.e: DDT is hardly broken down in the body. Each link in the chain takes in the poison from all the prey it has eaten, so the amount was highest in birds of prey.
109984.m: Some poisons build up more and more at each level of the food chain.

109985.q: Which link in the chain “dandelion, brown hare, fox” is the plant eater?
109985.e: The brown hare eats the dandelion and is itself eaten by the fox.
109985.m: The second link of a food chain is usually a plant eater.

109986.q: Why does a food web describe nature better than a single chain?
a: Because most animals have several sources of food
Because animals only eat one single species
Because it shows fewer living things
109986.e: A fox, for example, eats mice, birds, beetles and berries. A single chain cannot show this.
109986.m: Nature is more like a web than a simple chain.

109987.q: What do predators in a food web often do when one prey species becomes rare?
a: They only eat the rare species
They go into hibernation at once
109987.e: Because there are many links in the web, predators can switch to other prey. This makes the system less vulnerable.
109987.m: In a food web there is often a replacement when one food source is missing.

109988.q: What is an ecosystem with many species and many links in its food web usually like?
109988.e: If one species disappears from a web with many species, other species can partly take over its role.
109988.m: Many species and links make a food web more stable.

109989.q: Besides fish, what prey does the grey heron often eat?
109989.e: The grey heron hunts fish, frogs and mice by the water and in meadows. This links it to many food chains.
109989.m: The grey heron catches fish, frogs and mice.

109990.q: Which animal species was brought back to Yellowstone National Park in 1995 and changed the whole food web?
109990.e: The wolves hunted elk, which then ate fewer young trees in some places. Experts see this as an example of how a predator also affects plants through the food web.
109990.m: A single predator can change a whole food web.

109991.q: What is a species called whose disappearance changes a food web especially strongly?
109991.e: A keystone species has a much bigger influence on its ecosystem than its numbers would suggest.
109991.m: If a keystone species disappears, the whole food web is thrown into disorder.

109992.q: Sea otters eat sea urchins. What often happens to the kelp forests when the sea otters disappear?
a: Sea urchins eat the kelp forests bare
The kelp forests grow twice as fast
The kelp forests turn into coral
109992.e: Without sea otters, sea urchins multiply a lot and eat the large brown seaweeds. This shows how predators, plant eaters and plants are connected in the web.
109992.m: The sea otter protects the kelp forests by eating sea urchins.

109993.q: Which animal in the food web of a Swiss forest is both prey and predator?
109993.e: The wood mouse eats seeds and also insects. At the same time, it is eaten by foxes, owls and weasels.
109993.m: Many animals in a food web both eat and are eaten.

109994.q: In ecology, what are living things called that make their own food?
109994.e: Producers build energy-rich nutrients from simple substances such as water and carbon dioxide. They are mainly plants and algae.

109995.q: Through which process do green plants make sugar?
109995.e: In photosynthesis, plants use light energy to build glucose from water and carbon dioxide.
109995.m: Through photosynthesis, plants turn light into food.

109996.q: Which source of energy do producers on land use?
109996.e: Green plants capture sunlight and store its energy in sugar.
109996.m: Plants get their energy from sunlight.

109997.q: Who are the most important producers in the sea?
109997.e: Phytoplankton is made up of microscopic algae that carry out photosynthesis. It is the basis of almost all food chains in the sea.
109997.m: In the sea, tiny algae are the most important food producers.

109998.q: In the end, what do all the animals in an ecosystem live on?
a: Only the water in the ground
109998.e: Plants and algae use sunlight to make nutrients. Plant eaters eat them, and meat eaters eat the plant eaters.
109998.m: All animals depend on the producers.

109999.q: Which producers live at hot springs in the dark deep sea?
a: Bacteria that get energy from sulphur compounds
109999.e: There is no light in the deep sea. There, bacteria use chemical energy from sulphur compounds to make nutrients; this is called chemosynthesis.
109999.m: Even without light there are producers that use chemical energy.

110000.q: Which of these living things is a producer?
110000.e: The beech carries out photosynthesis. Fungi such as the cep have no chlorophyll and cannot make food from light.
110000.m: Fungi are not producers because they do not carry out photosynthesis.

110001.q: What is typical of a consumer in ecology?
a: It feeds on other living things
It makes its food from light
110001.e: Consumers cannot make their own food. They eat plants or other animals.
110001.m: Consumers have to eat other living things.

110002.q: In ecology, what are animals called that eat plants directly?
110002.e: Plant eaters are the first consumers after the producers. They are also called first-order consumers.

110003.q: A fox eats a mouse that has eaten grain. What kind of consumer is the fox?
110003.e: The grain is the producer and the mouse is the primary consumer. Whatever eats the mouse is a secondary consumer.
110003.m: Anything that eats a plant eater is a secondary consumer.

110004.q: What kind of consumer is the pike in the chain “alga, water flea, perch, pike”?
110004.e: The alga is the producer, the water flea the primary consumer, the perch the secondary consumer and the pike the tertiary consumer.
110004.m: You count consumers starting with the first animal after the producer.

a: Because they cannot carry out photosynthesis
Because they are too big for photosynthesis
Because they are only active at night
110005.e: Animals have no chlorophyll and cannot make food from light. They have to take in their energy with their food.
110005.m: Animals have to eat because they cannot make food from light.

110006.q: A great tit eats caterpillars that feed on the leaves of an oak. What is the great tit?
110006.e: The oak is the producer and the caterpillar is the plant eater. The great tit eats the caterpillar, so it is a secondary consumer.
110006.m: The great tit feeds its young lots of caterpillars.

110007.q: What does the Latin word “consumere”, which “consumer” comes from, mean?
110007.e: Consumers use up the substances and energy that the producers have built up.
110007.m: Consumers are the users in an ecosystem.

110008.q: What is a consumer called that mainly feeds on other animals?
110008.e: Meat eaters, also called carnivores, hunt or eat other animals. Examples are the lynx, the wolf and the pike.
110008.m: Meat eaters mainly feed on other animals.

110009.q: What is the underground network of fine fungal threads that breaks down wood and leaves called?
110009.e: The mushroom you can see is only the fruiting body. The actual fungus lives as a mycelium of fine threads in the soil or in wood and breaks down dead plant parts there.
110009.m: The mycelium is the real body of a fungus in the soil.

110010.q: Which living things are the most important decomposers?
110010.e: Bacteria and fungi break down dead matter into minerals, water and carbon dioxide.
110010.m: Bacteria and fungi break down dead living things.

110011.q: What forms when soil organisms break down fallen leaves?
110011.e: Soil organisms turn leaves and other remains into dark, fertile humus.

110012.q: What would happen in a forest without decomposers?
a: Dead plants and animals would pile up
There would be more minerals in the soil
110012.e: Without decomposers, nothing would be broken down. Leaves and dead animals would just lie there, and the nutrients would be locked inside them.
110012.m: Without decomposers, nature would choke on its own waste.

110013.q: Which soil animal pulls leaves into the ground and so helps to break them down?
110013.e: The earthworm pulls leaves into its tunnels and eats them. Its droppings are very fertile and are broken down further by bacteria.
110013.m: The earthworm turns leaves into fertile soil.

110014.q: Which substances do decomposers return to the soil so that plants can take them up again?
110014.e: Decomposers break down dead matter into simple minerals. Plants take these up again with water through their roots.
110014.m: Decomposers close the cycle of substances.

110015.q: Why does a compost heap get warm inside?
a: Because tiny organisms give off heat as they break things down
Because the sun heats it from the inside
110015.e: Bacteria and fungi break down the waste and release energy as heat. That is why it can get much warmer inside a compost heap.
110015.m: Composting produces heat through the work of tiny organisms.

110016.q: Why does an apple go off more slowly in the fridge?
a: Because cold slows down bacteria and fungi
Because there is no oxygen in the fridge
Because the apple grows in the fridge
110016.e: Bacteria and moulds work much more slowly in the cold. That is why chilling keeps food fresh for longer.
110016.m: Cold slows down the work of decomposers.

110017.q: What does a trophic level describe?
a: The level of a living thing in the food chain
The height at which an animal lives
110017.e: The trophic level shows at which feeding level a living thing is, for example producer or plant eater.
110017.m: The trophic level shows the feeding level of a living thing.

110018.q: On which trophic level are the producers?
110018.e: Producers are the basis of all food chains and so form the first trophic level.
110018.m: Plants form the first trophic level.

110019.q: On which trophic level are the plant eaters?
110019.e: Plant eaters eat the producers and are therefore one level higher, on the second level.
110019.m: Plant eaters form the second trophic level.

110020.q: What does the Greek word “trophe”, found in “trophic level”, mean?
110020.e: In Greek, trophe means nourishment or food. A trophic level is therefore a feeding level.
110020.m: Trophic levels are levels of feeding.

110021.q: Can an animal belong to several trophic levels?
a: Yes, if it eats plants and animals
Only if it lives in water
110021.e: An omnivore like the fox eats berries and mice. This puts it on the second and third levels at the same time.
110021.m: Omnivores are often on several trophic levels at once.

110022.q: On which trophic level is a wolf that eats a deer?
110022.e: Plants form the first level, the deer as a plant eater the second and the wolf the third.
110022.m: Anything that eats a plant eater is on the third trophic level.

110023.q: What is an animal on the highest trophic level called that has hardly any natural enemies?
110023.e: Apex predators such as the orca, the eagle or the wolf are at the very top of the food web and are hardly ever hunted as adults.
110023.m: Apex predators are at the very top of the food web.

110024.q: On which trophic level is the tawny owl in the chain “grass, grasshopper, shrew, tawny owl”?
110024.e: Grass is on the first level, the grasshopper on the second, the shrew on the third and the tawny owl on the fourth.
110024.m: You count trophic levels upwards starting from the plants.

110025.q: What does an ecological food pyramid show?
a: How numbers, mass or energy decrease from level to level
110025.e: Each level of the pyramid stands for a trophic level. The levels usually get narrower towards the top.
110025.m: The food pyramid gets narrower towards the top.

110026.q: Who forms the broad base of an ecological food pyramid?
110026.e: In an ecosystem, the producers have the most mass and energy. They support all the levels above them.
110026.m: Plants form the broad base of the pyramid.

110027.q: Which three types of ecological pyramid are there?
a: Pyramids of numbers, biomass and energy
Pyramids of water, air and earth
Pyramids of age, size and colour
Pyramids of summer, autumn and winter
110027.e: You can show the number of living things, their mass or the energy they contain at each level.
110027.m: Pyramids can show numbers, biomass or energy.

110028.q: Which ecological pyramid can never be upside down?
110028.e: Each level can only get part of the energy of the level below. That is why the energy is always greatest at the bottom.
110028.m: The pyramid of energy is always widest at the bottom.

110029.q: A single oak tree feeds thousands of caterpillars. What does the pyramid of numbers look like here?
a: It is narrower at the bottom than above
It is widest at the bottom
It is the same width everywhere
110029.e: One tree is set against thousands of caterpillars. In terms of numbers, the bottom level is therefore narrower than the second.
110029.m: Pyramids of numbers can be upside down.

110030.q: Why can the pyramid of biomass in the sea be upside down?
a: Because there are no producers in the sea
Because algae are bigger than whales
110030.e: The tiny algae live only a short time, but they divide very quickly and are constantly being eaten. That is why at any one time their mass is often smaller than that of the animals that live on them.
110030.m: In the sea, the mass of consumers can be greater than that of the producers.

110031.q: Unlike the ecological pyramid, what does the food pyramid of the Swiss Society for Nutrition show?
a: How to eat a balanced diet
Who eats whom in the forest
How much energy the sun provides
110031.e: The food pyramid is advice for healthy eating. It has nothing to do with trophic levels in an ecosystem.
110031.m: The food pyramid is advice about eating, not an ecological pyramid.

110032.q: Why are there far fewer foxes than mice in an area?
a: Because less energy reaches the top of the pyramid
Because foxes do not have young
Because foxes only eat in winter
110032.e: A fox needs many mice to live. Because energy is lost at every level, only a few animals can live at the top.
110032.m: The higher the level in the pyramid, the fewer animals live there.

110033.q: What usually happens to the number of predators when there are lots of prey animals?
a: It also rises a little later
It always stays exactly the same
110033.e: With lots of food, predators can raise more young. So their numbers grow after a short delay.
110033.m: Lots of prey leads to more predators later on.

110034.q: Which pair of animals from Canada is a famous example of rising and falling numbers of predators and prey?
110034.e: From the fur sales figures of a trading company, we know that the numbers of lynx and snowshoe hares went up and down in cycles of about ten years.
110034.m: The lynx and the snowshoe hare are the classic predator and prey example.

110035.q: How do the numbers of predators and prey often change over many years?
a: They rise and fall in waves
110035.e: When there is lots of prey, the predators multiply. Then prey becomes scarce, and later the predators decline too. This creates waves, which researchers have even described with equations.
110035.m: Predator and prey numbers go up and down in waves.

110036.q: Why do predator numbers follow prey numbers with a delay?
a: Because predators need time to multiply
Because prey animals feed the predators
110036.e: More food only shows up in the predators' next litters. That is why their curve lags behind the curve of the prey.
110036.m: The predator curve lags behind the prey curve.

110037.q: What is it called when a harmless animal like the hoverfly looks like an animal that can defend itself, such as the wasp?
110037.e: The hoverfly has no sting, but with its yellow and black stripes it looks like a wasp. That is why predators often leave it alone.
110037.m: Mimicry protects harmless animals because they look like dangerous ones.

110038.q: Which prey does the lynx mainly hunt in Switzerland?
110038.e: The lynx is an ambush hunter that mainly catches roe deer and chamois in Switzerland.
110038.m: In Switzerland, the lynx mainly hunts roe deer.

110039.q: What is the advantage for the prey population when predators often catch sick and weak animals?
a: The prey animals forget how to flee
110039.e: Sick and weak animals are easier to catch. When they are gone, diseases spread less in the prey population.
110039.m: Predators often help prey populations to stay healthy.

110040.q: Why do predators in nature not normally wipe out their prey?
a: Because when prey is scarce, predator numbers fall too
Because predators feel sorry for their prey
Because predators only hunt every other year
110040.e: When prey becomes rare, predators find too little food and have fewer young. The prey can then recover.
110040.m: Predators and prey keep each other in balance.

110041.q: How do young roe deer fawns protect themselves from predators in their first weeks of life?
a: They lie still and are well camouflaged
They attack predators with their horns
110041.e: Roe deer fawns have spotted coats and press themselves motionless into the long grass when there is danger. This makes them easy for predators to miss.
110041.m: Fawns protect themselves by camouflage and lying still.

110042.q: What is the scientific term for plant eaters?
110042.e: The word comes from the Latin “herba”, meaning grass or herb. Herbivores feed on plants.

110043.q: What are plant eaters such as cows, goats and chamois called that chew their food a second time?
110043.e: Ruminants bring their food back up from the first part of the stomach and chew it thoroughly again.

110044.q: What is the largest part of a cow's stomach called?
110044.e: The rumen is the largest of the four parts of the stomach. There, microorganisms break down the grass.
110044.m: The rumen is the largest stomach of the cow.

110045.q: Who helps plant eaters to digest the tough cellulose in plants?
110045.e: Mammals cannot break down cellulose themselves. Bacteria and other tiny organisms in the stomach or gut do this work.
110045.m: Without microorganisms, cows could hardly digest grass.

110046.q: How can you recognise a typical plant eater by its teeth?
a: By broad back teeth with grinding surfaces
110046.e: Plants have to be ground up thoroughly. For this, plant eaters have broad back teeth.
110046.m: Plant eaters grind their food with broad back teeth.

110047.q: What does the giant panda eat almost exclusively?
110047.e: Although the giant panda is a bear, it eats almost nothing but bamboo and has to eat large amounts of it every day.
110047.m: The giant panda lives almost entirely on bamboo.

110048.q: What does the koala mainly eat?
110048.e: Koalas eat almost only the leaves of certain eucalyptus trees. These leaves contain few nutrients, which is why koalas sleep a lot.
110048.m: The koala eats almost only eucalyptus leaves.

110049.q: What is it called when roe deer eat the buds of young trees?
110049.e: Roe deer and red deer like to eat the buds and shoots of young trees. This browsing can make it harder for the forest to grow back.
110049.m: Browsing damage happens when wild animals eat the buds of young trees.

110050.q: Which Swiss rodent eats only plants and likes to eat tree bark in winter?
110050.e: The beaver eats herbs, water plants and, in winter, mainly bark and twigs. It even fells trees to get them.
110050.m: The beaver fells trees to get at bark and twigs.

110051.q: What is the scientific term for animals that eat everything?
110051.e: The Latin “omnis” means “all”. Omnivores eat plants and animals.
110051.m: Omnivores eat both plant and animal food.

110052.q: Which of these Swiss wild animals is an omnivore?
110052.e: The wild boar eats acorns, roots, mushrooms, worms, insects and also carrion.
110052.m: The wild boar eats almost anything it finds.

110053.q: What does most of the brown bear's food consist of?
a: Plants such as berries, grasses and roots
110053.e: Brown bears are omnivores, but they usually eat more plant food than animal food. They also eat insects, carrion and sometimes wild animals.
110053.m: The brown bear mainly eats plants, even though it is a carnivore.

110054.q: Which types of teeth show that humans have the typical teeth of an omnivore?
110054.e: Humans have incisors for biting off, canines for holding and molars for grinding. This suits a mixed diet.
110054.m: Human teeth are built for a mixed diet.

110055.q: Which bird is a typical omnivore in Swiss towns and cities?
110055.e: Carrion crows eat seeds, fruit, worms, insects, rubbish and carrion. Swifts only catch insects, and falcons hunt animals.
110055.m: The carrion crow eats almost anything, which is why it does well in towns.

110056.q: Besides mice, what else does the red fox like to eat?
110056.e: The red fox mainly eats mice, but in late summer it also eats lots of berries and fallen fruit. It is an omnivore.
110056.m: The red fox eats mice and also sweet fruit.

110057.q: What advantage do omnivores have over animals that eat only one kind of food?
a: They find a replacement more easily when one food is missing
110057.e: If you can eat many different things, you depend less on a single source of food.
110057.m: Omnivores cope well when the food supply changes.

110058.q: Which food does the badger, an omnivore, especially like?
110058.e: The badger eats fruit, roots, insects and mice. But earthworms are often its most important food.
110058.m: The badger is a great lover of earthworms.

110059.q: Where does the energy of almost all ecosystems come from?
a: From the inside of the Earth
110059.e: Plants store the sun's energy in sugar. Through food chains, this energy reaches all animals.
110059.m: Almost all the energy in an ecosystem comes from the sun.

110060.q: According to the rule of thumb, roughly how much energy passes from one level of the food chain to the next?
110060.e: According to the ten percent rule, only about a tenth of the energy is built into the body mass of the next level. The rest is lost first.
110060.m: Only about a tenth of the energy reaches the next level.

110061.q: Where is most of the energy lost at each level?
a: As heat during breathing and movement
110061.e: Living things use most of their energy for breathing, moving and keeping warm. This energy goes into the surroundings as heat.
110061.m: Most energy is lost as heat.

110062.q: Why do we speak of an energy flow and not an energy cycle?
a: Because the energy is lost as heat and does not come back
Because the energy flows in a circle
110062.e: Substances are recycled by decomposers, but energy is not. It flows in one direction only and has to be supplied by the sun all the time.
110062.m: Substances go round in cycles; energy flows in one direction only.

110063.q: Roughly what share of the sunlight falling on them do plants store in nutrients?
110063.e: A large part of the light is reflected, passes through or is turned into heat. Only a few percent is turned into chemical energy.
110063.m: Plants only use a small part of the sunlight.

110064.q: What happens to the energy in droppings, fallen leaves and dead animals?
a: It flows back to the sun
It disappears without a trace at once
110064.e: Bacteria, fungi and soil animals break down the dead matter and use the energy stored in it for themselves. In the end, this energy is also given off as heat.
110064.m: Decomposers also live on the energy in dead matter.

110065.q: In terms of energy, why is it better to eat plants directly than to eat meat from animals that have eaten plants?
a: Because a lot of energy is lost on the detour through animals
110065.e: An animal needs most of the energy in its food for itself. If people eat the plants directly, this loss does not happen.
110065.m: Every extra level in the food chain costs energy.

110066.q: In what form is the energy in our food stored?
110066.e: In photosynthesis, light energy is turned into chemical energy. It is found in sugar, fat and protein.

110067.q: Why do mammals and birds need more food than reptiles of the same weight?
a: Because they keep their body temperature constant
110067.e: Warm-blooded animals heat their bodies all the time. This uses a lot of energy, which reptiles save.
110067.m: Warm-blooded animals use a lot of energy to keep warm.

110068.q: In ecology, what is meant by biomass?
a: The mass of living things in an area
The mass of all the stones in an area
The weight of the water in a lake
The amount of air above a forest
110068.e: Biomass is the mass of all living organisms, or of material that comes from them, in a habitat.
110068.m: Biomass is the mass of living things.

110069.q: Which living things make up most of the Earth's biomass?
110069.e: According to scientific estimates, about four fifths of the biomass on Earth comes from plants, mainly trees.
110069.m: Most of the Earth's biomass is made up of plants.

110070.q: According to scientific estimates, which group of animals has the largest biomass among animals?
110070.e: Insects, spiders, crustaceans and other arthropods exist in huge numbers. Together they weigh more than all the other groups of animals.
110070.m: Together, arthropods make up the largest animal biomass.

110071.q: Which source of energy counts as biomass?
110071.e: Wood chips come from wood that has grown recently and count as renewable biomass. Natural gas, coal and oil are fossil fuels.
110071.m: Wood is a renewable source of energy from biomass.

110072.q: What is produced from slurry and green waste in a biogas plant?
110072.e: Bacteria break down the biomass without oxygen. This produces biogas, which is mainly methane.
110072.m: Biogas can be made from slurry and green waste.

110073.q: Why is biomass often measured as dry mass?
a: Because the water content can vary a lot
110073.e: Living things are largely made of water, and the amount keeps changing. Dried samples are easier to compare.
110073.m: For exact comparisons, biomass is weighed when dry.

110074.q: Where on land is the plant biomass per area especially large?
a: In the high mountains above the snow line
110074.e: Warmth, lots of rain and light all year round let huge trees grow in the rainforest.
110074.m: Tropical rainforests store especially large amounts of biomass.

110075.q: How does the biomass in a food pyramid usually change from bottom to top?
110075.e: Because energy is lost at every level, each level can build up less mass than the one below. The plants at the very bottom therefore usually have the largest biomass.
110075.m: Biomass is usually greatest at the level of the plants.

110174.q: Where does the outer ear canal of a human end?
110174.e: The outer ear canal leads inwards from the outer ear to the eardrum. Behind it the middle ear begins.
110174.m: The outer ear canal ends at the eardrum.

110175.q: Roughly how long is the outer ear canal in adults?
110175.e: In adults the outer ear canal is around 2.5 to 3.5 centimetres long. It is slightly curved in an S shape.
110175.m: The outer ear canal is only a few centimetres long.

110176.q: What does earwax do in the ear canal?
a: It protects against dirt and germs
110176.e: Earwax (cerumen) traps dust, keeps the skin supple and slows down bacteria. Over time it moves outwards by itself.
110176.m: Earwax is a natural protection for the ear canal.

110177.q: Why do doctors advise against cleaning the ear canal with cotton buds?
a: The earwax gets pushed further in
110177.e: Cotton buds often push earwax inwards, where it can form a plug. You can also injure the eardrum.
110177.m: Cotton buds do not belong deep in the ear canal.

110178.q: What is the wall of the outer third of the ear canal made of?
110178.e: The outer third of the ear canal has a wall of cartilage; the inner part lies in the temporal bone and is made of bone.
110178.m: The ear canal is cartilage on the outside and bone on the inside.

110179.q: Why should you let your ears dry well after swimming?
a: Damp skin in the ear canal gets inflamed more easily
Otherwise you only hear low notes
110179.e: If water stays in the ear canal, the skin softens. Germs then get in more easily and an ear canal infection can develop.
110179.m: After swimming you should let your ears dry well.

110180.q: What job does the outer ear canal do?
a: It carries sound to the eardrum
110180.e: The ear canal is a short tube leading inwards from the outer ear. Sound travels through it to the eardrum.
110180.m: The ear canal carries sound to the eardrum.

110181.q: Why does the doctor gently pull an adult's outer ear backwards and upwards before looking into the ear?
a: So that the curved ear canal becomes straighter
So that the earwax becomes runny
So that the semicircular canals rest
110181.e: The ear canal is curved. Pulling the outer ear backwards and upwards straightens it, so the eardrum can be seen better.
110181.m: A straightened ear canal gives a view of the eardrum.

110182.q: How many ear bones does each human ear have?
110182.e: In each middle ear lie the hammer, anvil and stirrup. Together they form the chain of ear bones.
110182.m: Each ear has three ear bones.

110183.q: In which part of the ear are the ear bones?
110183.e: The ear bones lie in the air-filled cavity of the middle ear. They connect the eardrum to the inner ear.
110183.m: The ear bones sit in the middle ear.

110184.q: What job do the ear bones do?
a: They pass vibrations from the eardrum to the inner ear
110184.e: The eardrum vibrates when sound hits it. The hammer, anvil and stirrup pass this vibration on to the inner ear.
110184.m: The ear bones carry sound into the inner ear.

110185.q: In what order do the ear bones pass sound on from the eardrum?
110185.e: The hammer sits on the eardrum, the anvil lies in the middle, and the stirrup presses on the oval window of the inner ear.
110185.m: Sound goes from hammer to anvil to stirrup.

110186.q: Which ear bone passes the vibrations directly to the inner ear?
110186.e: The hammer sits on the eardrum, the anvil in the middle. The stirrup is the last little bone and pushes the vibrations into the inner ear.
110186.m: The stirrup is the last ear bone before the inner ear.

110188.q: Where is the smallest skeletal muscle in the human body?
110188.e: The stapedius muscle in the middle ear is only a few millimetres long. With very loud noises it tightens and dampens the vibrations a little.
110188.m: The smallest skeletal muscle is in the middle ear.

110189.q: What happens if the stirrup in the ear becomes fixed and can no longer vibrate?
a: You can no longer smell anything
110189.e: The stirrup must vibrate freely to carry sound into the inner ear. If it becomes fixed, less sound arrives. An operation can often help.
110189.m: A fixed stirrup makes hearing worse.

110191.q: Which part of the ear is the hammer firmly attached to?
110191.e: The handle of the hammer is attached to the eardrum. When the eardrum vibrates, the hammer moves with it.
110191.m: The hammer hangs on the eardrum.

110192.q: In which part of the ear is the hammer?
110192.e: The hammer is one of the three ear bones. Together with the anvil and stirrup, it lies in the middle ear, just behind the eardrum.
110192.m: The hammer lies in the middle ear behind the eardrum.

110193.q: What is the rounded upper part of the hammer called?
110193.e: The hammer consists of a head, neck and handle. The head of the hammer lies at the top of the middle ear cavity.
110193.m: The upper part of the hammer is its head.

110194.q: Which ear bone is the hammer connected to by a small joint?
110194.e: There is a tiny joint between the hammer and the anvil. The vibration is passed on through it.
110194.m: The hammer and anvil are connected by a joint.

110195.q: What is the tiny muscle attached to the hammer in the ear for?
a: It dampens the vibration a little with loud noises
110195.e: The tensor tympani pulls on the hammer and tightens the eardrum. It then vibrates less strongly, which protects the inner ear a little from loud sounds.
110195.m: A tiny muscle on the hammer dampens loud noises a little.

110196.q: What can a doctor often see through the eardrum when looking with an otoscope?
110196.e: The eardrum is thin and slightly see-through. The attached handle of the hammer shows on it as a light stripe.
110196.m: You can see the handle of the hammer through the eardrum.

110197.q: Which of the three ear bones is the longest?
a: They are all the same length
110197.e: The hammer is around 8 to 9 millimetres long, the anvil only about 5 to 7 millimetres. The stirrup is the shortest.
110197.m: The hammer is the longest ear bone.

110198.q: Where does the hammer in the ear get its name from?
a: From its shape, which looks like a hammer
110198.e: The little bone looks like a small hammer. The anvil and stirrup are also named after their shapes.
110198.m: The hammer is named after its shape.

110199.q: How big is a newborn baby's anvil compared with an adult's?
a: About a tenth of the size
110199.e: The ear bones are already fully grown and fully turned to bone at birth. They do not grow any more after that.
110199.m: The ear bones are already fully grown at birth.

110200.q: In which part of the ear is the anvil?
110200.e: The hammer, anvil and stirrup lie in the middle ear behind the eardrum. They pass sound on to the inner ear.
110200.m: The anvil lies in the middle ear.

110201.q: Which tool is the anvil in the ear named after?
110201.e: The blacksmith puts the hot iron on an anvil and strikes it with a hammer. The ear bone has a similar shape.
110201.m: The hammer and anvil are named after blacksmith's tools.

110202.q: Which little bone is the long process of the anvil connected to?
110202.e: The long process of the anvil reaches to the head of the stirrup. There is a small joint there.
110202.m: The anvil passes the vibration on to the stirrup.

110203.q: How many ear bones does one ear have?
110203.e: In each middle ear there are three ear bones: the hammer, anvil and stirrup. They are the smallest bones in the body.
110203.m: Each ear has three ear bones.

110204.q: What job do the hammer, anvil and stirrup do?
a: They pass on the vibrations of the eardrum
They protect the ear from water
110204.e: Sound makes the eardrum vibrate. The three ear bones pass these vibrations on, amplified, to the inner ear.
110204.m: The ear bones carry sound into the inner ear.

110205.q: What happens if the connection between the anvil and stirrup is broken after an accident?
a: You hear much worse in that ear
You lose your sense of smell
110205.e: If the chain is broken, the vibration no longer reaches the inner ear properly. This causes conductive hearing loss, which can often be treated with an operation.
110205.m: A broken chain of ear bones makes hearing worse.

110206.q: How many joints does the anvil have with neighbouring ear bones?
110206.e: The anvil is connected by a joint to the hammer and by another to the stirrup. That makes two joints in total.
110206.m: The anvil is joined to two neighbours.

110207.q: In which part of the ear is the cochlea?
110207.e: The cochlea lies in the inner ear, well protected in the petrous bone. There sound is turned into nerve signals.
110207.m: The cochlea lies in the inner ear.

110208.q: What is the cochlea filled with?
110208.e: The passages of the cochlea contain fluids, the perilymph and the endolymph. The stirrup sets them in motion.

110209.q: Which cells in the cochlea turn vibrations into nerve signals?
110209.e: The hair cells carry tiny hairs. When these are bent, the cells send signals to the brain through the hearing nerve.
110209.m: Hair cells turn sound into nerve signals.

110210.q: Roughly how many turns does the human cochlea have?
110210.e: The human cochlea winds about two and a half times around a bony axis. That is why it looks like a snail shell.
110210.m: The cochlea has about two and a half turns.

110211.q: Which sounds do older people often hear worse first?
110211.e: The hair cells for high sounds sit at the start of the cochlea and wear out first. That is why older people often hear high sounds worse.
110211.m: In old age you often hear high sounds worse first.

110212.q: What is converted in the cochlea?
110212.e: In the cochlea, sound waves make a fluid vibrate. Hair cells turn this into nerve signals that go to the brain.
110212.m: The cochlea turns sound into nerve signals.

110213.q: Why is protection from noise so important for the hair cells?
a: Destroyed hair cells do not grow back in humans
Hair cells need noise to grow
Otherwise hair cells move out of the ear
Otherwise hair cells turn into bone
110213.e: Very loud noise can permanently damage the delicate hair cells. In humans they do not form again, so the hearing loss stays.
110213.m: Destroyed hair cells do not come back.

110214.q: Which device can directly stimulate the hearing nerve in the cochlea with electricity in cases of very severe hearing loss?
110214.e: A cochlear implant has an electrode that is inserted into the cochlea. It stimulates the hearing nerve with electrical signals.
110214.m: A cochlear implant does the work of the hair cells.

110215.q: How is the cochlea protected from injury?
a: It lies deep in the hard skull bone
It lies in the soft outer ear
It is surrounded by thick hair
110215.e: The cochlea lies in the petrous bone, part of the skull. It is one of the hardest bones in the body.
110215.m: The cochlea is protected in the hard skull bone.

110216.q: How many semicircular canals does each inner ear have?
110216.e: Each inner ear has three semicircular canals. Together with two little sacs they form the organ of balance.
110216.m: Each inner ear has three semicircular canals.

110217.q: Which movements do the semicircular canals detect?
110217.e: The semicircular canals react to rotation, for example when nodding, shaking or tilting your head. That way the brain knows how the head is turning.
110217.m: The semicircular canals sense turns of the head.

110218.q: How are the three semicircular canals arranged in relation to each other?
a: Roughly at right angles in three planes
One behind the other in a row
In circles one inside the other
110218.e: The three semicircular canals are roughly at right angles to each other. That way every turn in space can be detected.
110218.m: The three semicircular canals cover all three directions in space.

110219.q: What is inside the semicircular canals of the inner ear?
110219.e: The semicircular canals are filled with fluid. When you turn, it lags behind a little and bends tiny sensory hairs.
110219.m: Fluid moves in the semicircular canals.

110220.q: Where in the body are the semicircular canals?
110220.e: The semicircular canals are well protected in the skull bone in the inner ear. The cochlea lies right next to them.
110220.m: The semicircular canals lie in the inner ear.

110221.q: After spinning fast in the playground, why does everything still seem to turn even though you are standing still?
a: The fluid in the semicircular canals keeps moving
Your eyes grow for a moment
The ear canal fills with air
110221.e: Because of its inertia, the endolymph keeps flowing for a moment after you stop. So the brain reports a turn that is no longer happening.
110221.m: After spinning, the fluid in the semicircular canals keeps moving for a moment.

110222.q: Which organ tells the brain whether we are standing upright or lying down?
a: The organ of balance in the inner ear
110222.e: The organ of balance contains tiny chalk crystals that gravity pulls downwards. That way the brain senses how the head is tilted.
110222.m: The organ of balance senses gravity.

110223.q: Through which nerve do the signals from the semicircular canals reach the brain?
110223.e: The vestibular nerve (nervus vestibularis) forms the eighth cranial nerve together with the hearing nerve. It carries the signals from the semicircular canals.
110223.m: The vestibular nerve reports turns to the brain.

110224.q: Besides the semicircular canals, which senses help the brain to keep its balance?
a: The eyes and the position sense in muscles and joints
110224.e: The brain compares the messages from the organ of balance with what the eyes see and what muscles and joints report. That is why you wobble more with your eyes closed.
110224.m: Balance comes from several senses working together.

110225.q: Which two spaces does the Eustachian tube connect?
a: The middle ear and the upper throat
The outer ear and the mouth
The inner ear and the brain
The ear canal and the nose
110225.e: The Eustachian tube, also called the auditory tube, leads from the middle ear cavity to the upper throat behind the nose.
110225.m: The Eustachian tube connects the middle ear and the throat.

110226.q: What is the Eustachian tube mainly for?
a: Balancing the pressure in the middle ear
110226.e: When it opens, air can flow into or out of the middle ear. That way the pressure is the same on both sides of the eardrum.

110227.q: What is another name for the Eustachian tube?
110227.e: The Eustachian tube is also called the auditory tube. It connects the middle ear with the upper throat.
110227.m: The Eustachian tube is also called the auditory tube.

110228.q: What helps when your ears start to feel blocked as a plane comes in to land?
a: Holding your breath for a long time
110228.e: When you swallow or yawn, the Eustachian tube opens briefly. This balances the pressure in the middle ear.

110229.q: How do divers balance the pressure in their ears?
a: Pinch their nose and gently push air in
Hold their breath for a long time
110229.e: With your nose pinched, you gently push air through the Eustachian tube into the middle ear. This balances the pressure.
110229.m: You can balance ear pressure by pinching your nose.

110230.q: Why do young children get middle ear infections more often than adults?
a: Their Eustachian tube is shorter and flatter
They do not have an eardrum yet
Their ear canal is full of water
110230.e: In children the Eustachian tube is shorter, narrower and lies flatter. Germs from the throat can get into the middle ear more easily.
110230.m: A short, flat Eustachian tube makes middle ear infections more likely.

110231.q: Why does your ear often feel dull and blocked when you have a bad cold?
110231.e: With a cold, the lining swells and closes the Eustachian tube. Then the pressure can no longer balance out.
110231.m: A blocked Eustachian tube makes the ear feel dull.

110232.q: Roughly how long is the Eustachian tube in adults?
110232.e: In adults the Eustachian tube is around 3.5 centimetres long. Part of it is bone, the larger part is cartilage.
110232.m: The Eustachian tube is only a few centimetres long.

a: A noise in the ear with no outside source
An inflammation of the outer ear
A loud echo in the mountains
110233.e: With tinnitus you hear whistling, rushing or humming, even though no matching sound is coming from outside.
110233.m: Tinnitus is a noise in the ear that only you can hear.

110234.q: Which language does the word “tinnitus” come from?
110234.e: The word comes from the Latin “tinnire”, which means “to ring”.

110235.q: What is a common cause of tinnitus in teenagers?
110235.e: Very loud music in headphones or at concerts can damage the hair cells. Whistling afterwards is a warning sign.
110235.m: Loud music can cause noises in the ears.

110236.q: According to experts, after how long is tinnitus called chronic?
110236.e: Tinnitus that lasts longer than around three months is considered chronic. Before that it is called acute tinnitus.
110236.m: Tinnitus lasting over three months is considered chronic.

110237.q: How can you best protect yourself from tinnitus at a loud concert?
a: With ear protection and distance from the speakers
By standing as close to the speakers as possible
110237.e: Ear protection lowers the sound level in the ear. The further you are from the loudspeakers, the quieter it also gets.
110237.m: Ear protection and distance protect your ears.

110238.q: Is tinnitus a disease in itself or a symptom?
110238.e: Tinnitus is a sign of illness. It can occur, for example, after noise, with sudden hearing loss or with stress.
110238.m: Tinnitus is a symptom, not a disease in itself.

110239.q: What helps many people with long-lasting tinnitus to live better with the noise?
a: Learning to pay less attention to the noise
Blocking their ears with cotton wool for ever
110239.e: With chronic tinnitus, people learn in therapy to pay less attention to the noise. The brain often gets used to it this way.
110239.m: You can learn to pay less attention to tinnitus.

110240.q: What is tinnitus called that only the person affected can hear and nobody else can measure?
110240.e: Almost all ear noises are subjective and arise in the hearing pathway. Objective tinnitus is rare, for example a rushing of blood that others can hear.

110241.q: When do many people affected notice their tinnitus most strongly?
a: In quiet surroundings, for example when falling asleep
110241.e: In silence there are no other sounds to cover the tinnitus. That is why it is often most bothersome in bed at night.
110241.m: In silence, an ear noise is especially noticeable.

a: The length of the ear canal
110242.e: Decibels show how loud a sound is. Pitch, on the other hand, is measured in hertz.

110243.q: Which sound level roughly matches the hearing threshold of a healthy young person?
110243.e: 0 decibels does not mean silence; it is roughly the quietest sound that a healthy young ear can just hear at 1,000 hertz.
110243.m: 0 decibels is at the hearing threshold.

110244.q: Roughly how loud is a normal conversation?
110244.e: A normal conversation at a distance of one metre is around 60 decibels. A vacuum cleaner, at around 70 to 80 decibels, is much louder.

110245.q: Roughly from what sound level does sound start to hurt your ears?
110245.e: The pain threshold is around 120 to 130 decibels, about as loud as a jet plane close up.

110246.q: Why is there an upper volume limit at concerts in Switzerland?
a: So that the musicians use less electricity
So that the loudspeakers last longer
So that the drinks stay cool
110246.e: Very loud music over a long time can permanently damage hearing. That is why a regulation limits the sound level at events.
110246.m: Concerts have a volume limit to protect people's ears.

110247.q: What is the best way to protect your hearing at a loud concert?
a: With a hat over your eyes
110247.e: Earplugs reduce the sound by many decibels. Keeping your distance from the loudspeakers and taking breaks somewhere quiet also help.
110247.m: Ear protection lowers the volume in your ear.

110248.q: Why can listening to music through headphones for a long time at high volume damage your hearing?
a: The louder and longer the sound, the more hair cells are damaged
Headphones cool down the inner ear
110248.e: For hearing damage, what counts is the sound dose made up of level and time. Even from about 85 decibels over a long time, the hair cells can suffer.
110248.m: Loud music does more harm the longer it lasts.

110249.e: Quiet whispering is around 30 decibels, so it is much quieter than a normal conversation.

a: A sudden loss of hearing, usually in one ear
Slow hearing loss in old age
110250.e: With sudden hearing loss, you suddenly hear worse or hardly at all in one ear, usually for no obvious reason.
110250.m: Sudden hearing loss is hearing that goes suddenly.

110251.q: Which part of the ear does sudden hearing loss affect?
110251.e: Sudden hearing loss is a disorder in the inner ear, that is, in the cochlea with its hair cells.
110251.m: Sudden hearing loss happens in the inner ear.

110252.q: What feeling do people often describe with sudden hearing loss?
a: As if there were cotton wool in the ear
As if the ear were itching
As if the ear were ice-cold
As if they could hear better
110252.e: Many feel a dull pressure, as if there were cotton wool in the ear. Often there is also a noise in the ear.
110252.m: Sudden hearing loss often feels like cotton wool in the ear.

110253.q: What should you do if you suddenly can hardly hear anything in one ear?
a: Rinse the ear with cotton buds
110253.e: Sudden hearing loss should be checked by a doctor soon. That way other causes can be ruled out and treatment can be started.
110253.m: With sudden hearing loss, you go to the doctor soon.

110254.q: Which medicine is often used for sudden hearing loss?
110254.e: Cortisone is meant to reduce inflammation and swelling in the inner ear. It is the most common treatment for sudden hearing loss.
110254.m: Sudden hearing loss is often treated with cortisone.

110255.q: Which ear symptom often also occurs with sudden hearing loss?
a: Hair growing in the ear canal
110255.e: Many people with sudden hearing loss also hear whistling or rushing, that is, tinnitus.
110255.m: Sudden hearing loss often comes with a noise in the ear.

110256.q: How is sudden hearing loss different from acoustic trauma caused by a bang?
a: With sudden hearing loss, usually no cause can be found
With sudden hearing loss you hear better
Acoustic trauma only affects the nose
110256.e: Acoustic trauma has a clear cause, for example a firework close to the ear. With sudden hearing loss, the reason is usually not found.
110256.m: With sudden hearing loss, the cause usually stays unknown.

110257.q: How does mild sudden hearing loss turn out in many cases?
a: The ear always stops working completely
110257.e: In mild cases, hearing often improves within days or weeks, even without treatment. It should still be checked by a doctor.
110257.m: Mild sudden hearing loss often heals by itself.

110258.q: Why do you easily feel sick when reading in the car?
a: Your eyes and sense of balance report different things
There is too little light in the car
110258.e: Your eyes see a still book, but the organ of balance in your ear feels movement. This contradiction can make you feel sick.
110258.m: Travel sickness happens when the senses report different things.

110259.q: At what age does sudden hearing loss happen most often?
110259.e: Sudden hearing loss can happen at any age. It most often affects adults around 50; in children it is rare.
110259.m: Sudden hearing loss mostly affects middle-aged adults.

110260.q: Which is a typical sign of travel sickness?
110260.e: Typical signs are feeling sick, looking pale, cold sweat and being sick. When the movement stops, the symptoms usually go away soon.
110260.m: Travel sickness makes you feel sick.

110261.q: What helps against travel sickness in the car?
a: Looking out of the window into the distance
110261.e: If you look forwards into the distance, you see the movement that the organ of balance feels. Then the senses match better.
110261.m: Looking into the distance helps against travel sickness.

110262.q: Where is the best place to sit on a ship if you tend to get seasick?
a: In the middle of the ship
Right at the front in the bow
Right at the top of the mast
Right at the back in the stern
110262.e: In the middle of the ship it rocks the least. At the front and back the up and down movements are stronger.
110262.m: In the middle of a ship it rocks the least.

110263.q: What is the travel sickness called that astronauts can get when weightless?
110263.e: When weightless, the organ of balance is missing the usual signals from gravity. Many space travellers feel sick in the first few days.
110263.m: You can get travel sick in space too.

110264.q: Which age group is especially often affected by travel sickness?
110264.e: Children between about 2 and 12 are especially prone to it. Babies, on the other hand, are rarely affected.
110264.m: Schoolchildren get travel sick especially often.

110265.q: Which plant is often used as a natural remedy for travel sickness?
110265.e: Ginger has been used against nausea for a long time. Studies show a slight effect in some people.
110265.m: Ginger can help with travel sickness.

110266.q: What does spinning dizziness feel like?
a: As if everything were turning in a circle
As if you were very tired
As if your legs had gone to sleep
110266.e: With spinning dizziness, your surroundings or your own body seem to turn, like after a ride on a merry-go-round.
110266.m: With spinning dizziness, everything seems to turn.

110267.q: Why do you still feel dizzy for a moment after a merry-go-round ride?
a: The fluid in the organ of balance keeps turning
Blood only flows into your feet
Your eyes go blind for a moment
110267.e: In the inner ear there are semicircular canals with fluid. After stopping, the fluid keeps moving for a moment, and the brain reports a turn.
110267.m: After spinning, the fluid in the inner ear keeps moving.

110268.q: What helps if you feel dizzy after spinning?
a: Sitting down and looking at a fixed point
Running quickly in the other direction
110268.e: Sitting prevents falls. A fixed point to look at helps the brain find its bearings again.
110268.m: When dizzy, you sit down and look at a fixed point.

110269.q: Why should you not ride a bike if you suddenly feel spinning dizziness?
a: You can lose your balance and fall
110269.e: With spinning dizziness, your sense of balance is no longer right. Anyone who rides a bike then can easily fall.
110269.m: You do not ride a bike when you have spinning dizziness.

110270.q: Which complaint often also occurs with strong spinning dizziness?
110270.e: When the organ of balance and the eyes do not match, many people feel sick. Some even have to be sick.
110270.m: Strong spinning dizziness often makes you feel sick.

110271.q: How do ballet dancers stop themselves getting dizzy during pirouettes?
a: They fix their gaze on a point
110271.e: With “spotting”, the gaze stays on one point for as long as possible and then the head turns quickly. This reduces the dizziness.
110271.m: A fixed point to look at helps against spinning dizziness.
