111018.e: The sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems work as opposites. The sympathetic steps on the accelerator, the parasympathetic brakes and supports recovery and digestion.
111018.m: The parasympathetic nervous system is the opposite of the sympathetic.

111019.q: When is the parasympathetic nervous system especially active?
111019.e: The parasympathetic nervous system is also called the rest nerve. It looks after recovery and stimulates digestion.
111019.m: The parasympathetic nervous system is at work at rest.

111020.q: How does the parasympathetic nervous system affect the heartbeat?
111020.e: Through the vagus nerve, the parasympathetic nervous system slows the heart. That way it beats more slowly at rest.
111020.m: The parasympathetic nervous system calms the heart.

111021.q: How does the parasympathetic nervous system affect the stomach and gut?
111021.e: The parasympathetic nervous system stimulates the production of digestive juices and the movements of the gut.
111021.m: The parasympathetic nervous system gets digestion going.

111022.q: How does the parasympathetic nervous system change breathing?
a: It becomes faster and more hectic
It has nothing to do with it
111022.e: The parasympathetic nervous system brings calm and recovery. Breathing and heartbeat become slower.
111022.m: The parasympathetic nervous system calms breathing.

111023.q: How do the pupils change under the influence of the parasympathetic nervous system?
111023.e: The parasympathetic nervous system tightens the ring muscle of the iris. This makes the pupil narrower.
111023.m: The parasympathetic nervous system makes the pupils narrow.

111024.q: What happens to the flow of saliva when the parasympathetic nervous system is active?
a: It has nothing to do with it
111024.e: The parasympathetic nervous system prepares the body for digestion. That is why the mouth makes more saliva.
111024.m: The parasympathetic nervous system stimulates the flow of saliva.

111025.q: What is the relationship between the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems called?
111025.e: The two have opposite effects on most organs; for example, one speeds up the heart and the other slows it down.
111025.m: The sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems are opponents.

111026.q: What happens in the brain during an epileptic seizure?
a: Many nerve cells fire at the same time and excessively
A blood vessel in the brain bursts
The brain gets too little sugar
The membranes around the brain become inflamed
111026.e: During a seizure, many nerve cells send signals out of control at the same time. This can lead to jerking movements or loss of awareness.
111026.m: In an epileptic seizure, many nerve cells fire at the same time.

111027.q: What should you never do when another person is having a seizure?
a: Cushion their head with something soft
Time how long the seizure lasts
111027.e: Objects in the mouth can break teeth or block breathing. The right thing is to protect the person from injury and stay with them.
111027.m: During a seizure, nothing should go into the person's mouth.

111028.q: Which organ is affected by epilepsy?
111028.e: Epilepsy is a condition of the brain. An EEG measures brain waves to detect it.
111028.m: Epilepsy is a condition of the brain.

111029.q: What are medicines called that are meant to prevent epileptic seizures?
111029.e: Anti-epileptics make nerve cells less excitable. With them, many people with epilepsy become free of seizures.

111030.q: Which emergency number do you call in Switzerland if a seizure lasts longer than five minutes?
111030.e: 144 is the number of the ambulance service. 117 is the police, 118 the fire brigade and 1414 the Rega air rescue.
111030.m: In Switzerland you reach the ambulance service on 144.

111031.e: Epilepsy is a condition of the brain and is not passed from person to person.

111032.q: Which stimulus can trigger a seizure in some people with epilepsy?
111032.e: In photosensitive epilepsy, flashing lights or flickering screens can trigger seizures.
111032.m: Flickering light can trigger seizures in some people.

111033.q: What can a small epileptic seizure look like in children?
a: The child stares blankly for a moment and does not react
The child sneezes several times in a row
The child has tummy ache after eating
111033.e: In a so-called absence seizure, the child stares blankly for a few seconds. Then they carry on as if nothing had happened.
111033.m: A short blank stare can be a small seizure.

111035.q: What does a migraine headache typically feel like?
a: Throbbing and often on one side
Slightly pressing all over the head
111035.e: Migraine usually shows itself as a strong, throbbing headache that often affects only one side of the head.
111035.m: Migraine often throbs on one side of the head.

111036.q: Which other complaints often occur with migraine?
111036.e: During an attack, many people feel sick and are sensitive to light and noise.
111036.m: With migraine, light and noise are often bothersome.

111037.q: What are the visual disturbances called, such as flickering or zigzag lines, that sometimes come before a migraine?
111037.e: Some people experience an aura before the headache, usually with flickering or flashes of light in their field of vision.
111037.m: An aura can announce a migraine attack.

111038.q: According to the medical definition, how long does an untreated migraine attack last in adults?
111038.e: According to the international classification of headaches, a migraine attack without treatment lasts 4 to 72 hours.
111038.m: A migraine attack can last up to three days.

111039.q: Who is more often affected by migraine in adulthood?
111039.e: Adult women suffer from migraine about two to three times as often as men.
111039.m: Women get migraines more often than men.

111040.q: What helps many people during a migraine attack?
111040.e: Because light and noise are bothersome, many people go to a quiet, dark room and lie down.
111040.m: Rest and darkness help with migraine.

111041.q: What is a headache diary for in migraine?
111041.e: If you note down attacks, sleep, food and activities, it is easier to see what can trigger a migraine, such as lack of sleep or skipped meals.
111041.m: A headache diary helps to find migraine triggers.

111042.q: Where does the word “migraine” come from?
a: From the Greek word for “half skull”
111042.e: Migraine goes back to the Greek “hemikrania”, which means “half skull”. That fits the pain, which is often on one side.
111042.m: The word migraine originally means “half skull”.

111043.q: Unlike migraine, what does the common tension headache usually feel like?
111043.e: Tension headache is often described as a tight band around the head. It is usually milder than migraine and does not get worse with movement.
111043.m: Tension headache usually presses on both sides of the head.

111044.q: Roughly how fast is light in glass?
111044.e: In glass, light is about a third slower than in a vacuum. The refractive index of glass is about 1.5, and 300,000 ÷ 1.5 gives 200,000 km per second.
111044.m: In glass, light is much slower than in a vacuum.

111045.q: Which letter stands for the speed of light in physics?
111045.e: The symbol c comes from the Latin word “celeritas”, which means swiftness.
111045.m: The speed of light has the symbol c.

111046.q: Roughly how many times could light travel round the Earth's equator of 40,000 km in one second?
111046.e: In one second light travels about 300,000 km. 300,000 ÷ 40,000 = 7.5.
111046.m: In one second, light could go more than seven times round the Earth.

111047.q: According to Einstein's theory of relativity, can a spaceship reach the speed of light in a vacuum?
a: No, no object with mass can reach it
Yes, if it is built very light
111047.e: The closer an object gets to the speed of light, the more energy it needs to speed up further. To reach it, it would need infinite energy.
111047.m: Nothing with mass can go as fast as light.

111048.q: How does the speed of light change when light passes from air into water?
111048.e: In water light only travels at about 225,000 km per second. That is why it is refracted at the water's surface.
111048.m: Light is slower in water than in air.

111049.q: How was it first shown in the 17th century that light needs time to travel?
a: By observing a moon of Jupiter
111049.e: The astronomer Ole Rømer noticed that Jupiter's moon Io was eclipsed earlier or later depending on its distance from Earth. Light needed more time for the longer path.
111049.m: A moon of Jupiter revealed that light needs time.

111050.q: A radio signal takes 10 minutes to reach a space probe. Roughly how far away is the probe?
111050.e: Radio waves travel at the speed of light. 10 minutes are 600 seconds, and 600 times 300,000 km gives 180,000,000 km.
111050.m: Radio signals are as fast as light.

111051.q: Which unit is defined today using the speed of light?
111051.e: Since 1983 a metre has been the distance light travels in a vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second.
111051.m: The metre is defined by the speed of light.

111052.q: What does the unit light-year measure?
111052.e: A light-year is the distance light travels in a vacuum in one year. Despite the word “year”, it is a unit of length.
111052.m: A light-year is a distance, not a time.

111053.q: Roughly how many kilometres long is a light-year?
111053.e: 300,000 km/s times about 31.6 million seconds in a year gives about 9.46 trillion kilometres.
111053.m: A light-year is almost ten trillion kilometres.

111054.q: Roughly how far away is Proxima Centauri, the nearest star after the sun?
111054.e: Proxima Centauri is about 4.2 light-years from us. So its light takes over four years to reach Earth.
111054.m: The nearest star after the sun is just over four light-years away.

111055.q: Why are you looking into the past when you look at very distant stars?
a: Because their light took a very long time to reach us
Because the Earth spins more slowly
111055.e: We see a star as it was when its light set off. For a star 100 light-years away, that was 100 years ago.
111055.m: Looking at distant stars is looking into the past.

111056.q: Roughly how large is the diameter of the disc of our Milky Way?
111056.e: Depending on the method of measurement, the disc of the Milky Way is about 100,000 light-years across or a little more.
111056.m: The Milky Way is about 100,000 light-years wide.

111057.q: A star is 10 light-years away. When did the light we see today leave the star?
111057.e: Light travels exactly one light-year in one year. So for 10 light-years it needs 10 years.
111057.m: For each light-year of distance, the light travels for one year.

111058.q: Which abbreviation is used in English for the unit light-year?
111058.e: In English the light-year is abbreviated as ly; in German it is Lj, from “Lichtjahr”.

111059.q: How does light travel in a uniform substance such as air?
111059.e: In a uniform substance light always travels in straight lines. That is why you can't see round a corner.

111060.q: What is a ray of light in physics?
a: A model for the path of light
111060.e: A ray of light is drawn as a straight line with an arrow. It is an imagined model that describes the path of light.
111060.m: A ray of light is a model for the path of light.

111061.q: What do you call many rays of light coming from a lamp through an opening?
111061.e: A beam of light is made of many rays. It can be parallel, spreading out or coming together.
111061.m: Many rays of light together form a beam.

111062.q: Which of these is a source that gives off its own light?
111062.e: The sun produces its own light. The moon, mirrors and walls are only lit up and reflect light.
111062.m: The sun shines by itself; the moon is only lit up.

111063.q: Why can we see an object that does not give off its own light?
a: It reflects light into our eyes
It stores light from the day before
It produces its own heat rays
111063.e: We only see when light enters our eyes. Lit objects reflect part of the light, and this light reaches the eye.
111063.m: We see things because light from them enters our eyes.

111064.q: Why can you see the beam of a headlight in fog, but hardly in clear air?
a: Water droplets scatter light sideways into the eye
111064.e: Fog droplets scatter part of the light to the side. This light reaches our eyes, so the path of the beam becomes visible.
111064.m: You only see a beam of light when particles scatter light towards you.

111065.q: What happens when two rays of light cross in the air?
a: They cancel each other out completely
111065.e: Rays of light do not affect each other when they cross. After the crossing point, each carries on in its original direction.
111065.m: Crossing rays of light do not disturb each other.

111066.q: Can light travel through empty space?
a: Yes, light doesn't need a material
111066.e: Unlike sound, light does not need a material to travel through. That is why the light of the sun and stars reaches us through the vacuum.
111066.m: Light can also travel through a vacuum.

111067.q: Which light source is best for showing a very narrow ray of light that hardly spreads?
111067.e: A laser sends out a very narrow, almost parallel beam of light. Candles and lamps, on the other hand, shine in all directions.
111067.m: A laser produces a particularly narrow ray of light.

111068.q: A ray of light hits a flat mirror at an angle of incidence of 60 degrees. What angle does the reflected ray make with the mirror surface?
111068.e: The angle of reflection is also 60 degrees and is measured from the normal. That leaves 90 − 60 = 30 degrees to the mirror surface.
111068.m: The normal and the mirror surface always form a right angle.

111069.q: A ray of light hits a mirror at an angle of incidence of 30 degrees. What is the angle of reflection?
111069.e: According to the law of reflection, the angles of incidence and reflection are equal, so the angle of reflection is also 30 degrees.
111069.m: The reflected ray leaves the mirror at the same angle.

111070.q: A ray of light makes an angle of 40 degrees with the mirror surface. What is the angle of reflection?
111070.e: The angles are measured from the normal, not from the mirror surface. So the angle of incidence is 90 − 40 = 50 degrees, and the angle of reflection is the same.
111070.m: In the law of reflection, angles are always measured from the normal.

111071.q: What is the angle between the reflected ray and the normal called?
111071.e: The reflected ray makes the angle of reflection with the normal. The incoming ray makes the angle of incidence with the normal.
111071.m: The angle of reflection lies between the reflected ray and the normal.

111072.q: How do the incoming ray, the normal and the reflected ray relate to each other?
a: They are all at right angles to each other
They lie in three different planes
111072.e: The law of reflection also says that the incoming ray, the normal and the reflected ray lie in the same plane.
111072.m: Incoming ray, normal and reflected ray lie in one plane.

111073.q: A ray of light hits a flat mirror at right angles. Where is it reflected?
111073.e: The ray travels exactly along the normal. According to the law of reflection, it must therefore go back the same way.
111073.m: A ray hitting at right angles is reflected straight back.

111074.q: You can see your friend's eyes in a mirror. What is then certainly true?
a: She can also see your eyes in the mirror
She can't see you at all
111074.e: Light paths are reversible. If light travels from her eyes to yours, it can also travel the same way in reverse.
111074.m: A light path can also be travelled in the opposite direction.

111075.q: Does the law of reflection also apply to a rough surface such as paper?
a: Yes, on every tiny part of the surface
111075.e: A rough surface is made of many tiny surfaces at different angles. The law of reflection applies to each, but their normals point in different directions.
111075.m: The law of reflection also applies to every tiny part of a rough surface.

111076.q: Between which two lines is the angle of incidence measured?
a: Between the incoming ray and the normal
Between the incoming ray and the mirror surface
Between the normal and the mirror surface
Between the mirror and the floor
111076.e: The angle of incidence lies between the incoming ray of light and the normal at the point where it hits, not between the ray and the surface.
111076.m: The angle of incidence is measured between the ray and the normal.

111077.q: What is meant by the normal when talking about the angle of incidence?
a: A line at right angles to the surface where the ray hits
A line parallel to the surface
111077.e: The normal is an imaginary line that stands exactly perpendicular, at a right angle, to the surface at the point where the ray hits.
111077.m: The normal is perpendicular to the surface.

111078.q: What is the angle of incidence when a ray of light hits a surface exactly at right angles?
111078.e: When hitting at right angles, the ray lines up with the normal. So the angle between them is 0 degrees.
111078.m: Hitting at right angles means an angle of incidence of zero degrees.

111079.q: What is the largest possible angle of incidence on a mirror?
111079.e: A ray that skims almost parallel over the surface makes almost 90 degrees with the normal. The angle of incidence can't be bigger.
111079.m: The angle of incidence is always between zero and ninety degrees.

111080.q: Which Greek letter is often used for the angle of incidence?
111080.e: In many school books the angle of incidence is called α (alpha) and the angle of reflection α' or β.
111080.m: The angle of incidence is often called alpha.

111081.q: Which school tool is easiest for measuring the angle of incidence on a drawing?
111081.e: A protractor has a scale for angles. You place the centre on the point where the ray hits and read off the angle between the ray and the normal.
111081.m: Angles are measured with a protractor.

111082.q: What happens to a ray of light that passes exactly at right angles from air into water?
a: It carries on without changing direction
It is bent sharply to the side
It turns at a right angle
111082.e: If light hits the boundary at right angles, it is not bent when passing into another substance, only slowed down.
111082.m: Light hitting at right angles is not refracted.

111083.q: How does the angle of reflection change if you increase the angle of incidence by 10 degrees?
111083.e: Because the angles of incidence and reflection are always equal, they always change by the same amount.
111083.m: If the angle of incidence grows, the angle of reflection grows by the same amount.

111084.q: What is put on the back of the glass in an ordinary glass mirror?
a: A very thin layer of metal
111084.e: Today a wafer-thin layer of silver or aluminium is usually used. The smooth metal reflects almost all light in one direction, and the glass protects the layer.
111084.m: A mirror reflects thanks to a thin layer of metal.

111085.q: You stand 2 metres in front of a flat mirror. How far are you from your reflection?
111085.e: The image seems to be 2 metres behind the mirror. So from you to the image it is 2 + 2 = 4 metres.
111085.m: The distance to your reflection is twice the distance to the mirror.

111086.q: A ray of light is to be turned through 90 degrees with a flat mirror. What angle of incidence does the ray need?
111086.e: The angle of incidence and the angle of reflection together make the angle between the two rays. 45 + 45 = 90 degrees.
111086.m: To turn a ray through 90 degrees, it must hit at 45 degrees.

111087.q: Why is the image in a flat mirror called a virtual image?
a: It cannot be caught on a screen
It can only be seen on a computer
111087.e: No light arrives behind the mirror. The image only appears because the eye extends the reflected rays backwards in straight lines.
111087.m: A virtual image cannot be caught on a screen.

111088.q: Why is the word AMBULANCE written in mirror writing on many ambulances?
a: So it reads correctly in the rear-view mirror
111088.e: A mirror swaps the sides. The mirror writing appears the right way round in the rear-view mirror of the car in front.
111088.m: Mirror writing reads correctly in a mirror.

111089.q: How tall must a wall mirror be, at least, for you to see your whole body in it?
111089.e: According to the law of reflection, light from your head and feet hits the mirror halfway between your eyes and head, and halfway between your eyes and feet. So half your height is enough.
111089.m: For a full reflection, a mirror half your height is enough.

111090.q: Which device uses two flat mirrors to see over an obstacle?
111090.e: In a periscope, two angled mirrors turn the light twice. This lets you look above the water's surface from a submarine, for example.
111090.m: A periscope uses two mirrors to see round obstacles.

111091.q: You walk towards a flat mirror at 1 metre per second. How fast do you get closer to your reflection?
111091.e: You approach the mirror at 1 m/s, and your image approaches the mirror from behind at 1 m/s too. Together that makes 1 + 1 = 2 m/s.
111091.m: Your reflection comes towards you as fast as you walk towards the mirror.

111092.q: How many images of a candle do you see between two mirrors set at a right angle?
111092.e: With two mirrors at an angle w, there are 360 ÷ w − 1 images. At 90 degrees that is 360 ÷ 90 − 1 = 3 images.
111092.m: Two mirrors at a right angle show three images.

111093.q: Why is a satellite dish curved inwards?
a: It focuses the signals onto the receiver at the focal point
It is more stable in the wind
It protects the receiver from rain
It scatters the signals in all directions
111093.e: For radio waves a satellite dish works like a concave mirror. The weak signals are concentrated onto the receiver head at the focal point.
111093.m: A satellite dish collects signals like a concave mirror.

111094.q: What happens to parallel light hitting a concave mirror?
a: It is collected at the focal point
It is scattered in all directions
111094.e: A concave mirror reflects rays parallel to the axis so that they meet at one point, the focal point.
111094.m: A concave mirror collects parallel light at the focal point.

111095.q: A concave mirror has a radius of curvature of 40 centimetres. Roughly what is its focal length?
111095.e: For a spherical concave mirror, the focal length is about half the radius of curvature: 40 ÷ 2 = 20 centimetres.
111095.m: The focal length of a concave mirror is about half the radius of curvature.

111096.q: Where must the bulb sit in a headlight with a concave mirror so that a parallel beam is produced?
a: At the edge of the mirror
111096.e: Light from the focal point is reflected parallel by the concave mirror. This is how torches and car headlights shine far.
111096.m: A lamp at the focal point of a concave mirror gives parallel light.

111097.q: What can happen if you hold dark paper at the focal point of a concave mirror pointing at the sun?
111097.e: The concave mirror collects sunlight from a large area into a small point. It gets so hot there that paper can start to burn.
111097.m: At the focal point of a concave mirror, sunlight can start a fire.

111098.q: Why do you see yourself magnified in a make-up mirror?
a: It is a concave mirror and your face is within the focal length
111098.e: If an object is closer to a concave mirror than the focal point, an upright, magnified, virtual image is formed.
111098.m: Close to a concave mirror you see yourself magnified.

111099.q: How do you see yourself in the inside of a spoon when you hold it at arm's length?
a: Exactly as in the bathroom mirror
111099.e: The inside of the spoon works like a concave mirror. If your face is further away than the focal point, an upside-down image is formed.
111099.m: A concave mirror can turn images upside down.

111100.q: In which astronomy instrument does a large concave mirror collect the light of distant stars?
111100.e: Reflecting telescopes use a large concave mirror to collect as much light as possible. This makes even very faint objects in the sky visible.
111100.m: Reflecting telescopes use a concave mirror to collect light.

111101.q: What shape does a concave mirror have that collects parallel light at exactly one point?
111101.e: In a parabolic mirror, all rays parallel to the axis meet exactly at the focal point. A spherical concave mirror only manages this roughly.
111101.m: A parabolic mirror collects parallel light exactly at the focal point.

111102.q: How does your image in a convex mirror change when you move away from it?
111102.e: In a convex mirror, the further away the object, the smaller the image. It always stays upright.
111102.m: The further you are from a convex mirror, the smaller the image.

111103.q: What is the image like in a convex mirror?
111103.e: A convex mirror always produces an upright, smaller and virtual image.
111103.m: A convex mirror shows everything smaller and upright.

111104.q: What happens to parallel light hitting a convex mirror?
a: It is collected at one point
111104.e: A convex mirror reflects parallel rays as if they came from a point behind the mirror. The light spreads out.
111104.m: A convex mirror spreads light out.

111105.q: Why are convex mirrors often hung at exits where it's hard to see?
a: They show a wide field of view
They are cheaper than flat mirrors
111105.e: Because the convex mirror makes the image smaller, a much bigger stretch of road fits into it.
111105.m: A convex mirror gives a wide view.

111106.q: Why do cars in a curved wing mirror seem further away than they really are?
111106.e: The smaller image makes cars look smaller and therefore further away. That is why some mirrors carry a warning.
111106.m: In a convex mirror things look further away than they are.

111107.q: Which everyday object works like a convex mirror?
111107.e: The outside of a shiny ball curves outwards. In it you see a small, upright image of the whole room.
111107.m: A shiny ball reflects like a convex mirror.

111108.q: Where is the focal point of a convex mirror?
a: In front of the mirror in the middle
111108.e: The reflected rays seem to come from a point behind the mirror. This is called a virtual focal point.
111108.m: The focal point of a convex mirror seems to lie behind it.

111109.q: What is the technical term for a mirror that curves outwards?
111109.e: Convex means curved outwards. A mirror curved inwards is called a concave mirror, and a flat one a plane mirror.
111109.m: A mirror curving outwards is a convex mirror.

a: Light is reflected in many directions
Light is reflected in one direction
111110.e: On a rough surface, light is scattered in all directions. This is also called scattered reflection.
111110.m: In diffuse reflection light is scattered in all directions.

111111.q: On which surface is light mainly reflected diffusely?
111111.e: Under a microscope, paper is rough and fibrous. So it reflects light in many directions instead of showing a mirror image.
111111.m: Rough surfaces such as paper reflect diffusely.

111112.q: Why can you see a book from every direction in a room?
a: Because it scatters light diffusely in all directions
Because it gives off its own light
Because it creates a mirror image
111112.e: A lit book sends part of the light in all directions. So light reaches our eyes from every position.
111112.m: Thanks to diffuse reflection we see objects from everywhere.

111113.q: What is the opposite of diffuse reflection called, as it happens on a mirror?
111113.e: In specular reflection, parallel light is reflected back parallel. This creates a clear mirror image.
111113.m: A mirror reflects specularly, a rough surface diffusely.

111114.q: Why does a wet road often dazzle more at night than a dry one?
a: The water reflects light in a more focused way
Wet tarmac gives off its own light
Wet roads are a lighter colour
111114.e: The film of water fills the rough patches and acts like a mirror. The headlight beams are then reflected together in one direction.
111114.m: A wet road acts like a mirror and dazzles.

111115.q: Why should you wear sunglasses in the snow in the mountains?
a: Snow reflects a lot of sunlight
Snow gives off its own light
111115.e: Fresh snow scatters most of the sunlight back. Together with stronger UV light at altitude, this can damage the eyes.
111115.m: Snow reflects a lot of light and can dazzle the eyes.

111116.q: Why is a cinema screen made of matt white fabric?
a: So that everyone in the audience can see the picture
So that it swallows the light
So that it gives off its own light
So that it works like a mirror
111116.e: A matt screen reflects diffusely. So light from every point of the picture reaches every seat in the cinema.
111116.m: A matt screen spreads the picture to every seat.

111117.q: How does the light of the full moon reach us?
a: It reflects light like a mirror
It stores light from the day
111117.e: The moon does not shine by itself. Its rough, dusty surface scatters sunlight in all directions, including towards Earth.
111117.m: The moon scatters the sun's light towards us.

111118.q: Does a reflector glow in total darkness without any other light?
a: No, it needs light from outside
Yes, if it was in the sun before
111118.e: A reflector is not a light source. It only reflects light that falls on it, for example from car headlights.
111118.m: A reflector only shines when light falls on it.

111119.q: Why does a reflector look dark to a pedestrian beside the road but bright to the driver?
a: It sends light back mainly towards the headlight
Car headlights are a different colour
111119.e: A reflector sends light back to the light source in a narrow cone. Someone standing off to the side hardly gets any of it.
111119.m: A reflector shines mainly for whoever lights it up.

111120.q: How are the small mirror surfaces arranged in a cat's eye reflector?
a: Three surfaces are each at right angles to each other
There is only one single surface
111120.e: Each element is built like the corner of a cube. After three reflections the light goes back parallel. This is called a corner reflector.
111120.m: A cat's eye is made of many tiny cube corners.

111121.q: What is often mixed into road marking paint so the lines look bright in headlights at night?
111121.e: The little glass balls work like many tiny reflectors and send the headlight beams back to the car.
111121.m: Glass beads make road markings easy to see at night.

111122.q: Which astronauts set up a reflector on the moon in 1969?
111122.e: Apollo 11 took a reflector to the moon. Using laser beams that it reflects, the distance to the moon is still measured today.
111122.m: A reflector on the moon helps to measure its distance.

111123.q: On which bicycle parts are extra yellow reflectors often fitted that move as you ride?
111123.e: Pedal reflectors move up and down as you pedal. Drivers notice this movement especially well in their headlights.
111123.m: Pedal reflectors make cyclists stand out through their movement.

111124.q: Why should pedestrians wear reflective clothing at night?
111124.e: Reflective strips send the headlight beams back. This lets pedestrians be seen from much further away than in dark clothing.
111124.m: Reflectors make pedestrians easy to see at night.

111125.q: What colour are the reflectors at the back of cars and bikes?
111125.e: Reflectors facing backwards are red, like the rear lights. That way you can tell at night that you are seeing a vehicle from behind.
111125.m: Reflectors at the back of vehicles are red.

111126.q: Which way does the image in a pinhole camera appear?
a: Upside down and reversed left to right
Upright and the right way round
Upright but reversed left to right
Upside down but the right way round
111126.e: The rays of light cross in the small hole. Light from the top lands at the bottom, light from the left lands on the right.
111126.m: A pinhole camera shows an inverted image.

111127.q: Which property of light does the pinhole camera rely on?
a: That it travels in straight lines
111127.e: Each point of the object sends light in a straight line through the hole to one point on the back wall. This creates an image without a lens.
111127.m: A pinhole camera works because light travels in straight lines.

111128.q: What happens to the image if you make the hole of a pinhole camera bigger?
111128.e: More light comes through a bigger hole, but each point of the object makes a bigger patch of light. The patches overlap and the image becomes blurred.
111128.m: A bigger hole makes the image brighter but blurrier.

111129.q: What does the Latin name “camera obscura” for the pinhole camera mean?
111129.e: Camera means room and obscura means dark. The image can only be seen well in a dark room.

111130.q: A tree is 10 m tall and 20 m from a pinhole camera. The camera is 10 cm deep. How tall is the image?
111130.e: Image height divided by object height equals camera depth divided by distance: 10 m times 0.1 m divided by 20 m gives 0.05 m, which is 5 cm.
111130.m: In a pinhole camera the image size depends on the ratio of the distances.

111131.q: How does the image change if you make the pinhole camera longer, so the screen is further from the hole?
111131.e: Behind the hole the rays of light spread further apart. The further away the screen, the bigger but also fainter the image.
111131.m: A greater distance to the screen makes the image bigger.

111132.q: What do you see on the screen if a pinhole camera has two small holes side by side?
111132.e: Each hole creates its own inverted image. So with two holes there are two slightly offset images.
111132.m: Each hole of a pinhole camera creates its own image.

111133.q: Why is a pinhole camera good for watching a solar eclipse?
a: You don't look directly at the sun
It magnifies the sun a lot
111133.e: The pinhole camera projects an image of the sun onto a screen. So you can follow the eclipse without exposing your eyes to the dangerous radiation.
111133.m: With a pinhole camera you can watch the sun without looking at it.

a: An area that no light from any source reaches
An area lit by only one lamp
The brightest part of a room
The shadow of a light bulb itself
111134.e: In the umbra, the light from all light sources is blocked by the object. That is why it is the darkest.

a: An area lit by only some of the light sources
111135.e: With two lamps, an area can be in the shadow of one but in the light of the other. It is then only partly lit.
111135.m: Only part of the light reaches the penumbra.

111136.q: What kinds of shadow form behind an object lit by a single point-like lamp?
111136.e: With a point light source there is only light or shadow. A single, sharply edged shadow forms.
111136.m: A point-like lamp makes a sharp shadow.

111137.q: How many penumbras form behind a rod lit by two lamps, if the shadows partly overlap?
111137.e: Each lamp makes its own shadow. Where they overlap is the umbra; the two remaining parts are penumbras.
111137.m: Two lamps make one umbra and two penumbras.

111138.q: In which shadow is the moon during a total lunar eclipse?
a: In the shadow of a cloud
111138.e: In a total lunar eclipse, the Earth is between the sun and the moon. The moon moves completely into the Earth's umbra.
111138.m: In a total lunar eclipse the moon is in the Earth's umbra.

111139.q: Why does the moon often look reddish during a total lunar eclipse?
a: The Earth's atmosphere bends red light into the Earth's shadow
Mars reflects its light onto the moon
111139.e: Sunlight is refracted and scattered in the Earth's atmosphere. Mainly red light gets into the umbra and faintly lights up the moon.
111139.m: Red light from the Earth's atmosphere colours the eclipsed moon.

111140.q: Where must you be to see a total solar eclipse?
a: On the night side of the Earth
111140.e: During a solar eclipse, the moon casts its shadow on the Earth. Only people in the small umbra see the sun completely covered. In the penumbra the eclipse is only partial.
111140.m: You only see a total solar eclipse in the moon's umbra.

111141.q: How does the shadow of your hand on the wall change when you hold it closer to the lamp?
111141.e: The closer your hand is to the lamp, the more light it blocks. The edges of the shadow spread further apart and the shadow gets bigger.
111141.m: The closer an object is to the lamp, the bigger its shadow.

111142.q: Why does the shadow from a large, flat lamp have a soft, blurred edge?
a: Because light comes from many points of the lamp
Because the wall swallows the light
111142.e: An extended light source consists of many points of light. At the edge, some of them reach the wall, creating a smooth change from umbra to penumbra.
111142.m: Large light sources make soft shadow edges.

111143.q: In which canton is Parc Ela?
111143.e: Parc Ela is in the canton of Grisons, in the region around the Albula valley and Surses.
111143.m: Parc Ela is a nature park in the Grisons.

111144.q: What is Parc Ela named after?
a: After a woman who founded it
111144.e: The name comes from Piz Ela, a striking peak in the Albula Alps.
111144.m: Parc Ela takes its name from Piz Ela.

111145.q: What is special about Parc Ela compared with Switzerland's other regional nature parks?
111145.e: With around 550 square kilometres, Parc Ela is the largest regional nature park in Switzerland by area.
111145.m: Parc Ela is the largest regional nature park in Switzerland.

111146.q: Which three languages are spoken in the area of Parc Ela?
111146.e: In Parc Ela people speak Romansh and German, and in Bivio also Italian. That makes it a park with three languages.
111146.m: In Parc Ela you come across three national languages.

111147.q: Which famous railway structure stands near Filisur in Parc Ela?
111147.e: The Landwasser Viaduct on the Albula line is one of the best-known structures of the Rhaetian Railway and is near Filisur.
111147.m: The Landwasser Viaduct near Filisur is a landmark of the Albula line.

111148.q: Which railway company runs the Albula line, which goes through Parc Ela?
111148.e: The Albula line belongs to the Rhaetian Railway. Together with the Bernina line, it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2008.
111148.m: The Rhaetian Railway's Albula line is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

111149.q: Which two Alpine passes are in the area of Parc Ela?
111149.e: The Albula Pass links the Albula valley with the Engadine, and the Julier Pass leads from Surses into the Upper Engadine. Both are in Parc Ela.
111149.m: The Albula Pass and the Julier Pass belong to Parc Ela.

111150.q: What is the route from Preda to Bergün known for in winter?
a: As an ice channel for bobsleighs
111150.e: In winter, the pass road between Preda and Bergün becomes a popular sledging run, and the train takes people back up.
111150.m: In winter, people sledge down the pass road between Preda and Bergün.

111151.q: Which dog breed carries the name of the Entlebuch region?
111151.e: The Entlebucher Mountain Dog is the smallest of the four Swiss mountain dogs. It originally comes from the Entlebuch and helped farmers drive their cattle.
111151.m: The Entlebucher Mountain Dog comes from the Entlebuch.

111152.q: In which canton is the UNESCO Biosphere Entlebuch?
111152.e: The Entlebuch lies in the canton of Lucerne, between Lucerne and Bern. It has been a UNESCO Biosphere since 2001.
111152.m: The UNESCO Biosphere Entlebuch is in the canton of Lucerne.

111153.q: Which kind of landscape is the UNESCO Biosphere Entlebuch especially known for?
111153.e: A large part of the area is made up of raised bogs and fens. The Entlebuch is one of the areas of Switzerland with the most bogs.
111153.m: The Entlebuch is rich in bogs.

111154.q: Which holiday resort with a ski area on the Brienzer Rothorn is in the UNESCO Biosphere Entlebuch?
111154.e: Sörenberg belongs to the municipality of Flühli and is the best-known tourist resort in the Entlebuch.
111154.m: Sörenberg is the largest holiday resort in the Entlebuch.

111155.q: What are karren, like those you can see on the limestone mountains of the Entlebuch?
a: Grooves that rainwater has eaten into the limestone
Marks left by glaciers in sand
111155.e: Rainwater slowly dissolves limestone. This creates deep grooves and cracks called karren, for example on the Schrattenflue.
111155.m: Karren are grooves in limestone washed out by rain.

111156.q: What is the aim of a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve like the Entlebuch?
a: To protect nature and do business sustainably
To move all the people out of the area
To cut down the whole forest
111156.e: People live and work in a biosphere. They are meant to preserve nature while running farms, businesses and tourism sustainably.
111156.m: A biosphere combines nature protection with sustainable business.

111157.q: What is the UNESCO programme called that the Entlebuch Biosphere belongs to?
111157.e: Biosphere reserves belong to the UNESCO programme “Man and the Biosphere”.
111157.m: Biosphere reserves belong to the UNESCO programme “Man and the Biosphere”.

111158.q: Which three zones is a biosphere reserve like the Entlebuch divided into?
a: Core zone, buffer zone, transition zone
Town zone, village zone, mountain zone
Water zone, forest zone, rock zone
Summer zone, winter zone, quiet zone
111158.e: In the core zone nature comes first, the buffer zone protects the farmed landscape, and in the transition zone business is done sustainably.
111158.m: A biosphere reserve has a core zone, a buffer zone and a transition zone.

111159.q: Which two cantons is Gantrisch Nature Park spread over?
111159.e: Gantrisch Nature Park lies between the cities of Bern, Fribourg and Thun and includes municipalities from the cantons of Bern and Fribourg.
111159.m: Gantrisch Nature Park is in the cantons of Bern and Fribourg.

111160.q: What is Gantrisch Nature Park named after?
111160.e: The Gantrisch is a striking peak in the Bernese Pre-Alps that gives the park its name.
111160.m: The Gantrisch is a mountain in the Bernese Pre-Alps.

111161.q: Between which three cities is Gantrisch Nature Park?
111161.e: The park is close to three cities and is therefore an important area for outings and relaxation for Bern, Fribourg and Thun.
111161.m: Gantrisch Nature Park is close to Bern, Fribourg and Thun.

111162.q: What does Gantrisch Nature Park campaign against with its dark sky park project?
111162.e: Lots of lamps make the night bright, so you can hardly see the stars and animals that are active at night are disturbed. In the Gantrisch area the sky is still especially dark.
111162.m: A dark sky park protects the dark night from too much artificial light.

111163.q: Which animals suffer especially from too much artificial light at night?
111163.e: Moths and other insects fly to lamps and often die there from exhaustion. Bats and migrating birds are also disturbed.
111163.m: Artificial light at night harms many insects.

111164.q: Which well-known mountain lake in the canton of Fribourg is in the area of Gantrisch Nature Park?
111164.e: The Schwarzsee in the Sense district of Fribourg is part of the park. It is a popular place for outings in summer and winter.
111164.m: The Schwarzsee is in the Fribourg part of Gantrisch Nature Park.

111165.q: Which pass road leads through the Gantrisch area?
111165.e: The road over the Gurnigel leads from Riggisberg into the Gantrisch area and is popular with day trippers in summer.
111165.m: You reach the Gantrisch area over the Gurnigel Pass.

111166.q: What kind of park is the Jurapark Aargau?
a: A theme park with roller coasters
A city park with a playground
111166.e: The Jurapark Aargau is a regional nature park in the Aargau Jura. It protects nature and the landscape and at the same time supports the region.
111166.m: The Jurapark Aargau is a regional nature park.

111167.q: In which part of Switzerland is the Jurapark Aargau?
a: In the north, near the border with Germany
In the south, near the border with Italy
In the west, on Lake Geneva
In the east, in the Engadine
111167.e: The Jurapark Aargau is in the north of Switzerland between the Aare and the Rhine. There the Rhine forms the border with Germany. One municipality of the park is in the canton of Solothurn.
111167.m: The Jurapark Aargau is in the north of Switzerland.

111168.q: Which dinosaur was found in large numbers in the clay pit at Frick in the Fricktal?
111168.e: Many skeletons of the plant-eating Plateosaurus were found in the clay pit at Frick. They are on display in the Dinosaur Museum in Frick.
111168.m: Lots of Plateosaurus skeletons were found in Frick.

111169.q: Which fruit is the Fricktal, where part of the Jurapark Aargau lies, especially known for?
111169.e: There are many tall cherry trees in the Fricktal. In spring they have white blossom, and in summer the cherries are harvested.
111169.m: The Fricktal is well known for cherries.

111170.q: What used to be mined from the mountain at Herznach in the Jurapark Aargau?
111170.e: Until the 1960s there was a mine in Herznach where iron ore was extracted. Today a museum recalls it.
111170.m: Iron ore used to be mined in Herznach.

111171.q: Between which two rivers is the Jurapark Aargau?
111171.e: The park stretches from the Aare valley in the south to the Rhine on the border with Germany in the north.
111171.m: The Jurapark Aargau lies between the Aare and the Rhine.

111172.q: How was the limestone in the Jurapark Aargau formed?
111172.e: Many millions of years ago there was a shallow sea here. Shells and lime mud were deposited and turned into rock, which is why ammonites are often found.
111172.m: Jura limestone formed from the deposits of a prehistoric sea.

111173.q: Which two types of Jura are there in the Jurapark Aargau?
111173.e: In the north, the layers of rock lie almost flat like tables (Tabular Jura); in the south, they are folded into ridges (Folded Jura).
111173.m: The Aargau Jura is made up of Tabular Jura and Folded Jura.

111174.q: Which federal office awards the label “park of national importance” in Switzerland?
111174.e: The Federal Office for the Environment (FOEN) checks the cantons' applications and awards the park label.
111174.m: The FOEN awards the label for parks of national importance.

111175.q: What does a regional nature park have to do to keep its label?
a: Show that it is reaching its goals
Choose a new name every year
Charge all visitors an entrance fee
111175.e: The label only applies for a certain time. After that, it is checked whether the park has protected nature and the landscape and strengthened the region.
111175.m: A nature park has to show that it is reaching its goals.

111176.q: Which three categories of parks of national importance are there in Switzerland?
a: National park, nature park, nature discovery park
City park, forest park, lake park
Mountain park, valley park, river park
111176.e: Swiss law distinguishes between national parks, regional nature parks and nature discovery parks.
111176.m: Switzerland has three categories of parks of national importance.

111177.q: How big is a regional nature park in Switzerland usually?
a: It is as small as a garden
It covers the whole of Switzerland
It is made up of a single farm
111177.e: A regional nature park is a large area. Usually many municipalities take part together.
111177.m: A regional nature park covers several municipalities.

111178.q: Who decides whether a municipality takes part in a regional nature park?
111178.e: Taking part is voluntary. In each municipality, the people or the municipal assembly vote on it.
111178.m: Municipalities take part in a nature park voluntarily.

111179.q: Who pays part of the costs of the parks of national importance in Switzerland?
111179.e: The parks are based on the Federal Act on the Protection of Nature and Cultural Heritage. The federal government supports them with money, and the cantons and municipalities also contribute.
111179.m: The federal government supports the Swiss parks with money.

111180.q: What does the label “Swiss Parks Product” on food stand for?
111180.e: The label is given to cheese, meat, bread or crafts made mostly in the park. This way the park strengthens the local economy.
111180.m: The label “Swiss Parks Product” shows that something comes from a park.

111181.q: What is allowed in a regional nature park, unlike in the Swiss National Park?
111181.e: A regional nature park is a lived-in, farmed landscape. People live, farm and work there, but they are meant to look after nature.
111181.m: People live and work in a regional nature park.

111182.q: Besides protecting nature and the landscape, what aim does a regional nature park have?
a: To build as many tower blocks as possible
111182.e: A regional nature park is meant to preserve nature and the landscape and at the same time support the sustainable economy of the region, for example gentle tourism.
111182.m: Nature parks combine nature protection with the local economy.

111183.q: Which two parts make up the Zurich Wilderness Park?
111183.e: The Zurich Wilderness Park includes the natural forest of Sihlwald and the Langenberg animal park.
111183.m: The Zurich Wilderness Park is made up of Sihlwald and Langenberg.

111184.q: What is the Langenberg in the Zurich Wilderness Park?
a: An animal park with native wild animals
111184.e: The Langenberg is a wildlife park south of Zurich. Animals such as bears, wolves, lynx and deer live there.
111184.m: The Langenberg is an animal park with native wild animals.

111185.q: What is special about the history of the Langenberg animal park?
a: It is the oldest wildlife park in Switzerland
It is the newest zoo in Switzerland
It used to be an airport
It used to be a mine
111185.e: The Langenberg was founded in 1869 and is thought to be the oldest wildlife park in Switzerland.
111185.m: The Langenberg is the oldest wildlife park in Switzerland.

111186.q: Why is the Sihlwald called a wilderness forest?
a: Nature is allowed to develop freely there
111186.e: No more wood is cut in the Sihlwald. Trees grow, die and rot as nature wants.
111186.m: In the Sihlwald, nature is allowed to develop by itself.

111187.q: Which river flows through the Zurich Wilderness Park?
111187.e: The Sihl flows through the Sihl valley and gave the Sihlwald its name. It flows into the Limmat in Zurich.
111187.m: The Sihl flows through the Sihlwald.

111188.q: Which type of tree shapes the Sihlwald most?
111188.e: The Sihlwald is one of the largest continuous mixed beech forests on the Swiss Central Plateau.
111188.m: Mainly beeches grow in the Sihlwald.

111189.q: What happens to fallen trees in the Sihlwald?
a: They are left where they lie
111189.e: No wood has been used from the Sihlwald since the year 2000. Dead wood is left lying and gives fungi, beetles and woodpeckers food and a home.
111189.m: Dead wood is an important habitat in the forest.

111190.q: Which animals can you see in the Langenberg animal park?
111190.e: The Langenberg is home to animals that are native to Europe or used to be, such as bears, wolves, lynx and elk.
111190.m: Native wild animals live in the Langenberg.

111191.q: What is the Swiss Alps Jungfrau-Aletsch area?
a: A UNESCO World Natural Heritage Site
A national park with a zoo
A ski area in the Grisons
111191.e: UNESCO added the area to its list as a World Natural Heritage Site in 2001. It was the first natural World Heritage Site in the Alps.
111191.m: Jungfrau-Aletsch is a UNESCO World Natural Heritage Site.

111192.q: Which glacier in the Jungfrau-Aletsch World Heritage Site is the longest in the Alps?
111192.e: The Great Aletsch Glacier is about 20 kilometres long, making it the longest and largest glacier in the Alps.
111192.m: The Great Aletsch Glacier is the longest glacier in the Alps.

111193.q: Which two cantons is the Jungfrau-Aletsch World Heritage Site spread over?
111193.e: The World Heritage Site is in the Bernese Alps. The north side belongs to the canton of Bern, and the south side with the Aletsch Glacier to Valais.
111193.m: The Jungfrau-Aletsch World Heritage Site is in Bern and Valais.

111194.q: How does a large glacier like the Great Aletsch Glacier form?
a: Several streams of ice flow together
A lake freezes over every year
Rain freezes on a rock face
111194.e: At Concordiaplatz, several branches of glaciers flow together and form the Great Aletsch Glacier. The ice there is several hundred metres thick.
111194.m: The Great Aletsch Glacier forms from several streams of ice.

111195.q: Which type of tree shapes the Aletsch Forest above the glacier?
111195.e: Very old Swiss stone pines grow in the Aletsch Forest, some of them several hundred years old. The area is a Pro Natura nature reserve.
111195.m: Centuries-old Swiss stone pines stand in the Aletsch Forest.

111196.q: Which three famous peaks stand on the northern edge of the Jungfrau-Aletsch World Heritage Site?
111196.e: The trio of Eiger, Mönch and Jungfrau can be seen clearly from the Bernese Oberland and the Central Plateau.
111196.m: The Eiger, Mönch and Jungfrau form the famous trio of peaks.

111197.q: Why has the Great Aletsch Glacier been getting shorter and thinner for decades?
111197.e: Rising temperatures make more ice melt in summer than is added as snow in winter. That is why the glacier is retreating.
111197.m: Global warming is making the Alpine glaciers melt.

111198.q: What mainly shapes the Jungfrau-Aletsch World Heritage Site?
111198.e: The World Heritage Site covers the glaciated Bernese Alps with the Great Aletsch Glacier and peaks such as the Jungfrau and the Bietschhorn.
111198.m: In the Jungfrau-Aletsch World Heritage Site, glaciers and peaks shape the landscape.

111199.q: Which country does the Val Müstair border?
111199.e: The Val Müstair is in the far east of the Grisons and borders South Tyrol in Italy.

111200.q: Which building in the Val Müstair is a UNESCO World Cultural Heritage Site?
111200.e: The Benedictine Convent of St John in Müstair has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1983.
111200.m: The Convent of St John in Müstair is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

111201.q: According to legend, which ruler founded the monastery in Müstair?
111201.e: Legend says that Charlemagne founded the monastery around the year 800. What is certain is that it dates from Carolingian times.
111201.m: The monastery in Müstair dates from Carolingian times.

111202.q: What is the monastery church of Müstair especially famous for?
111202.e: Wall paintings from around the year 800 have survived in the church. They are among the oldest large picture cycles in Europe.
111202.m: In Müstair you can see wall paintings more than 1200 years old.

111203.q: Which language do the local people in the Val Müstair mainly speak?
111203.e: In the Val Müstair people speak a Romansh dialect called Jauer.
111203.m: In the Val Müstair people speak Romansh.

111204.q: With which area does the Val Müstair form a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve?
111204.e: The Biosfera Val Müstair and the Swiss National Park together form the UNESCO Biosphere Reserve Engiadina Val Müstair.
111204.m: The Val Müstair and the National Park together form a UNESCO Biosphere.

111205.q: Into which sea does the water from the Val Müstair flow?
111205.e: The Rom flows into Italy and into the Adige, which flows into the Adriatic. The rest of the Engadine, on the other hand, drains via the Inn into the Black Sea.
111205.m: The water from the Val Müstair reaches the Adriatic via the Adige.

111206.q: Over which pass do you get from the Engadine into the Val Müstair?
111206.e: The road over the Ofen Pass leads from Zernez through the National Park into the Val Müstair.
111206.m: The Ofen Pass links the Engadine with the Val Müstair.

111207.q: Which border does the river Doubs form for a long stretch in the Parc du Doubs?
111207.e: For many kilometres, the Doubs flows exactly along the national border between Switzerland and France.
111207.m: For a long stretch, the Doubs is a border river with France.

111208.q: Which three cantons is the Parc du Doubs spread over?
111208.e: The Parc du Doubs includes municipalities in the cantons of Jura, Neuchâtel and Bern.
111208.m: The Parc du Doubs stretches across three Jura areas.

111209.q: Which medieval little town on the Doubs is in the canton of Jura?
111209.e: Saint-Ursanne lies right on the Doubs and, with its old bridge and collegiate church, is a well-known place to visit.
111209.m: Saint-Ursanne is a medieval little town on the Doubs.

111210.q: Which breed of horse comes from the Franches-Montagnes, which belong to the Parc du Doubs?
111210.e: The Freiberger is the only native horse breed of Switzerland. It comes from the Franches-Montagnes, called Freiberge in German.
111210.m: The Freiberger is the Swiss horse breed from the Jura.

111211.q: What is the famous waterfall of the Doubs near Les Brenets called?
111211.e: At the end of Lac des Brenets, the Doubs plunges about 27 metres as the Saut du Doubs.
111211.m: The Saut du Doubs is the great waterfall of the Doubs.

111212.q: Which highly endangered fish, called “Roi du Doubs” in French, now lives only in the Doubs in Switzerland?
111212.e: The Rhone streber, called “Roi du Doubs” in French, is now found only in the Doubs in Switzerland. It is critically endangered and strictly protected.
111212.m: The Rhone streber is one of the rarest fish in Switzerland.

111213.q: Which river does the Doubs finally flow into in France?
111213.e: The Doubs flows back into France and into the Saône. The Saône flows into the Rhône and so into the Mediterranean.
111213.m: The Doubs is a tributary of the Saône.

111214.q: Which language is mainly spoken in the Parc du Doubs?
111214.e: The Parc du Doubs is in western Switzerland, and the municipalities are French-speaking.
111214.m: In the Parc du Doubs people speak French.

111215.q: In which canton is Thal Nature Park?
111215.e: Thal Nature Park covers the district of Thal in the Solothurn Jura.
111215.m: Thal Nature Park is in the canton of Solothurn.

111216.q: Which municipality is the main town of the district of Thal?
111216.e: Balsthal is the largest place and the main town of the district of Thal.
111216.m: Balsthal is the main town of the Thal.

111217.q: Which large wild animals have been living in a forest enclosure in Thal Nature Park since 2022?
111217.e: A trial with European bison has been running near Welschenrohr since 2022. The aim is to find out whether these wild cattle can live in Switzerland again.
111217.m: The return of the European bison is being tested in the Thal.

111218.q: Which is the largest land mammal in Europe?
111218.e: The European bison is a European wild ox. Bulls can weigh almost a tonne, more than any other land animal in Europe.
111218.m: The European bison is the heaviest land animal in Europe.

111219.q: What is a narrow valley that cuts through a Jura ridge called, like the ones near Balsthal?
111219.e: A cluse is a cross valley where a river cuts through a Jura ridge. There are cluses like this near Balsthal.
111219.m: A cluse is a valley that cuts through a Jura ridge.

111220.q: The river from the Thal flows into a large Swiss river at Olten. Which one?
111220.e: The Dünnern flows through Balsthal and the Gäu and flows into the Aare at Olten.
111220.m: At Olten, the Dünnern flows into the Aare.

111221.q: In which mountain range is Thal Nature Park?
111221.e: The Thal is a valley between two Jura ridges in the canton of Solothurn.
111221.m: Thal Nature Park lies between Jura ridges.

111222.q: The Swiss abbreviation BLN stands for the German name of which inventory?
a: Federal Inventory of Landscapes and Natural Monuments
Federal League for Air and Nature
Federal Office for Agriculture and Nature
111222.e: BLN is the abbreviation for the Federal Inventory of Landscapes and Natural Monuments of National Importance.
111222.m: The BLN lists the most valuable landscapes in Switzerland.

111223.q: What is listed in the Federal Inventory of Landscapes and Natural Monuments (BLN)?
a: All the hotels in the Alps
111223.e: The BLN lists landscapes and natural monuments of national importance. It has existed since 1977.
111223.m: The BLN lists the most valuable landscapes in Switzerland.

111224.q: Roughly how many sites does the Federal Inventory of Landscapes and Natural Monuments include?
111224.e: The BLN includes 162 landscapes and natural monuments of national importance (as of 2025).
111224.m: More than 160 sites are listed in the BLN.

111225.q: Roughly what share of Switzerland's area belongs to BLN areas?
111225.e: The BLN areas cover just under 20 percent of the country's area.
111225.m: About a fifth of Switzerland is in BLN areas.

111226.q: Which natural monument is listed in the Federal Inventory of Landscapes and Natural Monuments?
111226.e: The Rhine Falls near Schaffhausen is a natural landscape of national importance. The other answers are buildings.
111226.m: The Rhine Falls is a protected natural monument.

111227.q: Which federal office is responsible for the Federal Inventory of Landscapes and Natural Monuments?
111227.e: The Federal Office for the Environment (FOEN) manages the BLN and advises the authorities on projects in these areas.
111227.m: The FOEN looks after the BLN.

111228.q: What does the BLN require when the federal government builds something in such an area?
a: To spare the landscape as much as possible
To cut down all the trees first
111228.e: When the federal government carries out its tasks, a BLN area is to be preserved undiminished or at least spared as much as possible.
111228.m: In BLN areas, the landscape is to be spared as much as possible.

111229.e: Natural monuments are striking natural features, for example a large boulder left by a glacier, a waterfall or a rock formation.
111229.m: A natural monument is a natural feature worth protecting.

111230.q: Which trees are typical of a softwood floodplain forest by a river?
111230.e: Willows and alders cope well with floods and grow back quickly. That is why they stand close to the water.
111230.m: Willows and alders like to grow in floodplains.

111232.q: Why are floodplains so valuable for nature?
a: They are very rich in species
111232.e: Floodplains cover only a small area of Switzerland, but they are home to a large share of the native animal and plant species.
111232.m: Floodplains are among the habitats richest in species.

111233.q: Which small green frog that is good at climbing is a typical inhabitant of ponds in floodplains?
111233.e: The tree frog spawns in warm, shallow ponds like those that form in floodplains after floods. In Switzerland it is rare and protected.
111233.m: The tree frog needs shallow, sunny ponds.

111234.q: Which colourful bird hunts small fish in floodplains and nests in steep riverbanks?
111234.e: The kingfisher dives into the water to catch fish. It digs its nesting burrow into steep, sandy banks.
111234.m: The kingfisher is a typical bird of floodplains.

111235.q: Why are floods important for a floodplain?
a: They create new areas of gravel and ponds
They drive all animals away for ever
111235.e: Floods tear open banks and deposit gravel and sand in new places. This keeps creating young habitats for pioneer plants and animals.
111235.m: Floods renew the habitats in a floodplain.

111236.q: What is it called when a river that has been built up gets more space and natural banks again?
111236.e: In a revitalisation, embankments are moved back and banks are made natural. This lets new floodplains form.
111236.m: Revitalisation gives a river more space again.

111237.q: In which canton is the floodplain area of the Bolle di Magadino on Lake Maggiore?
111237.e: The Bolle di Magadino are a delta with floodplains, reeds and ponds where the Ticino flows into the lake. Many migrating birds rest there.
111237.m: The Bolle di Magadino are a floodplain area in Ticino.

111238.q: Roughly how high is the Gantrisch?
111238.e: The Gantrisch is 2175 metres high. This makes it not a high mountain peak but a mountain of the Pre-Alps.
111238.m: The Gantrisch is a peak in the Pre-Alps just over 2000 metres high.

111239.q: Why had European bison disappeared from Switzerland?
a: They were hunted and lost their habitat
They moved to Africa of their own accord
They were wiped out by wolves
They could not cope with snow
111239.e: European bison used to live in Switzerland too. Because of hunting and the clearing of forests, they died out here many centuries ago.
111239.m: Hunting and clearing forests wiped out the European bison in Switzerland.

111240.e: The Sihlwald has belonged to the city of Zurich since the Middle Ages. In the past it supplied building wood and firewood for the city.
111240.m: The Sihlwald is owned by the city of Zurich.

111330.q: According to the psychologist George Miller, roughly how many units of information can short-term memory hold at once?
111330.e: In 1956 George Miller described the “magical number seven, plus or minus two”. Newer research even suggests it is closer to about four units.
111330.m: Short-term memory can only hold a few things at once.

111332.q: Without repeating it, roughly how long does information stay in short-term memory?
111332.e: Without repetition, information in short-term memory usually fades after about 15 to 30 seconds. After that it is lost unless it has been processed further.
111332.m: Short-term memory forgets quickly if you do not repeat.

111333.q: Which technical term is often used for short-term memory when you actively work with information in it, for example in mental arithmetic?
111333.e: Working memory briefly holds information and processes it at the same time. In mental arithmetic you remember intermediate results and keep calculating with them.
111333.m: In working memory we hold things and work with them at the same time.

111334.q: What happens to most of the things we see and hear but do not pay attention to?
a: They stay in our memory for ever
They go straight into long-term memory
111334.e: Our senses constantly take in a huge amount. Only what we pay attention to reaches short-term memory; the rest is gone after fractions of a second.
111334.m: We can only briefly remember what we pay attention to.

111335.q: What helps most to keep information in short-term memory for longer?
111335.e: Repeating it in your head, for example saying it quietly to yourself, keeps information active. If you get distracted, it is quickly lost.
111335.m: Repeating keeps information alive in short-term memory.

111336.q: Why do you often forget a number straight away if someone speaks to you while you are trying to remember it?
111336.e: Short-term memory has only a little space. New information pushes out the old before it is firmly stored.
111336.m: Distraction pushes information out of short-term memory.

111337.q: Which part of the brain is working memory mainly based in?
111337.e: The front part of the cerebral cortex, the frontal lobe or prefrontal cortex, is especially important for working memory. It also controls planning and attention.
111337.m: The frontal lobe helps us keep things in our head briefly and plan.

111338.q: When does something you have learned get into long-term memory best?
a: When you repeat it several times
When you only skim it once
When you watch TV at the same time
When you forget it again immediately
111338.e: Through repetition, information is activated again and again in the brain. That way it becomes firmly stored and stays for a long time.
111338.m: Repetition brings knowledge into long-term memory.

111339.q: According to the well-known “forgetting curve”, when do we forget most of what we have learned?
a: Never, once you have read it
111339.e: The forgetting curve shows that most is lost in the first hours after learning. Anyone who reviews soon remembers much more.
111339.m: Without repetition, we forget most things soon after learning.

111340.q: According to research, which way of learning works especially well against forgetting?
111340.e: Spaced repetition, with breaks over several days, anchors knowledge better in long-term memory. This is called the spacing effect.
111340.m: If you spread your learning over several days, you remember more.

111341.q: Why do you hardly ever forget how to ride a bike, even if you have not ridden for years?
a: Sequences of movements are stored especially well
Your legs remember the bike themselves
Bikes are always built the same way
You learn it completely new every time
111341.e: The brain stores practised movements like cycling or swimming in a separate area of memory. These skills are hardly ever lost.
111341.m: Practised movements like riding a bike stay stored for a long time.

111342.q: Which memories belong to the personal experiences in long-term memory?
a: What your last birthday was like
What the capital of Switzerland is called
111342.e: We remember our own experiences with place, time and feelings. General knowledge such as arithmetic or capital cities, on the other hand, is stored differently.
111342.m: Personal experiences are stored with place and time.

111343.q: What happens during sleep to what we learned during the day?
a: It only stays in short-term memory.
It is stored in the muscles.
111343.e: During sleep the brain replays what it has learned and strengthens it. That is why enough sleep before a test is important.
111343.m: Good sleep strengthens what we have learned.

111344.q: According to current knowledge, how big is the storage capacity of long-term memory?
111344.e: Unlike short-term memory, long-term memory has no known upper limit, as far as we know today. The problem is more about finding the information again.
111344.m: Long-term memory has a huge amount of space.

111345.q: Why do you remember things better that are linked with strong feelings?
111345.e: The amygdala, the emotion centre, works closely with the hippocampus. That is why emotional experiences are stored more strongly.
111345.m: What moves us stays in our memory better.

111346.q: Which learning method actively tests your own knowledge, for example with flashcards, and so strengthens long-term memory?
111346.e: With active recall, the brain has to work hard to find the answer. This testing effect strengthens knowledge better than simply rereading.
111346.m: Testing yourself strengthens knowledge better than just reading.

111347.q: Which hormone from the adrenal cortex is considered a typical “stress hormone” during long-lasting stress?
111347.e: Cortisol is made in the adrenal cortex and provides the body with energy. If its level stays high for a long time, this can harm your health.
111347.m: Cortisol is an important stress hormone of the body.

111348.q: What is the ancient stress reaction called that prepares the body for fighting or running away?
111348.e: In danger, the body switches in a flash to fight or flight. Pulse, breathing and muscle tension rise.
111348.m: In danger, the body gets ready to fight or run away.

111349.q: What is positive stress called that spurs us on, for example before a competition?
111349.e: We feel eustress as stimulating and motivating. Negative, draining stress is called distress.
111349.m: Positive stress spurs us on, negative stress weighs us down.

111350.e: Stress is how the body and mind respond to pressure, for example before a test. Pulse and breathing get faster and the muscles tense up.
111350.m: Stress is the body's reaction to pressure.

111351.q: Which part of the nervous system becomes active under stress and gets the body ready for action?
111351.e: The sympathetic nervous system is the “accelerator” part of the autonomic nervous system. Afterwards the parasympathetic nervous system brings back calm and recovery.
111351.m: The sympathetic system accelerates, the parasympathetic system brakes.

111352.q: What has been shown to work well for reducing stress?
111352.e: Exercise breaks down stress hormones and lifts your mood. Enough sleep and breaks also help against stress.
111352.m: Exercise is a good remedy for stress.

111353.q: What can long-lasting stress do in the body?
a: The body no longer needs sleep.
111353.e: Stress hormones that stay high for a long time can weaken the body's defences. You then get ill more easily, for example.
111353.m: Constant stress weakens the body's defences.

111354.q: What is it called when your mind suddenly goes blank in a test because of fear?
111354.e: With strong fear, stress hormones temporarily block access to what you have learned. The knowledge is not gone; it is just hard to recall for a moment.
111354.m: In a blackout, knowledge is only blocked for a moment, not lost.

111355.q: What is most likely to help if your mind goes blank in a test?
a: Breathe deeply and do an easier question
Hand in the paper straight away
Read the question again and again
111355.e: Calm breathing lowers the tension. With an easier question you gain confidence, and your memory often comes back.
111355.m: Breathing deeply and starting with something easy helps against a blackout.

111356.q: What are thoughts like “I won't manage it anyway” called, which make test anxiety worse?
111356.e: Negative thoughts make fear stronger. If you replace them with realistic, encouraging sentences, you can become calmer.
111356.m: Encouraging thoughts help against test anxiety.

111357.q: Why does a practice test at home help against test anxiety?
a: You no longer need to study.
Your heart then stops beating altogether.
111357.e: If you practise a test, you know the situation better. Familiar things are less frightening than unknown things.
111357.m: Practising under test conditions takes the fear out of a test.

111358.q: What is a typical physical sign of test anxiety?
111358.e: Before or during the test, your heart can race, your hands can sweat or your tummy can hurt. These are effects of the stress hormones.
111358.m: Test anxiety often shows itself with a pounding heart and sweaty hands.

111359.q: What is the breathing exercise called in which you breathe in slowly through your nose and out even more slowly through your mouth to calm down before a test?
111359.e: In belly breathing, your tummy rises and falls, and breathing out takes longer than breathing in. This calms your pulse and nerves before a test.
111359.m: Slow breathing into your belly calms you before a test.

111360.q: What helps against test anxiety weeks before the test?
a: Making a study plan with fixed stages
Putting everything off until the last day
111360.e: A study plan divides the material into manageable portions. If you know you are well prepared, you go into the test more calmly.
111360.m: An early study plan takes a lot of pressure off a test.

111361.q: In Switzerland, who can you turn to if test anxiety becomes very strong?
a: The teacher or the school psychology service
111361.e: Teachers, parents and the school psychology service can give advice. Strong test anxiety can be tackled well with support.
111361.m: If test anxiety is strong, it is best to get help.

111362.q: What is motivation called that comes from enjoying the thing itself?
111362.e: Intrinsic means “from within”. You do something because it is fun or interesting.
111362.m: If you do something out of enjoyment, you are intrinsically motivated.

111363.q: What is motivation called that comes from reward or punishment from outside?
111363.e: Extrinsic means “from outside”. Examples are marks, money or praise.
111363.m: Rewards from outside create extrinsic motivation.

111364.q: Which messenger substance in the brain plays an important part in the reward system and in motivation?
111364.e: Dopamine is released when we expect a reward. It drives us to pursue a goal.
111364.m: Dopamine drives us to reach goals.

111365.q: Which psychologist is the well-known hierarchy of needs named after?
111365.e: Abraham Maslow arranged human needs in levels that build on each other. Showing them as a pyramid was later made popular by others.
111365.m: The hierarchy of needs comes from Abraham Maslow.

111366.q: What is at the very bottom of Maslow's hierarchy of needs?
111366.e: At the very bottom are needs such as eating, drinking and sleeping. Only when they are met do higher needs come to the fore.
111366.m: Basic needs such as food and sleep form the base of the pyramid.

111367.q: According to research, which kind of goals motivate best?
a: Goals that are as vague as possible
111367.e: Specific and realistic goals show what needs to be done. If you reach small stages, you stay motivated.
111367.m: Clear and achievable goals keep motivation high.

111368.q: What is it called when you keep putting important tasks off until later?
111368.e: Procrastination means “putting off”. It helps to split tasks into small steps and simply get started.
111368.m: If you split tasks into small steps, you put things off less.

111369.q: What can happen if you reward someone for something they enjoy doing anyway?
a: Their inner enjoyment of it can drop.
111369.e: This is called the overjustification effect. Rewards from outside can weaken intrinsic motivation.
111369.m: Too much reward can dampen the enjoyment of something.

111370.q: In psychology, what is the belief called that you can manage a task by your own efforts?
111370.e: The psychologist Albert Bandura coined the term self-efficacy. People who believe in their abilities are more likely to try difficult tasks.
111370.m: If you believe in yourself, you dare to do more.

111371.q: According to Albert Bandura, what makes self-confidence grow most strongly?
111371.e: If you master a challenge yourself, you experience yourself as capable. Such successes strengthen self-confidence the most.
111371.m: Your own successes are the best source of self-confidence.

111372.q: What is the difference between self-confidence and arrogance?
111372.e: Self-confident people trust their own abilities without making others feel small. Arrogance shows itself as acting superior towards others.
111372.m: Real self-confidence does not need arrogance.

111373.q: What is the attitude called that you can improve your abilities through practice?
111373.e: The psychologist Carol Dweck called this attitude a “growth mindset”. Mistakes then count as chances to learn.
111373.m: Mistakes are chances to learn if you believe in growing.

111374.q: Which is more likely to strengthen self-confidence?
111374.e: If you know your strengths, you feel more secure in yourself. Constant comparing, for example on social media, can weaken self-confidence.
111374.m: If you know your strengths, you feel more secure in yourself.

111375.q: What is the value you give yourself as a person called?
111375.e: Self-esteem describes how much you value yourself. It is closely linked with self-confidence.
111375.m: Self-esteem shows how much you value yourself.

111376.q: Which posture generally comes across as self-confident?
a: Standing up straight with eye contact
Hunched over with your head down
Arms in front of your face
Turning away from the other person
111376.e: An upright posture and eye contact come across as confident to others. Body language can also affect how you feel yourself.
111376.m: An upright posture comes across as self-confident.

111377.q: What does being able to say “no” mean for self-confidence?
a: It shows that you respect your own limits.
It shows a lack of self-confidence.
111377.e: If you say no in a friendly but clear way, you take your own needs seriously. That is part of healthy self-confidence.
111377.m: If you know and show your limits, you have healthy self-confidence.

a: Being consciously in the moment without judging
Doing as much as possible at once
