112633.q: What does the Latin word “mellitus” in the name diabetes mellitus mean?
112633.e: In the past, doctors tested the urine of sick people and noticed that it tasted sweet. Hence the name “honey-sweet flowing through”.

112634.q: Which parts of the body are often damaged when blood sugar is too high for a long time?
112634.e: Permanently high sugar damages the fine blood vessels and nerves. That is why the eyes and kidneys are checked regularly in diabetes.
112634.m: In the long run, high blood sugar harms the eyes, kidneys and nerves.

112635.q: Why should people with diabetes check their feet regularly?
a: They often no longer feel small wounds
Their toenails fall off every month
112635.e: Diabetes can damage the nerves in the feet. Small injuries then go unnoticed and heal badly, because the blood supply also suffers.

112636.q: Which type of diabetes is the most common worldwide?
112636.e: About nine out of ten people with diabetes have type 2. In this type, insulin no longer works properly.
112636.m: Type 2 is the most common form of diabetes.

112637.q: Which lifestyle habits increase the risk of type 2 diabetes?
a: Lack of exercise and being very overweight
Lots of vegetables and lots of water
112637.e: People who move little and are very overweight have a higher risk. Genes also play a part.
112637.m: Exercise and healthy eating lower the risk of type 2 diabetes.

112638.q: How are people with type 1 diabetes treated?
a: They give themselves insulin from outside
They have a leg put in plaster
112638.e: Because the body hardly produces any insulin of its own, it must be given with a syringe, pen or insulin pump.
112638.m: In type 1 diabetes, the missing insulin is replaced.

112639.q: Which signs are typical of untreated diabetes?
a: Great thirst and needing to wee often
Red eyes and a runny nose
112639.e: If there is too much sugar in the blood, the kidneys get rid of sugar with lots of water. The body loses fluid, so you feel very thirsty.
112639.m: Strong thirst can be a warning sign of diabetes.

112640.q: Where did the insulin used to treat diabetes in the first decades come from?
a: From the pancreases of cattle and pigs
112640.e: For a long time, insulin was obtained from animal pancreases from slaughterhouses. Since the 1980s, human insulin has been made by genetic engineering.
112640.m: In the past, insulin for medicines came from animals.

112641.q: Why is there a World Diabetes Day every year?
a: To raise awareness of the disease diabetes
To have a holiday without school
112641.e: On World Diabetes Day in November, organisations provide information about diabetes, prevention and treatment. The day remembers Frederick Banting, one of the discoverers of insulin.
112641.m: World Diabetes Day raises awareness of diabetes.

a: There is too much salt in the blood
112642.e: In hypoglycaemia, the body, especially the brain, gets too little glucose from the blood.
112642.m: In hypoglycaemia, there is too little sugar in the blood.

112643.q: What can hypoglycaemia easily be mistaken for?
112643.e: When the brain lacks sugar, you become confused, speak unclearly and stagger. That is why it is important to think of hypoglycaemia.
112643.m: Confusion can be a sign of a lack of sugar.

a: Shaking, sweating and sudden strong hunger
112644.e: When sugar falls, the body releases alarm hormones. You shake, sweat, turn pale and get very hungry.
112644.m: Shaking and sudden strong hunger can be signs of hypoglycaemia.

112645.q: What helps a conscious person with hypoglycaemia fastest?
a: Glucose tablets or a sugary drink
112645.e: Glucose tablets and sugary drinks reach the blood very quickly. Cheese contains hardly any sugar, so it does not help quickly.
112645.m: In hypoglycaemia, sugar is needed quickly.

112646.q: What is the right thing to do for an unconscious person with hypoglycaemia?
a: Give nothing by mouth and call 144
Pour a glass of cola into their mouth
Put them under a cold shower
112646.e: An unconscious person can choke. You call the ambulance on 144 and put the person in the recovery position.
112646.m: Never give an unconscious person anything to drink.

112647.q: What can trigger hypoglycaemia in people with diabetes who take medicines that lower blood sugar?
a: A glass of milk as a mid-morning snack
112647.e: If the medicine is taken as usual but a meal is missed, there is no fresh supply of sugar. Lots of sport without extra carbohydrates can also lower the level too much.
112647.m: People who take diabetes medicines should not skip meals.

112648.q: Why does the brain notice hypoglycaemia particularly quickly?
a: It needs glucose as its main source of energy
It is made mainly of sugar
It stores a great deal of sugar
112648.e: The brain has hardly any sugar stores of its own and depends on a constant supply. If this is missing, you become confused, cannot concentrate or even lose consciousness.
112648.m: The brain constantly needs sugar from the blood.

112649.q: Why is hypoglycaemia dangerous when cycling in traffic?
112649.e: With a lack of sugar, the brain works more slowly. You react later and miss dangers more easily.
112649.m: With a lack of sugar, you react too slowly in traffic.

112651.e: If you heat the greyish-black iodine crystals, a violet vapour rises. The name comes from the Greek “iodes”, meaning violet-coloured.

112652.q: Why was iodine deficiency once particularly common in the Alps?
a: The soil and water there contain little iodine
The mountains suck iodine out of the air
The mountain people ate too much fish
Cold destroys iodine in the body
112652.e: Over a long time, glaciers and rain washed the iodine out of the soil in the Alps. Vegetables and milk from there therefore contained little iodine.
112652.m: Alpine soils are naturally low in iodine.

112653.q: Why does Switzerland give iodine tablets to households near nuclear power stations?
a: To protect the thyroid from radioactive iodine in an accident
112653.e: If you take potassium iodide tablets in time, the thyroid is filled up with normal iodine. Radioactive iodine is then hardly absorbed any more.
112653.m: Iodine tablets protect the thyroid in a nuclear power station accident.

112654.q: What is the chemical symbol of the element iodine?
112654.e: The symbol I comes from the element’s international name, “iodum” in Latin. In the periodic table, iodine is one of the halogens.

112655.q: Which organ needs iodine to make its hormones?
112655.e: The thyroid gland in the neck builds iodine into its hormones. These hormones stimulate the metabolism throughout the body.
112655.m: The thyroid needs iodine for its hormones.

112656.q: What effect did severe iodine deficiency once have on some children?
a: Problems with physical and mental development
112656.e: Thyroid hormones are needed for the development of the brain and bones. If iodine was missing even before birth, serious developmental problems could result.
112656.m: Children need iodine for healthy development.

112657.q: Which symptoms fit an underactive thyroid?
a: Tiredness, feeling cold and lack of energy
A racing heart, sweating and restlessness
Ringing in the ears and nosebleeds
112657.e: Too little thyroid hormone slows down the metabolism. You are tired, feel cold easily and often put on weight.
112657.m: An underactive thyroid slows down the whole body.

112658.q: Which surgeon from Bern received the Nobel Prize in 1909 for his research on the thyroid?
112658.e: Theodor Kocher operated on thousands of people with goitre in Bern and researched the functions of the thyroid. He was the first Swiss winner of the Nobel Prize in Medicine.
112658.m: Theodor Kocher from Bern became famous for his goitre research.

112659.q: Where on the body can you see a goitre?
a: At the front of the neck
At the back of the head
On the sole of the foot
112659.e: The thyroid lies at the front of the neck below the larynx. If it gets bigger, the neck bulges forwards.
112659.m: A goitre shows at the front of the neck.

112660.q: What is the medical term for a goitre?
112660.e: Struma is the Latin word for goitre. Doctors use it for any enlargement of the thyroid.
112660.m: In medicine, a goitre is called a struma.

112661.q: What does an overactive thyroid often cause?
112661.e: With an overactive thyroid, the gland produces too much hormone. The body then runs at full speed: the heart races, you are restless and you sweat.
112661.m: Too much thyroid hormone makes you restless and your heart race.

112662.q: Why does the thyroid grow when there is a lack of iodine?
a: It is constantly driven to make more hormone
It is blown up by bacteria
112662.e: Because there is too little thyroid hormone in the blood, the pituitary gland sends more and more control hormone. This constant stimulation makes the gland tissue grow.
112662.m: Constant stimulation to work makes the thyroid grow.

112663.q: How has goitre in Switzerland changed since iodised salt was introduced?
a: It has stayed just as common
It only occurs in animals now
112663.e: In the past, a great many people in some Alpine valleys had a goitre. With iodised salt, the disease declined sharply.
112663.m: Iodised salt has made goitre almost disappear in Switzerland.

112664.q: What shape is the thyroid gland?
112664.e: The thyroid has two lobes joined by a narrow bridge. It looks like a butterfly.
112664.m: The thyroid is shaped like a butterfly.

112665.q: Which examination can measure the size of the thyroid painlessly?
112665.e: For an ultrasound, a probe is placed on the neck. You can see the gland on the screen and measure its size and any lumps.
112665.m: Ultrasound shows the thyroid without radiation.

112666.q: Which problems can a very large goitre cause?
112666.e: A large goitre presses on the gullet and windpipe, which lie directly behind it. Then swallowing or breathing becomes difficult.
112666.m: A large goitre can narrow the windpipe and gullet.

112667.q: What building blocks are endorphins made of?
112667.e: Endorphins are peptides, short chains of amino acids. They are cut out of a larger precursor protein.

112669.q: What effect do endorphins have in the body?
a: They relieve pain and lift your mood
112669.e: Endorphins act like the body’s own painkillers. They can also give you a good feeling.
112669.m: Endorphins relieve pain and put you in a good mood.

112670.q: During which activity are particularly large amounts of endorphins released?
112670.e: After running or cycling for a long time, some people report a feeling of great happiness. This is also called the “runner’s high”.
112670.m: Endurance sport can release happiness hormones.

112671.q: Where in the body are endorphins mainly produced?
112671.e: Endorphins are mainly made in the pituitary gland and the hypothalamus. From there they act in the nervous system.
112671.m: Endorphins are made in the brain.

112672.q: During which activity did researchers also find signs that endorphins are released?
112672.e: Studies from Finland and England showed that laughing together releases endorphins in the brain. This probably also strengthens the feeling of belonging together.

112673.q: From which plant does the substance morphine come, which endorphins act similarly to?
112673.e: Morphine is obtained from the milky sap of the seed capsules of the opium poppy. It is a strong painkiller that is only available on prescription.
112673.m: Morphine comes from the opium poppy.

112674.e: The body makes endorphins itself, mainly in the brain. That is why they are called the body’s own painkillers.
112674.m: Endorphins are painkillers made by your own body.

112675.q: What happens to blood sugar when you are under a lot of stress?
112675.e: Stress hormones release sugar reserves so that the muscles and brain have enough energy to fight or run away.

112676.q: In which glands is adrenaline produced?
112676.e: Adrenaline is made in the inner part of the adrenal glands, the adrenal medulla. In a fright or danger, it enters the blood within seconds.
112676.m: Adrenaline comes from the adrenal glands.

112677.q: Where exactly are the adrenal glands?
a: Like caps on top of the kidneys
112677.e: Each kidney has a small gland on top like a hat. That is where the name adrenal gland comes from, meaning “next to the kidney”.
112677.m: The adrenal glands sit on top of the kidneys.

112678.q: How does adrenaline affect the heart when you get a fright?
a: It makes the heart beat faster
It has no effect on the heart
112678.e: Adrenaline prepares the body to fight or run away. The heart beats faster and pumps more blood to the muscles.
112678.m: Adrenaline makes the heart beat faster.

112679.q: Why do you often turn pale when you get a big fright?
a: Adrenaline narrows the blood vessels in the skin
Blood flows out of the body
The heart stops for a short time
112679.e: Adrenaline sends blood away from the skin to the muscles, heart and brain. That is why the face often looks pale after a fright.
112679.m: You turn pale after a fright because adrenaline draws blood away from the skin.

112680.q: Why do you often have a dry mouth when you are very nervous?
a: The production of saliva is reduced
You breathe in too little air
112680.e: In the stress reaction, the body slows down everything that is not needed at that moment, including digestion. That is why less saliva flows.
112680.m: When you are nervous, the body produces less saliva.

112681.q: What does the stress hormone cortisol do in the body?
a: It makes energy available to the body
112681.e: Cortisol makes sugar and fat move from the reserves into the blood. That way the body has enough energy during longer periods of strain.
112681.m: Cortisol supplies the body with energy during stress.

112682.q: What are substances derived from cortisol used for, for example in creams and sprays?
112682.e: Cortisone and similar active ingredients calm the body’s defence reactions. They are used, for example, for eczema, asthma or severe hay fever.
112682.m: Cortisone medicines calm inflammation and allergies.

112683.q: Which hormone is closely related to adrenaline and also acts as a messenger at nerve endings?
112683.e: Noradrenaline differs from adrenaline only by a small group on the molecule. It is released in the adrenal medulla and at the nerve endings of the sympathetic nervous system.
112683.m: Noradrenaline is a close relative of adrenaline.

112684.q: Which organ uses a hormone to tell the brain that you are hungry?
112684.e: When the stomach is empty, it releases a hormone into the blood. This tells the brain that it is time to eat.
112684.m: The empty stomach tells the brain you are hungry.

112685.q: Fatty tissue produces a hormone that tells the brain there are enough reserves. What does this hormone dampen?
112685.e: Fat cells release a hormone that tells the brain there are enough energy reserves. This dampens hunger.

112686.q: Which of these glands is NOT a hormone gland?
112686.e: The sweat gland releases sweat through a duct to the outside onto the skin. Hormone glands, on the other hand, release their substances into the blood.
112686.m: Sweat glands release to the outside, hormone glands into the blood.

112687.q: What are the messenger substances that hormone glands release into the blood called?
112687.e: Hormone glands release messenger substances into the blood: hormones. They act in other places in the body.
112687.m: Hormones are messengers in the blood.

112688.q: How do hormones travel from the gland to their target organs?
112688.e: Hormone glands release their messengers into the blood. With the bloodstream they reach the whole body.

112689.q: Why does a hormone only act on certain cells, even though it is everywhere in the blood?
a: Only these cells have matching receptors
Only these cells have a nucleus
Only these cells are warm enough
Only these cells are coloured red
112689.e: Like a key, a hormone only fits certain receiving sites, the receptors. Cells without a matching receptor do not react.
112689.m: Hormones work on the lock-and-key principle.

112690.q: How does control by hormones usually differ from control by nerves?
a: Hormones act more slowly, but for longer
Hormones only act in the legs
112690.e: Nerve signals reach their target in a fraction of a second. Hormones have to travel through the blood, but their effect often lasts longer.
112690.m: Nerves are fast; hormones act more slowly and for longer.

112691.q: What are the usually four small glands behind the thyroid that control the calcium level in the blood called?
112691.e: The parathyroid glands are only about the size of lentils. Their hormone, parathyroid hormone, raises the calcium level in the blood.
112691.m: The parathyroid glands control the calcium content of the blood.

112692.q: In which organ is the hormone glucagon produced?
112692.e: The pancreas produces the two blood sugar hormones, insulin and glucagon. Glucagon was discovered shortly after insulin.

112693.q: When does the body release more glucagon?
a: When blood sugar is too low
112693.e: When the sugar level in the blood falls, the pancreas releases glucagon. It makes sure that sugar gets back into the blood.
112693.m: When blood sugar is low, glucagon is released.

112694.q: How do insulin and glucagon affect blood sugar?
a: They have no effect on it
112694.e: Insulin lowers blood sugar and glucagon raises it. Together they keep the level within a narrow range.
112694.m: Insulin and glucagon are opposites when it comes to blood sugar.

112695.q: Which organ releases sugar into the blood when it gets the signal from glucagon?
112695.e: The liver stores sugar as glycogen. Glucagon makes it break down this store and release sugar into the blood.
112695.m: Glucagon gets sugar out of the liver.

112696.q: Which emergency medicine can a companion give a person with diabetes during severe hypoglycaemia?
a: Glucagon as an injection or nasal spray
112696.e: Glucagon can be injected or sprayed into the nose and raises the sugar level again within minutes. Afterwards you call the ambulance.
112696.m: Glucagon is an emergency medicine for severe hypoglycaemia.

112697.q: How does glucagon help the body during a very long period without food?
a: The liver makes new sugar from other substances
The skin takes in sugar from the air
The heart makes its own sugar
112697.e: Glucagon promotes gluconeogenesis. In this process, the liver builds new sugar from building blocks such as amino acids.
112697.m: Glucagon makes the liver produce new sugar.

112698.q: Why does the glucagon level often rise during endurance sport?
a: The muscles use up a lot of sugar
The lungs need glucagon to breathe
You drink too much during sport
112698.e: Working muscles take a lot of sugar from the blood. Glucagon makes sure fresh supplies come from the stores.
112698.m: During sport, glucagon keeps blood sugar steady.

112699.q: What building blocks is the hormone glucagon made of?
112699.e: Glucagon is a peptide hormone, a short chain of 29 amino acids. Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins.
112699.m: Glucagon is a short chain of amino acids.

112700.q: What is meant by a vegetation zone?
a: A large area with similar plant life
An area with the same rock
An area with the same time
112700.e: A vegetation zone is a large area of the Earth where similar plant communities grow. It is closely linked to the climate.
112700.m: A vegetation zone is a large area with similar plant life.

112701.q: Which factor decides most strongly where the vegetation zones lie?
112701.e: Above all, temperature and rainfall decide which plants can grow where. That is why the vegetation zones largely follow the climate zones.
112701.m: The climate decides which plants grow in a region.

112702.q: Roughly how are the vegetation zones arranged on Earth?
a: As belts roughly along the lines of latitude
As strips along the lines of longitude
112702.e: Because the sun's rays get weaker from the equator to the poles, the zones stretch around the Earth like belts. But mountains, seas and winds make the borders irregular.
112702.m: The vegetation zones stretch around the Earth like belts.

112703.q: Which vegetation zone lies closest to the equator?
112703.e: At the equator it is hot and very humid all year. That is where the always-wet tropical rainforest grows.
112703.m: The tropical rainforest grows at the equator.

112704.q: In the northern hemisphere, which vegetation zone comes after the boreal conifer forest towards the pole?
112704.e: North of the conifer forest belt it gets too cold for trees. Next comes a treeless zone with mosses, lichens, grasses and dwarf shrubs.
112704.m: Towards the pole, the conifer forest is followed by the treeless tundra.

112705.q: What do you call the plant zones lying one above the other on a mountain?
112705.e: The higher you go, the cooler it gets, so plant life changes step by step. In the Alps, for example, broadleaf forest, conifer forest, Alpine meadows and rock follow one another.
112705.m: On mountains, plant life changes in altitude zones.

112706.q: What is the vegetation zone of the tropics with wet and dry seasons, grasses and scattered trees called?
112706.e: In the savannah, rainy and dry seasons alternate. Mainly grasses grow there, with scattered trees such as acacias or baobabs.
112706.m: The savannah is a tropical grassland with scattered trees.

112707.q: Which vegetation zone gets so little rain that only a few scattered plants grow?
112707.e: In deserts, often less than 250 millimetres of rain falls a year. Only specially adapted plants such as cacti or thorn bushes survive there.
112707.m: In the desert only a few plants grow because it is so dry.

112708.q: What is the line in the Alps called, above which no closed forests grow any more?
112708.e: Higher up, the summer is too short and too cool for closed forests. In the Swiss Alps this line lies between about 1,800 and 2,400 metres, depending on the region.
112708.m: No closed forests grow above the tree line.

112709.q: What do you call the structure of the tropical rainforest made of several layers one above the other?
112709.e: The rainforest is built like a house with storeys: from the ground layer through shrub and tree layers up to the tallest trees. Each storey has its own light and living conditions.
112709.m: The rainforest is built in layers.

112710.q: What are the single giant trees that rise above the closed leaf canopy of the rainforest called?
112710.e: These forest giants rise far above the other treetops. They are exposed to strong wind and blazing sun.
112710.m: Emergents are forest giants that rise above the canopy.

112711.q: What is the layer called that forms an almost closed roof of leaves in the rainforest?
112711.e: The tree crowns, pressing closely together, form a green roof about 30 to 40 metres up. It catches most of the sunlight.
112711.m: The canopy layer forms the leafy roof of the rainforest.

112712.q: Roughly how much of the sunlight reaches the floor of the tropical rainforest?
112712.e: The many layers of leaves above swallow almost all the light. So it is dim on the ground even during the day.
112712.m: Hardly any sunlight reaches the rainforest floor.

112713.q: How tall do the forest giants of the tropical rainforest often grow?
112713.e: The tallest trees in the rainforest often reach 50 to 60 metres, and some even more. That is as tall as a building with about 20 storeys.
112713.m: Forest giants often grow taller than 50 metres.

112714.q: Why is the soil of the tropical rainforest usually poor in nutrients?
a: The nutrients are almost all inside the plants
Because the soil freezes every winter
112714.e: Fallen leaves break down very quickly in the warmth, and the plants take up the nutrients again straight away. Also, the heavy rain washes the soil out.
112714.m: In the rainforest, the nutrients are stored mainly in the plants.

112715.q: In which layer of the rainforest do most animal and plant species live?
a: In the canopy of the treetops
In the leaf litter on the ground
112715.e: High up there is lots of light, flowers, fruit and leaves. That is why the canopy is the rainforest habitat richest in species.
112715.m: Most rainforest species live high up in the canopy.

112716.q: What are climbing plants called that grow from the ground up trees towards the light in the rainforest?
112716.e: Lianas root in the ground and use trees as supports to reach the light. Some become as thick as an arm and many metres long.
112716.m: Lianas climb up trees towards the light.

112717.q: What happens when a forest giant falls down in the rainforest?
a: Young trees grow quickly into the light
The gap stays empty for ever
A lake forms there straight away
The ground freezes at that spot
112717.e: Suddenly lots of light falls through the gap to the ground. Young trees that have waited a long time in the shade now grow quickly upwards and close the canopy again.
112717.m: A gap in the rainforest is quickly filled by young trees.

a: A plant that grows on another without tapping into it
A plant that takes sap from other plants
A fungus that breaks down wood
A plant that lives only in water
112718.e: Epiphytes are also called air plants. They only use their host tree as a base and take no nutrients from it.
112718.m: An epiphyte grows on another plant without harming it.

112719.q: Where do epiphytes get their water from?
a: From rain, fog and damp air
From the sap of the host tree
112719.e: Epiphytes have no contact with the soil. They catch rainwater and take in moisture from the air and fog.
112719.m: Epiphytes live on water from rain and the air.

112720.q: Which plant family do many epiphytes belong to that are popular as houseplants here?
112720.e: A large share of orchid species grow on trees in the tropics. The well-known moth orchid is also originally an air plant.
112720.m: In nature, many orchids grow on trees.

112721.q: How do many bromeliads collect water?
a: In a funnel formed by their leaves
112721.e: The leaves of many bromeliads form a kind of tank in which rainwater and leaves collect. The plant takes up water and nutrients from it.
112721.m: Bromeliads collect water in their leaf funnels.

112722.q: Which animals often grow up in the water funnels of bromeliads?
112722.e: Some poison dart frogs carry their tadpoles into the small pools of water in bromeliads. There they are protected from many enemies.
112722.m: Bromeliad funnels are nurseries for poison dart frogs.

112723.q: Why do epiphytes grow high up on trees?
a: To escape animals that eat roots
112723.e: On the dark forest floor there is not enough light for photosynthesis. On branches high up, epiphytes get enough sun without having to grow a trunk of their own.
112723.m: Epiphytes grow on trees to reach the light.

112724.q: Which roots of many orchids are covered by a spongy layer that soaks up water?
112724.e: The silvery covering is called velamen. It soaks up rain and moisture like a sponge.
112724.m: Orchids soak up water with their aerial roots.

112725.q: Why is mistletoe not considered a true epiphyte?
a: It takes water and mineral salts from the tree
It only grows on the ground
112725.e: Mistletoe is a semi-parasite: it does photosynthesis itself but takes water and minerals from the wood of its host tree. An epiphyte, by contrast, takes nothing from its host.
112725.m: Mistletoe is a semi-parasite, not a true air plant.

112726.q: Which living things often grow as air plants on tree bark in Switzerland?
112726.e: We have air plants here too: mosses and lichens often cover trunks and branches. They live on rainwater and dust.
112726.m: Mosses and lichens grow on trees in Switzerland too.

a: Flat, board-like roots at the foot of the trunk
Roots made of wooden boards in gardening
Roots that hang down from branches
112727.e: Buttress roots are upright, flat growths on the lower trunk that merge into the roots. They look like boards standing on their edges.
112727.m: Buttress roots look like boards at the foot of the trunk.

112728.q: What is the main job of buttress roots?
a: They store sugar for the winter
112728.e: Tall trees with heavy crowns need good support. Buttress roots work like supporting pillars and stop the tree from toppling over.
112728.m: Buttress roots support tall trees like pillars.

112729.q: Why do many trees in the tropical rainforest have rather shallow roots?
a: The nutrients are in the top layer of soil
Because the soil below is always frozen
Because there is salt water further down
112729.e: Nutrients from rotted leaves are found almost only in a thin top layer of soil. That is why the roots spread out flat instead of growing deep into the ground.
112729.m: Rainforest trees have shallow roots because the nutrients are at the top of the soil.

112730.q: Which tropical tree with huge buttress roots provides fibres for filling cushions?
112730.e: The kapok tree is one of the tallest trees in the tropics and has large buttress roots. The fluffy fibres from its fruits were used for cushions and life jackets.
112730.m: The kapok tree has buttress roots and provides fluffy fibres.

112731.q: What are the arched roots called with which mangroves stand in the mud?
112731.e: Mangroves grow on tropical coasts in the tidal zone. Their stilt roots grow in arches from the trunk into the soft ground and hold the tree firmly.
112731.m: Mangroves stand in the mud on stilt roots.

112732.q: In which vegetation zone are buttress roots especially common?
112732.e: Tall trees on shallow soils are typical of the always-wet tropics. Many tree species there grow buttress roots.
112732.m: Buttress roots are typical of trees in the tropical rainforest.

112733.q: How are buttress roots arranged around the trunk?
a: As a ring high up in the crown
112733.e: Buttress roots usually grow outwards from the trunk in a star shape. This way they support the tree against forces from different directions.
112733.m: Buttress roots spread out from the trunk in a star shape.

112734.q: What is typical of a cloud forest?
a: It is very often wrapped in cloud or fog
It loses all its leaves every winter
It only grows at sea level
112734.e: Cloud forests are found where clouds regularly get caught on mountain slopes. So the air is almost always very damp.
112734.m: A cloud forest is very often in the clouds.

112735.q: Where do tropical mountain cloud forests typically grow?
a: On mountain slopes in the tropics
112735.e: Damp air rises up tropical mountains, cools down and forms clouds. Mountain cloud forests grow in this cloud zone, for example in the Andes.
112735.m: Tropical cloud forests grow on mountain slopes at cloud level.

112736.q: Apart from rain, how do cloud forests get extra water?
a: Leaves and mosses comb droplets out of the fog
112736.e: Tiny fog droplets get caught on leaves, mosses and lichens and drip off. This fog drip can make up a large part of the water.
112736.m: Cloud forests comb water out of the clouds.

112737.q: What are the trees in a cloud forest often thickly covered with?
112737.e: The constant damp is ideal for plants that grow on branches. Trunks and branches are often covered as if with green fur.
112737.m: In a cloud forest, the trees are full of mosses and ferns.

112738.q: Which well-known cloud forest reserve is in Costa Rica?
112738.e: The Monteverde cloud forest reserve lies in the mountains of Costa Rica. It is known for its great variety of species and attracts many nature lovers.
112738.m: Monteverde in Costa Rica is a famous cloud forest.

112739.q: On which group of islands in the Atlantic do laurel forests grow that get lots of water from fog?
112739.e: On islands such as La Gomera, the damp trade wind clouds pile up against the mountain slopes. A laurel forest shaped by fog grows in Garajonay National Park.
112739.m: The Canary Islands have foggy, damp laurel forests.

112740.q: Why are cloud forests important for the water supply?
a: They store water and release it slowly into streams
They evaporate all the water at once
They keep the rain away from the valley
They turn rain into salt water
112740.e: Mosses and soils soak up water like a sponge and release it bit by bit. This way some cities in the tropics get part of their drinking water.
112740.m: Cloud forests work like a giant water sponge.

112741.q: Which bird with long green tail feathers lives in the cloud forests of Central America?
112741.e: The quetzal has shimmering green feathers, and the males have very long tail feathers. It is the national bird of Guatemala.
112741.m: The quetzal is a colourful bird of the cloud forests.

112742.q: What is typical of a monsoon forest?
a: Rainy seasons and dry seasons take turns
Rain on every day of the year
A climate with no rain at all
112742.e: Monsoon forests grow in the tropics, where the monsoon brings a strong rainy season. It is followed by a dry season lasting several months.
112742.m: In the monsoon forest, rainy and dry seasons take turns.

112743.q: Why do many monsoon forest trees drop their leaves in the dry season?
112743.e: A lot of water evaporates through the leaves. Without leaves, the tree loses hardly any water in the dry season.
112743.m: Without leaves, trees lose less water in the dry season.

112744.q: Which valuable wood comes from a typical tree of the monsoon forests?
112744.e: The teak tree grows in South and South-East Asia. Its hard, weatherproof wood is used for example for ship decks and garden furniture.
112744.m: Teak comes from the monsoon forests of Asia.

112745.q: In which region of the world are monsoon forests especially widespread?
112745.e: Countries such as India, Myanmar and Thailand are strongly shaped by the monsoon. There are large areas of monsoon forest there.
112745.m: Monsoon forests are found mainly in South and South-East Asia.

112746.q: Which big cat lives in the monsoon forests of India?
112746.e: Most of the world's wild tigers live in India. Many tiger reserves lie in monsoon and dry forests.
112746.m: Tigers live in India's monsoon forests.

112747.q: What are monsoon forests also called because they mainly have leaves in the rainy season?
112747.e: The trees grow new leaves when the rain comes and often stand bare in the dry season. That is why people speak of rain-green forest.

112748.q: Where does the word “monsoon” come from?
112748.e: The word goes back to the Arabic “mausim”, which means something like “season”. Sailors used the seasonal winds for their journeys from early on.
112748.m: The word “monsoon” comes from Arabic and means season.

a: A dense evergreen scrubland around the Mediterranean
112749.e: The macchia is made up of dense shrubs, usually about one to five metres tall. It is typical of the coastal countries around the Mediterranean.
112749.m: The macchia is a dense scrubland around the Mediterranean.

112750.q: What climate is found in areas with macchia?
a: Hot, dry summers and mild, wet winters
Frost and snow all year round
Cold summers and very cold winters
112750.e: This is the typical Mediterranean climate. Most rain falls in the winter half of the year, and the summers are long and dry.
112750.m: The macchia grows in the Mediterranean climate with dry summers.

112751.q: What kind of leaves do many macchia plants have to protect them from drying out?
a: Leaves that only grow at night
112751.e: Such plants are called sclerophylls (hard-leaved plants). Their thick outer skin protects them from losing too much water in the dry summer.
112751.m: Hard leaves protect macchia plants from drying out.

112752.q: Which herb grows wild in the macchia?
112752.e: Rosemary is a typical Mediterranean shrub and copes well with drought. Thyme, lavender and myrtle also belong to the fragrant plant life of these landscapes.
112752.m: Rosemary grows wild in the macchia.

112753.q: On which Mediterranean island is the macchia especially widespread?
112753.e: On Corsica the macchia covers large parts of the island. Its herby scent can be smelt even from the sea.
112753.m: Corsica is known for its fragrant macchia.

112754.q: How did the macchia often come about?
a: Through the cutting, grazing and burning of former forests
Through glaciers in the Ice Age
112754.e: Originally, hard-leaved forests with holm oaks grew in many places. Over centuries, people cleared them, grazed them and burnt them down.
112754.m: The macchia often grew where people had destroyed forests.

112755.q: Which danger is especially great in the macchia in summer?
112755.e: In the dry summer the shrubs are parched and often contain essential oils. So sparks or carelessness can start big fires.
112755.m: In the dry summer, the macchia catches fire easily.

112756.q: What is the macchia called in French?
112756.e: On Corsica and in southern France people speak of the “maquis”. The word was later also used for resistance groups who hid in the scrubland.
112756.m: In French the macchia is called “maquis”.

112757.q: Why do hardly any trees grow in steppes?
a: It is too warm all year round
112757.e: There is too little rain for trees, especially in the hot summers. Grasses cope better with drought and cold winters.
112757.m: The steppe is too dry for trees.

112758.q: Which country is strongly shaped by steppes and known for nomads living in yurts?
112758.e: Large parts of Mongolia are steppe. Traditionally, many people there move around with their herds and live in round felt tents.
112758.m: On the Mongolian steppe, nomads live in yurts.

112759.q: Which very fertile, dark soil formed under steppes?
112759.e: Under the thick grass, lots of humus built up over thousands of years. This created the fertile soil also called chernozem.
112759.m: Fertile black earth forms under steppes.

112760.q: Which cereal is grown today on many former steppe soils?
112760.e: The fertile steppe soils of Ukraine, Russia and Kazakhstan are important wheat-growing areas. That is why these regions are often called breadbaskets.
112760.m: A lot of wheat is grown on former steppes.

112761.q: Which wild horse has been brought back to the Mongolian steppe?
112761.e: Przewalski's horse had died out in the wild and survived only in zoos. Since the 1990s it has been living in Mongolia again.
112761.m: Przewalski's horse lives on the Mongolian steppe again.

112762.q: Which steppe grass has long, feathery awns?
112762.e: The long, feathery awns of feather grass shine silvery in the wind. They help spread the seeds far and wide.
112762.m: Feather grass is a typical grass of the steppe.

112763.q: Which steppe region stretches from Eastern Europe to East Asia?
112763.e: The Eurasian Steppe is a huge belt of grassland from Ukraine through Kazakhstan to Mongolia. Many peoples on horseback used to travel across it.
112763.m: The Eurasian Steppe stretches right across Europe and Asia.

112764.q: On which continent is the prairie?
112764.e: The prairie is the great grassland in the interior of North America. It reaches from Canada to Texas.
112764.m: The prairie is North America's grassland.

112765.q: Which large hoofed animal once roamed the prairie in huge herds?
112765.e: Millions of bison used to live on the prairie. In the 19th century they were almost wiped out, and today they live mainly in reserves.
112765.m: Bison used to roam the prairie in huge herds.

112766.q: Which rodent digs large underground colonies on the prairie?
112766.e: Prairie dogs are ground squirrels that live in burrows with many tunnels. Their colonies are called “towns” because so many animals live there.
112766.m: Prairie dogs live in large colonies underground.

112767.q: What naturally kept the prairie free of trees in the past?
a: Fire and the grazing of large herds
112767.e: Lightning kept starting prairie fires, and large herds ate young woody plants. Grasses survive this because their buds sit close to the ground.
112767.m: Fire and grazing herds kept the prairie open.

112768.q: Why is the grass taller on the eastern prairie than on the western prairie?
a: More rain falls in the east
The soil is saltier in the west
There is more sun in the east
No animals live in the west
112768.e: It gets drier and drier from east to west, because the Rocky Mountains keep the rain off. That is why the tallgrass prairie in the east is followed by the shortgrass prairie in the west.
112768.m: The prairie has taller grass in the wetter east.

112769.q: What has happened to most of the prairie since the 19th century?
a: It has been turned into farmland
112769.e: Settlers ploughed the fertile soil and planted wheat and maize. Only a small remnant of the original tallgrass prairie is left.
112769.m: Most of the prairie is farmland today.

112770.q: What was the “Dust Bowl” in the 1930s?
a: A time of severe dust storms caused by drought and erosion
A huge forest fire in Canada
112770.e: After the prairie was ploughed up, there was no grass left to protect the soil. During a long drought, the wind carried away huge amounts of earth.
112770.m: The “Dust Bowl” showed how erosion can destroy the prairie.

112771.q: Which country shares the North American prairie with the USA?
112771.e: The prairie reaches from the USA far into Canada. A lot of grain is grown in the Canadian Prairie Provinces.
112771.m: The prairie lies in the USA and Canada.

112772.q: What are the mounted cattle herders of the pampas called?
112772.e: For centuries, gauchos have herded cattle and horses on the pampas. They are a symbol of Argentina and Uruguay.
112772.m: The gauchos are the cattle herders of the pampas.

112773.q: Which branch of the economy is especially important on the pampas?
112773.e: Large herds of cattle graze on the wide grasslands. Argentina is known for its beef, and soya and wheat are grown as well.
112773.m: Lots of cattle are raised on the pampas.

112774.q: Which large, flightless running bird lives on the pampas?
112774.e: The rhea is the largest bird in South America. Like the African ostrich, it cannot fly but can run very fast.
112774.m: The rhea is the large running bird of the pampas.

112775.q: Which garden plant popular in our area is named after the pampas?
112775.e: Pampas grass comes from the grasslands of South America. It forms tall clumps with silvery-white feathery flower heads.
112775.m: Pampas grass comes from the pampas.

112776.q: Which capital city lies on the edge of the pampas on the Río de la Plata?
112776.e: The Argentine capital lies on the wide estuary of the Río de la Plata. The flat grassland begins to the west and south of it.
112776.m: Buenos Aires lies on the edge of the pampas.

112777.q: What did the word “pampa” originally mean?
112777.e: The word comes from Quechua, the language of the Andean peoples. It suits the flat, wide landscape well.

112778.q: What is the cool south-west wind called that often blows stormily across the pampas?
112778.e: The pampero is a cold, often stormy wind from the south-west. After hot days it brings a sudden cool-down and sometimes thunderstorms.
112778.m: The pampero is the cold storm wind of the pampas.

112779.q: Which Russian word is also used for the boreal conifer forest?
112779.e: The word comes from Russian. It stands for the huge conifer forests of the north, especially in Siberia.
112779.m: The boreal conifer forest is also called the taiga.

112780.q: Which trees shape the boreal zone?
a: Conifers such as spruces, pines and larches
112780.e: Conifers can stand long, very cold winters and short summers. Birches, poplars and willows grow there too.

112781.q: Which broadleaf tree with white bark often grows in the boreal conifer forest?
112781.e: Birches are very frost-hardy and grow quickly on open areas, for example after forest fires. Their white bark is easy to recognise.
112781.m: The frost-hardy birch often grows in the boreal forest.

112782.q: On which continents does the boreal zone lie?
112782.e: The boreal conifer forest stretches as a wide belt across the northern hemisphere. In the southern hemisphere there is no land at the right latitudes for it.
112782.m: The boreal conifer forest exists only in the northern hemisphere.

112783.q: Why are cone-shaped conifers well suited to snowy winters?
a: The snow slides off more easily
They melt the snow with heat
112783.e: The narrow cone shape and the flexible branches that slope downwards let snow slide off. So the branches break less often under the weight.
112783.m: Snow slides easily off cone-shaped trees.

112784.q: Which country has the largest share of the boreal conifer forest?
112784.e: Russia stretches across a huge part of northern Eurasia. A large part of its area is covered by northern conifer forest.
112784.m: Russia has the largest part of the boreal forest.

112785.q: Which large member of the deer family is typical of the northern conifer forest?
112785.e: The elk, called moose in North America, is the largest deer in the world. It eats twigs, buds and water plants and copes well with cold winters.
112785.m: The elk is a typical animal of the boreal forest.

112786.q: Why do fallen needles break down only slowly in the boreal forest?
a: Because it is cold there for a long time
Because there are no bacteria there
Because it is too wet to rot there
Because the needles are made of stone
112786.e: In the cold, soil creatures and fungi work only very slowly. So a thick layer of needles and raw humus builds up on the ground.
112786.m: In the cold, needles break down only slowly.

112787.q: Roughly how long is the growing season for plants in the boreal conifer forest?
112787.e: The summers are short and the winters long and very cold. So plants can only grow during a few warm months.
112787.m: In the boreal forest, the growing season is short.

112788.q: Which vegetation zone would naturally cover the Swiss Central Plateau without people?
112788.e: Without clearing, the Central Plateau would be mostly covered by mixed broadleaf forests, especially beech forests. Today fields, meadows and towns shape the landscape.
112788.m: The Central Plateau would naturally be covered with broadleaf forest.

112789.q: In which canton are Swiss beech forests that have been part of the UNESCO World Heritage site of the ancient beech forests of Europe since 2021?
112789.e: Beech forests that have hardly been used for a long time grow in the Valle di Lodano and neighbouring valleys. In 2021 they were added to the World Heritage site that spans several countries.
112789.m: Ancient beech forests in Ticino are part of the UNESCO World Heritage.

112790.q: How do fungi and trees in a broadleaf forest help each other?
a: Fungi supply water and minerals, the tree gives sugar
The tree protects the fungi from rain
112790.e: Fungal threads wrap around the fine tree roots and supply water and minerals. In return the fungi get sugar from the tree. This partnership is called mycorrhiza.
112790.m: Fungus and tree swap minerals for sugar.

112791.q: What do you call a forest where broadleaf and conifer trees grow together?
112791.e: In a mixed forest, for example, beeches, spruces and firs stand side by side. Such forests are usually more resistant to storms and pests.
112791.m: In a mixed forest, broadleaf trees and conifers grow together.

112792.q: Why do wood anemones flower so early in spring in the broadleaf forest?
a: Because then lots of light falls through the bare trees
Because they get too much water in summer
Because bees only fly in March
Because they need snow to flower
112792.e: Before the trees come into leaf, lots of sunlight reaches the forest floor. Early flowers use this short time to bloom and grow.
112792.m: Early flowers use the light before the trees have leaves.

112793.q: What climate is found in the zone of deciduous broadleaf forest?
a: A temperate climate with four seasons
A polar climate with permanent frost
A desert climate with almost no rain
112793.e: The summers are warm, the winters cool, and rain falls throughout the year. These conditions suit trees that rest in winter.
112793.m: Deciduous broadleaf forests grow in a temperate climate.

112794.q: Apart from Europe, where are there large deciduous broadleaf forests?
112794.e: Eastern North America and East Asia also have a damp, temperate climate. Large broadleaf forests with beautiful autumn colours grow there.
112794.m: The eastern USA also has large broadleaf forests.

112795.q: What forms from fallen leaves on the floor of a broadleaf forest?
112795.e: Worms, fungi and bacteria break down the leaves. This creates dark, nutrient-rich humus.
112795.m: Fertile humus forms from the leaves.

112796.q: Which bird drums on tree trunks with its beak in the broadleaf forest?
112796.e: Woodpeckers hammer holes into wood and look for insects inside. In spring they also mark their territory with loud drumming.
112796.m: The great spotted woodpecker drums on trees with its beak.

112797.q: How can you tell that a person is unconscious?
a: They do not respond to being spoken to or touched
They are breathing calmly and evenly
112797.e: An unconscious person does not respond when you speak to them loudly and hold their shoulders. Closed eyes alone do not mean unconsciousness, because sleeping people have their eyes closed too.
112797.m: Anyone who does not respond to voice or touch is considered unconscious.

112798.q: Why is unconsciousness particularly dangerous when lying on the back?
a: The tongue can fall back and block the airway
The heart beats too fast when lying on the back
Blood no longer flows into the legs
112798.e: When unconscious, the muscles go slack. The tongue can sink back into the throat and block the airway.
112798.m: In unconscious people, their own tongue can block the airway.

112799.q: Which protective reflexes does an unconscious person lack, so that vomit can get into the lungs?
112799.e: Without coughing and swallowing reflexes, an unconscious person cannot clear vomit or blood from the airway. That is why you must put them in a safe position.
112799.m: Without coughing and swallowing reflexes, an unconscious person’s airway is unprotected.

112800.q: For how long at most should you check whether an unconscious person is breathing normally?
112800.e: According to resuscitation guidelines, you check breathing for no more than about 10 seconds by looking, listening and feeling. Waiting longer costs valuable time.
112800.m: Checking breathing takes no longer than about ten seconds.

112801.q: How do you open the airway of an unconscious person?
a: Tilt the head back and lift the chin
Press the head forward onto the chest
Raise the legs and stretch the arms
Sit the person up and shake them
112801.e: Tilting the head back and lifting the chin lifts the tongue away from the throat. Air can then flow freely again.
112801.m: Tilting the head back and lifting the chin opens the airway.

112802.q: What is a short loss of consciousness lasting a few seconds called, for example after standing for a long time in the heat?
112802.e: Fainting usually happens because the brain briefly gets too little blood. The person normally comes round by themselves after a short time.
112802.m: Fainting is a short, usually harmless loss of consciousness.

112803.q: What is particularly important for an unconscious person who is breathing normally, after calling for help?
a: Put a pillow under their head
112803.e: Breathing can get worse or stop at any time. That is why you stay with the person and check their breathing until the ambulance arrives.
112803.m: Stay with an unconscious person and keep watching their breathing.

112804.q: Why must you not give an unconscious person anything to drink?
a: They could breathe the liquid into their lungs
The drink would raise their blood pressure too much
Liquid makes the unconsciousness last longer
Water cools the body down too much
112804.e: Without a swallowing reflex, liquid easily goes into the windpipe instead of the gullet. The person could choke on it.
112804.m: Unconscious people get neither food nor drink.

112805.q: When do you put a person in the recovery position?
a: When they are unconscious and breathing normally
When they are awake and have tummy ache
When they have broken a leg
112805.e: The recovery position is meant for unconscious people who are breathing normally by themselves. It keeps the airway open and lets fluid drain from the mouth.
112805.m: Unconscious people who are breathing normally belong in the recovery position.

112806.q: Which way does the mouth of a person in the recovery position point?
112806.e: The mouth is the lowest point of the head. This lets vomit, blood or saliva drain out instead of getting into the lungs.
112806.m: In the recovery position, the mouth points down so fluid can drain out.

112807.q: How is the head positioned in the recovery position?
112807.e: Tilting the head back keeps the airway open so the tongue does not fall into the throat. The person can then keep breathing freely.
112807.m: In the recovery position too, the head stays slightly tilted back.

112808.q: What is the bent upper leg for in the recovery position?
a: It stops the person rolling onto their front or back
It improves blood flow to the head
112808.e: The bent upper leg supports the body like a stand. This keeps the person lying steadily on their side.
112808.m: The bent leg keeps the person steady on their side.

112809.q: What do you do if a person in the recovery position suddenly stops breathing normally?
a: Turn them onto their back and start chest compressions
Turn them onto the other side
112809.e: If normal breathing is missing, cardiac arrest is likely. The person must then lie flat on their back so that you can press the chest effectively.
112809.m: If breathing stops, start chest compressions immediately.

112810.q: Why do you cover a person in the recovery position, for example with a foil blanket?
a: So they do not get too cold
112810.e: Injured and unconscious people lose body heat quickly, especially on cold ground. A blanket or foil blanket protects against hypothermia.
112810.m: Cover unconscious people so they do not get cold.

112812.q: What goes under the person’s cheek in the recovery position?
a: The back of their upper hand
112812.e: You place the back of the upper hand under the cheek. It supports the head so that it stays slightly tilted back and the mouth points downwards.
112812.m: In the recovery position, the cheek rests on the back of the upper hand.

112813.q: Where do you press when giving chest compressions to an adult?
a: In the middle of the chest on the breastbone
On the left side of the chest under the armpit
On the neck over the larynx
112813.e: The pressure point is in the middle of the chest on the lower half of the breastbone. There the heart is squeezed between the breastbone and the spine.
112813.m: For chest compressions, press on the middle of the chest.

112814.q: Roughly how many times per minute do you press during chest compressions?
112814.e: European and Swiss guidelines recommend a rate of 100 to 120 compressions per minute. That is about the beat of some well-known pop songs.
112814.m: You press about 100 to 120 times per minute.

112815.q: How do you hold your arms during chest compressions?
a: Straight and vertically above the chest
Stretched far forwards over the head
112815.e: With straight arms vertically above the pressure point, you press with your own body weight. That way you get tired less quickly and press evenly deep.
112815.m: During chest compressions, keep your arms straight and vertical.

112816.q: In what ratio do chest compressions and rescue breaths alternate in adults?
112816.e: When resuscitating adults, the ratio is 30 to 2. So 30 compressions are followed by two rescue breaths.
112816.m: For adults: press 30 times and give 2 breaths.

112817.q: What must you do after each press during chest compressions?
a: Let the chest come all the way back up
Take your hands off the body and clap
Rub the chest from the side
112817.e: Only when the chest rises completely can the heart fill with blood again. Your hands stay on the pressure point while this happens.
112817.m: After each press, let the chest come fully back up.

112818.q: What does a defibrillator do in ventricular fibrillation?
a: It gives an electric shock so that the heart beats in an orderly way again
It pumps oxygen into the lungs
112818.e: In ventricular fibrillation, the heart muscle twitches chaotically and pumps no blood. The shock interrupts this chaos so that the natural pacemaker can take over again.
112818.m: A defibrillator’s shock can get a fibrillating heart back into rhythm.

112819.q: What should a person lie on so that chest compressions are effective?
112819.e: On a soft surface, the mattress gives way and the chest is hardly pressed in. That is why you lay the person on the floor.
112819.m: Chest compressions are done on hard, flat ground.

112820.q: Why is it important to start chest compressions immediately in cardiac arrest?
a: The brain is damaged after just a few minutes without oxygen
Otherwise the blood immediately goes solid
The muscles cramp after one minute
112820.e: Without blood circulation, the brain no longer gets any oxygen. Permanent damage can occur after only about 3 to 5 minutes.
112820.m: In cardiac arrest, every minute counts for the brain.

112821.q: In which rescue breathing method does the helper close the mouth and blow air into the nose?
112821.e: In mouth-to-nose breathing, you hold the person’s mouth shut with your thumb and blow through the nose. Many experts recommend it, because the nose can be sealed well.
112821.m: In mouth-to-nose breathing, you blow through the nose and keep the mouth shut.

112822.q: How can you tell that a rescue breath is working?
112822.e: When air gets into the lungs, the chest rises. If the tummy swells instead, the air is going into the stomach.
112822.m: You can tell a good rescue breath by the chest rising.

112823.q: Roughly how long does a single rescue breath last during resuscitation?
112823.e: You blow air in calmly for about 1 second until the chest visibly rises. Then you let the air escape again.
112823.m: A rescue breath lasts about one second.

112824.q: How do you give rescue breaths to a baby?
a: Through the mouth and nose at the same time
Not at all, only by fanning
112824.e: A baby’s face is small, so the helper covers the mouth and nose at the same time with their own mouth. Only gentle puffs of breath are given.
112824.m: Give babies gentle rescue breaths through the mouth and nose together.

112825.q: Why does a helper’s breathed-out air contain enough oxygen for rescue breathing?
a: It still contains about 16 per cent oxygen
It contains more oxygen than fresh air
The helper breathes out pure oxygen
112825.e: Fresh air contains about 21 per cent oxygen, and breathed-out air still around 16 per cent. That is enough to supply a person with oxygen during rescue breathing.
112825.m: Even breathed-out air still contains plenty of oxygen.

112826.q: What can happen if you give rescue breaths too forcefully?
a: Air gets into the stomach and the person vomits
The lungs immediately become permanently healthy
112826.e: If the pressure is too high, the entrance to the stomach opens and air flows into the stomach. This can cause vomiting, which can let stomach contents get into the lungs.
112826.m: Breathing in too hard blows air into the stomach.

112827.q: What is a face shield or resuscitation mask in first aid?
a: A barrier that prevents direct contact with the mouth
A device that produces oxygen by itself
A cloth for wiping off sweat
112827.e: Breathing aids protect helpers from direct contact with saliva or blood. Many car first aid kits and keyrings contain such a shield.
112827.m: A resuscitation mask protects helpers from direct mouth contact.

112828.q: What do you do if you do not dare to give rescue breaths to a stranger?
a: Do chest compressions only, without stopping
112828.e: If you do not want to or cannot give rescue breaths, do continuous chest compressions. This is much better than doing nothing, because the blood still contains oxygen.
112828.m: Chest compressions alone are much better than no help at all.

112829.q: What is a pressure bandage for?
112829.e: A pressure bandage squeezes the wound together so that less blood comes out. It is applied to heavily bleeding wounds on the arms or legs.
112829.m: A pressure bandage stops heavy bleeding.

112830.q: What do you put directly on the wound when applying a pressure bandage?
a: An elastic bandage without a dressing
112830.e: First a germ-free dressing goes on the wound. On top come the pressure pad and a bandage that wraps everything firmly.
112830.m: A sterile dressing always goes on the wound first.

112831.q: What is the job of the pressure pad in a pressure bandage?
a: It presses precisely on the bleeding spot
It soaks up all the blood
It cushions the bone against knocks
112831.e: The pressure pad, for example an unopened dressing pack, is wrapped firmly over the wound dressing. It puts targeted pressure on the blood vessels.
112831.m: The pressure pad creates the pressure on the wound.

112832.q: What do you do if blood soaks through the first pressure bandage?
a: Put a second pressure bandage on top
Rip off the first bandage at once
112832.e: You leave the first bandage in place and put another pressure bandage on top. Removing it would disturb the clotting that has started.
112832.m: A blood-soaked pressure bandage stays on, and a second one goes on top.

112833.q: How should you also position an injured arm with a heavily bleeding wound?
a: Hold it up, above heart level
Move it hard back and forth
112833.e: If the wound is above the heart, less blood flows into it. Holding it up therefore helps to stop the bleeding.
112833.m: Hold a bleeding limb up high.

112834.q: How can you tell that a pressure bandage has been put on too tightly?
a: Fingers or toes turn blue, cold or tingle
112834.e: A bandage that is too tight disturbs the blood flow to the whole arm or leg. Then you must loosen it a little.
112834.m: Blue or cold fingers show that a bandage is too tight.

112835.q: What should you wear as a first aider before treating a bleeding wound?
112835.e: Disposable gloves protect against germs in the blood and also protect the wound from dirt. They belong in every car first aid kit.
112835.m: When there is blood, disposable gloves protect both helper and injured person.

112836.q: What is the first measure for a heavily bleeding wound on the arm, before the bandage is ready?
a: Press directly on the wound with your hand
Put the arm in cold water
112836.e: Direct pressure on the wound, ideally with a compress and gloves, slows the bleeding immediately. Then a pressure bandage is applied.
112836.m: With heavy bleeding, press directly on the wound at once.

112837.q: How do you cool a small burn on the hand correctly?
a: With lukewarm to cool tap water
With ice cubes directly on the skin
112837.e: Slightly cool tap water relieves pain and limits the damage. Ice can damage the skin further, and home remedies such as butter or flour encourage infection.
112837.m: Cool small burns with cool tap water, not with ice.

112838.q: How many degrees of burns are usually distinguished in medicine?
112838.e: First, second and third degree burns are distinguished, and some systems also name a fourth degree for charring. The higher the degree, the deeper the damage.
112838.m: The higher the degree of a burn, the deeper the skin is damaged.

112839.q: Which feature is typical of a second degree burn?
112839.e: In second degree burns, the dermis is also affected, blisters form and it hurts a lot. In even deeper burns, the skin can be white or charred black.
112839.m: Blisters are a sign of a second degree burn.

112840.q: What must you not do with a burn blister?
a: Cover it with a sterile dressing
112840.e: The blister protects the skin underneath from germs. If it is popped, germs can easily get in.

112841.q: What do you do if clothing is stuck to a burnt patch of skin?
a: Do not rip it off, leave it stuck
Set it alight so it melts
112841.e: Stuck clothing is left on the wound so as not to injure the skin further. Loose clothing, jewellery and watches, on the other hand, are removed before the area swells.
112841.m: Clothing stuck to burns stays on.

112842.q: Why must you be careful about cooling large burns for a long time?
a: There is a risk of hypothermia
112842.e: With large areas, and especially in children, the whole body cools down quickly. That is why large burns are only cooled briefly and the person is then covered up warmly.
112842.m: With large burns, cooling can lead to hypothermia.

112843.q: What do you cover a burn with after cooling it?
a: A sticking plaster directly on the blister
112843.e: A sterile dressing, for example a special burn dressing, protects against germs. Cotton wool can leave fibres in the wound.
112843.m: Cover burns with something germ-free and without cotton wool.

112844.q: How do you smother the flames when a person’s clothes are on fire?
a: Roll the person on the ground or cover them with a fire blanket
Fan air at them with a fan
112844.e: Running fans the fire because of the draught. Rolling on the ground or a fire blanket cuts off the flames’ oxygen.
112844.m: Put out burning clothes by rolling or with a fire blanket.

112845.q: What is shock in the medical sense?
a: A brief fright with no consequences
An electric shock from a socket
112845.e: In shock, the blood circulation is no longer enough to supply the organs with oxygen. This can happen, for example, after a large loss of blood.
112845.m: Medical shock is a life-threatening failure of the circulation.

112846.q: Which signs are typical of shock?
a: Pale, cold, sweaty skin and a fast pulse
A red face and a slow pulse
Great hunger and a good mood
Warm, dry skin and deep sleep
112846.e: The body draws blood away from the skin and limbs to supply the vital organs. That is why the skin becomes pale and cold, and the heart beats faster.
112846.m: Pale, cold skin and a fast pulse point to shock.

112847.q: How do you position a person showing signs of shock after blood loss, if no injuries rule it out?
a: Flat on their back with the legs slightly raised
On their front with the head raised
112847.e: In the shock position, blood flows from the legs back to the body and the vital organs. With some injuries or breathing difficulties, however, this position is not suitable.
112847.m: In shock, lay the person flat with legs slightly raised, if nothing rules it out.

112848.q: What do people with a severe wasp sting allergy often carry with them?
112848.e: After a sting, life-threatening allergic shock can develop. With the emergency pen, you inject yourself with adrenaline immediately.
112848.m: People with allergies carry an adrenaline pen for emergencies.

112849.q: Apart from calling for help, what do you do for a person in shock?
a: Cover them, calm them and do not leave them alone
112849.e: Keeping warm, calming down and being looked after help the body to stabilise the circulation. Until the ambulance arrives, you keep checking breathing and consciousness.
112849.m: Cover people in shock, calm them and stay with them.

112850.q: What is shock caused by a large loss of blood or fluid called?
112850.e: If a lot of blood or fluid is missing, there is too little volume in the circulation. This form of shock is called hypovolaemic shock.
112850.m: Hypovolaemic shock is caused by missing blood or fluid in the circulation.

112851.q: Why should a person showing signs of shock not eat or drink anything?
a: They may need an operation and could vomit
They would get better too quickly
112851.e: Shock may make an anaesthetic or operation necessary, for which the stomach should be as empty as possible. Also, their condition can get worse and the person can vomit.
112851.m: In shock, give nothing to eat and nothing to drink.

112852.q: With which injury must you not raise the legs of a person in shock?
a: An insect sting on the arm
112852.e: Raising a broken leg causes pain and can make the injury worse. The shock position is also unsuitable for head injuries or breathing difficulties.
112852.m: With leg injuries, do not raise the legs.

112853.q: What does the A in the ABC approach of first aid stand for?
112853.e: A stands for airway. It must be open so that any air can get into the lungs at all.
112853.m: A stands for airway and comes first in an emergency.

112854.q: What does the C in the ABC approach stand for?
112854.e: For C, you check and secure the blood circulation. This includes, for example, chest compressions or stopping heavy bleeding.
112854.m: In the ABC approach, C stands for circulation.

112855.q: Which language do the terms behind the letters of the ABC approach come from?
112855.e: The letters stand for Airway, Breathing and Circulation. The approach is used in many countries, including Switzerland.
112855.m: The ABC approach comes from English.

112856.q: Why are the steps of the ABC approach checked in exactly this order?
a: Because the greatest danger to life is dealt with first
Because they must be in alphabetical order
Because the order was chosen at random
112856.e: Without an open airway, breathing is no use, and without oxygen in the blood, the circulation does not help much either. So the order follows urgency.
112856.m: In the ABC approach, the most life-threatening thing comes first.

112857.q: Which extension of the ABC approach do ambulance services often use?
112857.e: The ABCDE approach adds D for neurological problems such as consciousness and E for examining the whole body.
112857.m: Professionals extend the ABC approach to the ABCDE approach.

112858.q: What do you check for B in the ABC approach?
a: Whether the person is breathing normally
112858.e: B is about breathing. You look, listen and feel whether the person is breathing normally, and give rescue breaths if necessary.
112858.m: B in the ABC approach is about breathing.

112859.q: What are the three basic steps that Swiss first aid courses use to sum up what to do at the scene of an accident?
112859.e: First you get an overview, then you consider what dangers there are and what needs to be done. Only after that do you act.
112859.m: At an accident: look, think and then act.

112860.q: What always comes first, before the ABC approach, when you arrive at the scene of an accident?
a: Paying attention to your own safety
Giving the injured person something to drink
112860.e: If you put yourself in danger, you cannot help anyone any more. That is why you first secure the scene, for example with a high-visibility vest and a warning triangle.
112860.m: At an accident, your own safety comes first.

112861.q: What has the umbrella organisation of the Samaritan associations in Switzerland been called since 2022?
112861.e: The former Swiss Samaritan Federation has been called Samariter Schweiz since 2022. Hundreds of Samaritan associations all over Switzerland belong to it.
112861.m: Switzerland’s Samaritan associations are organised in Samariter Schweiz.

112862.q: Which story does the word Samaritan go back to?
a: The parable of the Good Samaritan in the Bible
A town in the canton of Valais
112862.e: In the parable from the Gospel of Luke, a man from Samaria helps someone who has been attacked and whom others have walked past. The Samaritan thus became a symbol of helpfulness.
112862.m: Samaritans are named after the helpful man in the Bible.

112863.q: Which task do Samaritans often take on at festivals and sports events?
112863.e: Samaritan associations run first aid posts at many events. They treat minor injuries and give first aid until the ambulance arrives.
112863.m: Samaritans give first aid at events.

112864.q: Which large aid organisation is Samariter Schweiz linked to?
112864.e: Samariter Schweiz is one of the Red Cross rescue organisations and follows the principles of the Red Cross movement. Together they work for first aid among the population.
112864.m: Samariter Schweiz belongs to the Swiss Red Cross family.

112865.q: How do most Samaritans in Switzerland work?
112865.e: Members of Samaritan associations help in their free time. They regularly take further training in first aid.
112865.m: Samaritans help as volunteers in their free time.

112866.q: What are the youth groups of the Samaritans in Switzerland called?
112866.e: The Help Samaritan youth was founded in Basel in 1968. In the groups, children and young people learn first aid through play.
112866.m: The youth groups of the Swiss Samaritans are called Help.

112867.q: How long has there been a joint federation of Samaritan associations in Switzerland?
112867.e: In 1888, the first Samaritan associations founded the Swiss Samaritan Federation. Since 2022 it has been called Samariter Schweiz.
112867.m: The Samaritan federation has existed for more than 100 years.

112868.q: What do you need a first aid course for in Switzerland?
a: To apply for a learner driver’s permit
112868.e: Anyone in Switzerland who wants to learn to drive a car or ride a motorbike must show they have done a first aid course before getting a learner’s permit. The course teaches the basics of first aid.
112868.m: In Switzerland, you need a first aid course for a learner driver’s permit.

112869.q: What do you learn in a first aid course?
a: First aid in accidents and emergencies
112869.e: In a first aid course you learn, for example, how to secure the scene of an accident, make an emergency call and do chest compressions.
112869.m: In a first aid course, you learn first aid.

112870.q: Which object is used in the first aid course to secure the scene of an accident on the road?
112870.e: The warning triangle warns approaching vehicles of the accident. It is best to wear a highly visible high-visibility vest as well.
112870.m: A warning triangle warns other road users of an accident.

112871.q: When may you pull an injured person out of a car after an accident?
a: Only if there is acute danger, for example fire
Never, not even if there is a fire
112871.e: You only move an injured person if they are in danger. For this, you learn the Rautek rescue grip in the first aid course.
112871.m: Only move injured people if there is acute danger.

112872.q: Which number reaches Tox Info Suisse in Switzerland in cases of poisoning?
112872.e: Tox Info Suisse gives advice on poisoning around the clock on the emergency number 145. If symptoms are serious, you still call 144.
112872.m: For poisoning, the number 145 gives you advice.

112873.q: Which European emergency number also works in Switzerland?
112873.e: 112 is valid throughout Europe and in Switzerland is passed on to the police. 911 is used in the USA and 999 in Great Britain.

112875.q: Who hangs up first in an emergency call?
112875.e: The control centre often has more questions or gives instructions, for example on chest compressions. That is why you wait until they end the call.
112875.m: In an emergency call, the control centre ends the conversation.

112876.q: How can you tell that a person has choked and cannot get any air?
a: They clutch their throat and cannot speak
112876.e: If the airway is completely blocked, the person can neither speak, cough nor breathe. Clutching the throat is typical.
112876.m: Anyone who clutches their throat and cannot speak may be choking.

112877.q: What should a person do who has choked on something but can still cough strongly?
112877.e: Strong coughing is the best way to get an object out of the airway. You encourage the person to do so and stay with them.
112877.m: Anyone who can still cough should keep coughing hard.

112878.q: What do you do first if an adult has choked and can no longer cough effectively?
a: Give firm blows between the shoulder blades
Give them bread to swallow after it
Lay them on their back and wait
112878.e: You bend the person’s upper body forwards and strike firmly between the shoulder blades with the flat of your hand. If that does not help, the Heimlich manoeuvre follows.
112878.m: First come firm blows between the shoulder blades.

112879.q: How do you position a baby for back blows if it has choked?
a: Face down on the forearm with the head lower
Hanging upside down by the feet
112879.e: The baby lies on its tummy along the forearm, with the head supported and lower than the body. Gravity then helps to free the object.
112879.m: For back blows, lay babies face down on the forearm with the head lower.

112880.q: Which small objects are a particularly common choking risk for toddlers?
112880.e: Small, round, hard things fit exactly into a toddler’s windpipe. That is why people advise keeping nuts and small parts away from toddlers.
112880.m: Nuts and small parts do not belong in toddlers’ hands.

112881.q: Why should a person still be checked by a doctor after choking has been successfully cleared?
a: Bits could be in the lungs or injuries could have occurred
Because otherwise they will get a fever
Because otherwise they will not be able to swallow any more
112881.e: Small remains may have slipped into the lungs. Also, back blows or thrusts into the upper abdomen can cause internal injuries.
112881.m: After a choking emergency, a doctor should take a look.

112882.q: What do you do if a person with an object in their airway becomes unconscious?
a: Lay them down, call for help and start resuscitation
Hold them upright and shake them
Leave them alone and go to get help
112882.e: If the person becomes unconscious, you lay them on the floor and start chest compressions. The compressions can also free the object.
112882.m: If a choking person becomes unconscious, start resuscitation.

112883.q: When do you use the Heimlich manoeuvre?
a: When someone is in danger of choking on something they have swallowed
112883.e: If an object is stuck in the airway and the person can no longer breathe or cough, the Heimlich manoeuvre can push it out. It is named after the US doctor Henry Heimlich.
112883.m: The Heimlich manoeuvre helps when someone is in danger of choking.

112884.q: Where do you place your fist for the Heimlich manoeuvre?
a: In the upper abdomen between the belly button and the tip of the breastbone
On the back over the kidneys
112884.e: The helper stands behind the person, puts their arms around them and places the fist in the upper abdomen. Then they pull sharply inwards and upwards.
112884.m: In the Heimlich manoeuvre, the fist presses into the upper abdomen.

112885.q: How does the Heimlich manoeuvre work?
a: The pressure on the diaphragm forces air out of the lungs
It stimulates the stomach to digest
It lowers blood pressure in the head
112885.e: The sudden thrust pushes the diaphragm upwards. The air from the lungs shoots out and pushes the object out like a cork.
112885.m: In the Heimlich manoeuvre, air from the lungs pushes the object out.

112886.q: On whom must you not use the Heimlich manoeuvre?
112886.e: In babies, the risk of injuring the abdominal organs is too great. Instead of upper abdominal thrusts, chest thrusts with two fingers are used for them.
112886.m: For babies, chest thrusts replace the Heimlich manoeuvre.

112887.q: Where does the helper stand when doing the Heimlich manoeuvre on an adult?
a: Next to the person lying down
On a chair above the person
112887.e: The helper stands behind the person and puts both arms around them. That way they can pull strongly inwards and upwards.
112887.m: In the Heimlich manoeuvre, you stand behind the person.

112888.q: How many times at most do you repeat the Heimlich manoeuvre in one go before giving back blows again?
112888.e: According to the guidelines, up to 5 back blows and up to 5 abdominal thrusts alternate. Each time you check whether the object has come out.
112888.m: Back blows and Heimlich thrusts alternate in series of five.
